[MUQATIL:1:1-4/r1] MUQATIL, d. 150 · author | holds | Muqātil glosses praise of God as gratitude or thanks to God.
[MUQATIL:1:1-4/r2] MUQATIL, d. 150 · author | holds | The Lord of the worlds means jinn and humans, as in the description of the Qur'an as a warning to all worlds. | mentions 25:1
[MUQATIL:1:5-7/r8] MUQATIL, d. 150 · أبو هريرة عن النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم | reports | A report from Abū Hurayra says the Prophet related that God divided this sūra between Himself and the servant: praise is thanks, the two mercy names are praise, the King verse is glorification, and the rest belongs to the servant; seeking help is God's special acknowledgment of the servant's plea.
[FARRA:v1p1#2/r6] FARRA, d. 207 · القراء | reports | Reciters agree on reading al-ḥamdu in the nominative.
[FARRA:v1p3/r1] FARRA, d. 207 · author | reports | Bedouin speech has several variants for al-ḥamd li-llāh, including a form that raises both the dāl and lām.
[FARRA:v1p3/r2] FARRA, d. 207 · author | holds | Accusative al-ḥamda is possible because ḥamd is a verbal noun that can be replaced by a verb, as in “strike the necks.” | mentions 47:4
[FARRA:v1p3/r3] FARRA, d. 207 · author | holds | The same verbal-noun construction appears in “I seek refuge in God” and in Arabic expressions equivalent to “may God water you” or “care for you.” | mentions 12:79
[FARRA:v1p3/r4] FARRA, d. 207 · author | reports | Some lower the dāl in al-ḥamd because the frequent phrase has become one word and mixed short vowels are heavy; they analogize to ibil. | mentions [, ]
[FARRA:v1p3/r5] FARRA, d. 207 · بعضهم | reports | Those who raise the lām match the common Arabic pattern with two ḍammas, as in al-ḥilm and al-ʿuqab.
[FARRA:v1p3/r6] FARRA, d. 207 · author | holds | Frequent phrases can be reanalyzed as one word: bi-abī becomes bābā; Abū Tharwān’s verse attests the resulting vocative form. | mentions 
[FARRA:v1p3/r7] FARRA, d. 207 · أبو ثروان | reports | Abū Tharwān’s poem uses “yā bībā” as evidence for the contracted phrase.
[MAJAZ:v1p21/r6] MAJAZ, d. 209 · author | holds | Rabb al-ʿālamīn means the created beings, and the singular of ʿālamīn is ʿālam; Labīd’s line witnesses the plural.
[MAJAZ:v1p21/r7] MAJAZ, d. 209 · author | holds | Al-ʿAjjāj’s line uses ʿālam in the singular, supporting the stated singular form.
[AKHFASH:v1p12/r1] AKHFASH, d. 215 · author | reports | Al-Akhfash cites a rajaz couplet about every living being meeting death and every pair ending in separation, then says this usage is scarcely known; the witnessed word is ithnayn.
[AKHFASH:v1p12/r2] AKHFASH, d. 215 · author | holds | The lām makes li-llāh genitive, and rabb al-ʿālamīn al-raḥmān al-raḥīm is also genitive as an attribute of Allāh.
[AKHFASH:v1p12/r3] AKHFASH, d. 215 · author | holds | The open nūn in the sound masculine plural is an added marker that disappears in the singular; its fatḥa distinguishes it from the dual's always-kasra nūn. | mentions 5:23, 36:14
[AKHFASH:v1p12/r4] AKHFASH, d. 215 · author | holds | Sound masculine plurals use wāw for nominative and yāʾ for accusative and genitive, while the dual uses alif for nominative and yāʾ for the other two cases.
[AKHFASH:v1p12/r5] AKHFASH, d. 215 · author | holds | The plural nūn falls in annexation like the dual nūn; unlike the root nūn in broken plurals such as shayāṭīn, dahāqīn, and masākīn, which remains.
[AKHFASH:v1p12/r6] AKHFASH, d. 215 · author | holds | Al-ladhīna has an added open nūn because it disappears in singular alladhī; the text also cites the nominative form alladhūn.
[AKHFASH:v1p7/r1] AKHFASH, d. 215 · author | holds | In words beginning with the added alif-lām, the alif drops in connected speech and is always fatḥa when starting; the two letters function together like qad or bal.
[AKHFASH:v1p7/r2] AKHFASH, d. 215 · author | holds | The alif-lām is recognized as added because another alif-lām cannot be prefixed to words such as al-ḥamd, al-ʿālamīn, alladhī, and Allāh.
[AKHFASH:v1p7/r3] AKHFASH, d. 215 · author | holds | A preceding interrogative alif preserves and lengthens the article alif to distinguish a question from a statement; only a few Arabs leave it unlengthened. | mentions 10:59, 27:59, 10:91
[AKHFASH:v1p7/r4] AKHFASH, d. 215 · author | holds | With an interrogative alif before aṣṭafā or aftarā, the interrogative is open and the following hamzat waṣl drops. | mentions 37:153, 34:8
[AKHFASH:v1p8/r1] AKHFASH, d. 215 · author | holds | An initial alif is hamzat qaṭʿ when another article can be added, as with al-ilāh, alwāḥ, ilhām, and ilqāʾ. | mentions 7:59
[AKHFASH:v1p8/r2] AKHFASH, d. 215 · author | holds | The alif in ilā is also cut, but it is not an added article: ilā is a preposition rather than a noun, and its alif is kasra rather than fatḥa.
[AKHFASH:v1p8/r3] AKHFASH, d. 215 · author | holds | Al-ḥamdu is nominative as a subject begun without a preceding governing verb; the beginning raises subject and predicate, an explanation al-Akhfash says is more analogical. | mentions 48:29
[AKHFASH:v1p8/r4] AKHFASH, d. 215 · بعضهم | reports | Some grammarians say that the beginning raises both the subject and the predicate.
[AKHFASH:v1p8/r5] AKHFASH, d. 215 · بعضهم | reports | Other grammarians say that the predicate raises the subject; al-Akhfash accepts both accounts but prefers the first as more analogical.
[AKHFASH:v1p8/r6] AKHFASH, d. 215 · بعض العرب | reports | Some Arabs put al-ḥamdu in the accusative as a verbal noun in place of the verb, equivalent to saying a praise to God or I praise with praise.
[AKHFASH:v1p8/r7] AKHFASH, d. 215 · بعض العرب | reports | Some Arabs give al-ḥamdu a fixed kasra by treating it like indeclinable nouns; before and after are likewise fixed unless annexed, as the cited Qurʾanic examples show. | mentions 30:4, 57:10, 9:69, 59:10, 57:22, 12:100
[TUSTARI:1:2/r1] TUSTARI, d. 283 · author | holds | Praise means gratitude, which means obedience; obedience is God's guardianship, completed only by disavowing everything besides Him. | mentions 5:55
[TUSTARI:1:2/r2] TUSTARI, d. 283 · author | holds | The Lord of the worlds is creation's master, nurturer, caretaker, reformer, and governor, acting by prior knowledge, will, command, and decree; none is their lord but Him.
[TAB:1:2/r1] TAB, d. 310 · author | holds | Al-Tabari defines praise as pure thanks to God alone for countless gifts, including faculties for obedience, worldly provision without entitlement, and guidance to lasting bliss; all praise belongs to Him at first and last.
[TAB:1:2/r10] TAB, d. 310 · author | holds | Readers and scholars unanimously vocalize al-ḥamdu in the nominative; al-Tabari says the accusative would distort the meaning and merits punishment if knowingly read.
[TAB:1:2/r11] TAB, d. 310 · author | holds | God speaks both clauses: He praises Himself, then teaches and obliges His servants to recite them as a test, with an understood command to say them signaled by “You alone we worship.” | mentions 1:5
[TAB:1:2/r12] TAB, d. 310 · author | holds | The command “say” is omitted because Arabic speakers omit words recoverable from context; here the following worship clause reveals that the praise clause is also an instruction to servants. | mentions 1:5
[TAB:1:2/r13] TAB, d. 310 · author | holds | For rab as obedient master or chief, al-Tabari cites Labīd's “lord of Kinda” and al-Nābigha's “lord of my possessions.”
[TAB:1:2/r14] TAB, d. 310 · author | holds | Rab can mean one who repairs or tends something: al-Farazdaq calls an unrepaired hide “not tended,” while ʿAlqama describes another king tending his affairs.
[TAB:1:2/r15] TAB, d. 310 · author | holds | A third Arabic sense is owner: one who possesses a thing is called its rabb.
[TAB:1:2/r16] TAB, d. 310 · author | holds | God is the incomparable master, the one who sets His creatures' affairs right through His gifts, and the owner of creation and command.
[TAB:1:2/r17] TAB, d. 310 · ابن عباس | reports | Ibn ʿAbbas glosses “Lord of the worlds” as the one who owns all creation, the heavens, earth, their inhabitants, and all between them, known and unknown; nothing resembles Him.
[TAB:1:2/r18] TAB, d. 310 · author | holds | Al-ʿālamūn is the plural of ʿālam, while ʿālam is a collective noun with no singular form from the same word, like anām, rahṭ, and jaysh.
[TAB:1:2/r19] TAB, d. 310 · author | holds | Al-ʿālam names classes of peoples and each generation in its era; humans, jinn, and every other created kind form worlds. Al-ʿAjjāj's poem uses “this world” for his contemporaries.
[TAB:1:2/r2] TAB, d. 310 · ابن عباس | reports | Ibn ʿAbbas says Gabriel instructed Muhammad to say “praise be to God”; he glosses it as thanks, submission, and acknowledgment of God's blessing and guidance.
[TAB:1:2/r20] TAB, d. 310 · ابن عباس | reports | A report through ʿIkrima attributes to Ibn ʿAbbas the view that the worlds are jinn and humans.
[TAB:1:2/r21] TAB, d. 310 · ابن عباس | reports | A report through Saʿīd ibn Jubayr also attributes to Ibn ʿAbbas the gloss “Lord of the jinn and humans.”
[TAB:1:2/r22] TAB, d. 310 · سعيد بن جبير | reports | Saʿīd ibn Jubayr says Adam's descendants, jinn, and humans each constitute a distinct world.
[TAB:1:2/r23] TAB, d. 310 · مجاهد | reports | Mujāhid interprets “Lord of the worlds” as Lord of humans and jinn.
[TAB:1:2/r24] TAB, d. 310 · قتادة | reports | Qatāda says every kind is a world.
[TAB:1:2/r25] TAB, d. 310 · أبو العالية | reports | Abū al-ʿĀliya says humans and jinn are worlds, alongside either eighteen thousand or fourteen thousand other worlds (he is unsure), of angels on earth, 3,500 in each corner, created to worship God.
[TAB:1:2/r26] TAB, d. 310 · ابن جريج | reports | Ibn Jurayj interprets the worlds as jinn and humans.
[TAB:1:2/r3] TAB, d. 310 · الحكم بن عمير | reports | Al-Hakam ibn ʿUmayr reports the Prophet's statement that saying “praise be to God, Lord of the worlds” is gratitude to God and brings an increase.
[TAB:1:2/r4] TAB, d. 310 · قيل | reports | An unnamed view distinguishes praise of God through

 His beautiful names and attributes from thanks for His favors and gifts.

[TAB:1:2/r6] TAB, d. 310 · author | holds | Al-Tabari notes that Kaʿb's report does not clarify whether praise means praise through God's names and attributes or praise for His blessings.

[TAB:1:7/r54] TAB, d. 310 · أهل الإلحاد الطاعنون في القرآن | reports | Critics ask why al-Fātiḥa has seven verses when, they argue, the meaning of its remaining verses is already contained in “Master of Judgment Day” and “You alone we worship and ask for help.”
[TAB:1:7/r55] TAB, d. 310 · author | holds | Earlier scriptures each contain some meanings found together in the Qur'an: the Torah gives admonitions and detail, the Psalms praise and glorify, and the Gospel admonishes and reminds; the Qur'an gathers these and adds more.
[TAB:1:7/r56] TAB, d. 310 · author | holds | Al-Ṭabarī says the prior books lack a miracle certifying their recipients, whereas the Qur'an's unmatched composition defeats all attempts to produce even a short surah and proves Muhammad's prophethood.
[TAB:1:7/r57] TAB, d. 310 · author | holds | The Qur'an's varied contents—encouragement, warning, commands, prohibitions, stories, argument, and parables—also make its extended expression purposeful.
[TAB:1:7/r58] TAB, d. 310 · author | holds | Al-Fātiḥa's inimitable arrangement proves prophethood, while its praise and glorification direct people to recognize God's greatness, sovereignty, power, and dominion and to thank Him for His favors.
[TAB:1:7/r59] TAB, d. 310 · author | holds | The account of those favored through knowledge of God and His enabling teaches that every religious and worldly blessing comes from Him, directing requests to God rather than idols or rivals.
[TAB:1:7/r60] TAB, d. 310 · author | holds | Recounting punishments for disobedience warns people away from sin and from incurring God's anger, whose consequences lead to destruction.
[TAB:1:7/r61] TAB, d. 310 · رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم | reports | Abū Hurayra reports that the Prophet said God answers the worshipper's recitation: He calls al-ḥamdu praise, al-Raḥmān al-Raḥīm commendation, Mālik Yawm al-Dīn glorification, and the rest of the surah the servant's share.

[TAB:1:7/r63] TAB, d. 310 · رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم | reports | Jābir ibn ʿAbd Allāh reports the divine saying that the prayer is divided between God and His servant, with the servant receiving what he asks; the first three praises are God's, and what follows is for the servant.
[TAB-FULL:v1p136/r1] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · author | holds | Al-ḥamd lillāh is gratitude and praise owed exclusively to God for countless blessings, including capacity for worship, provision, and guidance to lasting bliss.
[TAB-FULL:v1p136/r2] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · عبد الله بن عباس | reports | Ibn ʿAbbās explains praise as gratitude, submission to God, and acknowledging His blessings, guidance, and originating gifts.
[TAB-FULL:v1p136/r3] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم | reports | A report from the Prophet says that saying “Praise belongs to God, Lord of the worlds” is gratitude for which God gives an increase.
[TAB-FULL:v1p136/r4] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · كعب الأحبار | reports | Kaʿb al-Aḥbār calls al-ḥamd praise of God; the narration does not specify whether he means praise for names and attributes or for blessings.
[TAB-FULL:v1p138/r1] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · الأسود بن سريع | reports | A prophetic report says nothing is more beloved to God than praise, and that He praised Himself with “Praise belongs to God.”
[TAB-FULL:v1p138/r2] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · author | holds | Arabic allows praise and thanks to overlap: the phrase “praise belongs to God, in thanks” works because each term can occupy the other’s place.
[TAB-FULL:v1p138/r3] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · author | holds | The definite article makes al-ḥamd signify all praise and complete gratitude belong to God; without it the wording would describe only this speaker’s praise.
[TAB-FULL:v1p138/r4] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · author | rejects | The inherited nominative reading al-ḥamdu preserves the intended universal claim; deliberately reading it accusative would distort the meaning and merits punishment.

[TAB-FULL:v1p141#2/r1] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · author | holds | Rabb can mean an obeyed master; Labīd and al-Nābigha use it for the lords of Kindah and the speaker’s patron.
[TAB-FULL:v1p141#2/r2] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · author | holds | Rabb can mean one who repairs or sets something right; al-Farazdaq’s unrepaired hide and ʿAlqama’s neglected affairs illustrate this sense.
[TAB-FULL:v1p141#2/r3] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · author | holds | Rabb can also mean owner; these lexical senses converge in God as incomparable sovereign, caretaker of creation, and possessor of command.
[TAB-FULL:v1p141#2/r4] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · عبد الله بن عباس | reports | Ibn ʿAbbās says the Lord owns all creation—heavens, earths, their inhabitants, and what lies between—known and unknown, and resembles nothing.
[TAB-FULL:v1p141/r1] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · author | holds | Arabic regularly omits words recoverable from context, as in poetic answers and farewell formulas; a known meaning makes the unspoken expression unnecessary. | mentions 1:5
[TAB-FULL:v1p141/r2] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · عبد الله بن عباس | reports | Ibn ʿAbbās’s report that Gabriel told Muhammad to say the praise confirms Ṭabarī’s implied command interpretation.
[TAB-FULL:v1p145/r1] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · author | holds | ʿĀlamīn is a plural collective with no singular of the same form; ʿālam denotes a class of peoples, and each species or generation is its own world.
[TAB-FULL:v1p145/r2] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · author | holds | The poet al-ʿAjjāj calls his own generation “this world,” illustrating how a time’s people form a distinct ʿālam.
[TAB-FULL:v1p145/r3] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · عبد الله بن عباس | reports | One report from Ibn ʿAbbās takes the worlds as all creation: the heavens, earth, their inhabitants, and what is known or unknown.
[TAB-FULL:v1p145/r4] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · عبد الله بن عباس | reports | Other reports from Ibn ʿAbbās define the worlds as jinn and humans; Saʿīd ibn Jubayr and Mujāhid report the same narrower gloss.

[TAB-FULL:v1p145/r6] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · مجاهد | reports | Mujāhid also interprets “Lord of the worlds” as referring to humans and jinn.

[NAHHAS:v1p169/r2] NAHHAS, d. 338 · الكسائي | reports | Al-Kisa'i makes al-ḥamdu nominative through the pronoun implied in its predicate, treating the lām like a verb.
[NAHHAS:v1p169/r20] NAHHAS, d. 338 · أبو حاتم | reports | Abū Ḥātim explains the accusative as an implied I praise Allah, Lord of the worlds.
[NAHHAS:v1p169/r21] NAHHAS, d. 338 · أبو إسحاق | reports | Abū Isḥāq permits the accusative as an annexed vocative.
[NAHHAS:v1p169/r22] NAHHAS, d. 338 · ابن كيسان | reports | Ibn Kaysān rejects an annexed-vocative parse because it would split the utterance into two clauses, and instead parses the accusative as praise.
[NAHHAS:v1p169/r23] NAHHAS, d. 338 · author | holds | Rabb al-ʿālamīn may also be nominative, with an implied huwa: he is Lord of the worlds.
[NAHHAS:v1p169/r24] NAHHAS, d. 338 · author | holds | The word rabb has extended forms rabbāhu, rabbahu, and rabbathu, developed through b-to-y and then y-to-t changes.
[NAHHAS:v1p169/r3] NAHHAS, d. 338 · الفراء | reports | Al-Farrāʾ makes al-ḥamdu nominative by the grammatical position of the lām, treating the preposition like a noun that stands independently.
[NAHHAS:v1p169/r4] NAHHAS, d. 338 · author | holds | The grammarians use different labels for prepositions: al-Kisa'i says attributes, al-Farrāʾ loci, and Basrans adverbial containers.
[NAHHAS:v1p169/r5] NAHHAS, d. 338 · ابن عيينة ورؤبة ابن العجاج | reports | Ibn ʿUyayna and Ruʾba ibn al-ʿAjjāj read al-ḥamdu in the accusative as a verbal noun, a usage of Qays and al-Ḥārith ibn Samāma.
[NAHHAS:v1p169/r6] NAHHAS, d. 338 · author | prefers | The nominative is preferable in wording because a definite noun is being reported about, and in meaning because it includes the speaker's praise and everyone else's.
[NAHHAS:v1p169/r7] NAHHAS, d. 338 · author | holds | The accusative reading does not include the speaker's own praise in the same way.
[NAHHAS:v1p169/r8] NAHHAS, d. 338 · الفراء | reports | Al-Farrāʾ transmits two further vocalized forms of al-ḥamdu lillāh.
[NAHHAS:v1p169/r9] NAHHAS, d. 338 · علي بن سليمان | reports | ʿAlī ibn Sulaymān says neither of al-Farrāʾ's two forms is acceptable to Basran grammarians.
[SULAMI:v1p33#3/r1] SULAMI, d. 412 · ابن عطاء | reports | Praise is thanks to God for the favor of teaching people how to praise Him.
[SULAMI:v1p33#3/r10] SULAMI, d. 412 · بعضهم | reports | God praised Himself for the worlds before their creation, knowing they could not fulfill His praise.
[SULAMI:v1p33#3/r11] SULAMI, d. 412 · بعضهم | reports | Calling the worlds His subjects and adding them to Himself is mercy for them.
[SULAMI:v1p33#3/r12] SULAMI, d. 412 · بعضهم | reports | Praise is due in both ease and hardship, while thanks is due only for blessings.
[SULAMI:v1p33#3/r2] SULAMI, d. 412 · بعضهم | reports | The phrase means that no one praises God except God Himself.
[SULAMI:v1p33#3/r3] SULAMI, d. 412 · بعضهم | reports | God is praised for all His attributes and states.
[SULAMI:v1p33#3/r4] SULAMI, d. 412 · الواسطي | reports | People praise at three levels: ordinary habit, gratitude for pleasure, and recognition that God did not leave them to sever blessings from witnessing His due.
[SULAMI:v1p33#3/r5] SULAMI, d. 412 · جعفر الصادق | reports | True praise knows God through oneness, sovereignty, and permanence, signified by the letters of hamd.
[SULAMI:v1p33#3/r6] SULAMI, d. 412 · الجنيد | reports | Junayd tells a speaker to complete praise with Lord of the worlds; created beings leave no trace when joined to the Eternal.
[SULAMI:v1p33#3/r7] SULAMI, d. 412 · عطاء | reports | Praise expresses believers' affirmation of oneness, monotheists' affirmation of singularity, and knowers' recognition of God's rightful lordship and majesty.
[SULAMI:v1p33#3/r8] SULAMI, d. 412 · بعضهم | reports | Believers praise through the Fatiha, seekers through secluded remembrance, and knowers through longing and intimacy.
[SULAMI:v1p33#3/r9] SULAMI, d. 412 · الحسين | reports | No blessing is better than praise; God is the praised, the servant the praiser, and praise is the state that connects to the seeker.
[SULAMI:v1p34/r1] SULAMI, d. 412 · بعضهم | reports | Praise comes from being immersed in blessing, whereas thanksgiving seeks an increase.
[SULAMI:v1p34/r2] SULAMI, d. 412 · بعضهم | reports | The phrase is the worlds' own utterance of praise.
[SULAMI:v1p34/r3] SULAMI, d. 412 · ابن عطاء | reports | God nurtures knowers with certainty, believers with patience and sincerity, seekers with honesty and loyalty, and knowers' hearts with reflection and insight.
[SULAMI:v1p34/r4] SULAMI, d. 412 · بعضهم | reports | God created and nurtured the worlds through mercy so they could glorify Him; He praised Himself in eternity without cause, while creaturely praise is mixed with motives.
[SULAMI:v1p34/r5] SULAMI, d. 412 · بعضهم | reports | God alone inspires the worlds to praise Him.
[SULAMI:v1p34/r6] SULAMI, d. 412 · بعضهم | reports | Knowing servants cannot adequately praise God, so He praised Himself in eternity and relieved them of an impossible burden; even the Messenger admits he cannot enumerate His praise.
[SULAMI:v1p34/r7] SULAMI, d. 412 · بعضهم | reports | God's self-praise accounts for abundant blessings and human inability, lifting the burden of seeing the benefaction from servants.
[SULAMI:v1p34/r8] SULAMI, d. 412 · جعفر بن محمد | reports | Jafar explains the letters of hamd through God's oneness, gentleness, prior self-praise, majesty, and Islam, whose abode and greeting are peace.
[THALABI:v1p103/r4] THALABI, d. 427 · النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم | reports | In the divine report dividing prayer between God and the servant, the basmala glorifies God, al-ḥamdu praises Him, al-Raḥmān al-Raḥīm extols Him, Mālik delegates the matter, the worship-and-help verse is shared, and guidance is granted to the servant.
[THALABI:v1p107/r3] THALABI, d. 427 · author | holds | God praises Himself as a favor to creation; the declarative wording functions as a command meaning “say: praise belongs to God.”
[THALABI:v1p107/r4] THALABI, d. 427 · ابن عباس | reports | Ibn ʿAbbās glosses al-ḥamd as gratitude.
[THALABI:v1p107/r5] THALABI, d. 427 · ابن الأنباري | reports | Ibn al-Anbārī says al-ḥamd is an inversion of al-madḥ, like the word-order reversals jabal/jalab and baḍḍ/ḍabb.
[THALABI:v1p108/r1] THALABI, d. 427 · قوم | reports | One distinction says praise concerns someone for what they are, while thanks concern what they do; praise can stand for thanks, but thanks cannot praise knowledge or forbearance.
[THALABI:v1p108/r2] THALABI, d. 427 · author | holds | Because praise is broader than thanks, the verse praises God for His lofty attributes and beautiful names and for all His acts and kindness to creation.
[THALABI:v1p108/r3] THALABI, d. 427 · قوم | reports | Another view makes praise verbal and thanks embodied in action, illustrated by commands to

say praise and to work in gratitude. | mentions 17:111, 27:59, 34:13
[THALABI:v1p108/r4] THALABI, d. 427 · قوم | reports | Another distinction says praise is for blessings granted, while thanks is for what God has withheld.
[THALABI:v1p108/r5] THALABI, d. 427 · قوم | reports | A further view assigns praise to outward blessings and thanks to hidden blessings. | mentions 31:20
[THALABI:v1p108/r6] THALABI, d. 427 · النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم | reports | The Prophet calls praise the head of gratitude and says no servant thanks God without praising Him.
[THALABI:v1p108/r7] THALABI, d. 427 · ابن عباس | reports | Ibn ʿAbbās says al-ḥamd is the word of gratitude spoken by the people of Paradise.
[THALABI:v1p109/r1] THALABI, d. 427 · قراء العامة | reports | The majority read al-ḥamdu with ḍamma on the dāl as a nominal subject whose predicate follows; another analysis fronts the predicate, meaning “to God belongs praise,” and another treats it as quotation.
[THALABI:v1p109/r10] THALABI, d. 427 · الحسين بن الفضل | reports | Al-Ḥusayn ibn al-Faḍl says rabb can mean staying in a place without moving, as in the usage rabb bi-l-makān.
[THALABI:v1p109/r11] THALABI, d. 427 · أبو سعيد ابن أوس الأنصاري | reports | Abū Saʿīd ibn Aws al-Anṣārī explains Zayd ibn ʿAlī’s accusative reading as an implied “I praise the Lord of the worlds.”
[THALABI:v1p109/r2] THALABI, d. 427 · هارون بن موسى الأعور ورؤبة بن العجاج | reports | Hārūn al-Aʿwar and Ruʾba read the dāl in the accusative, supplying “I praise praise,” since al-ḥamd is a verbal noun that is not dualized or pluralized.
[THALABI:v1p109/r3] THALABI, d. 427 · الحسن البصري | reports | Al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī reads the dāl with kasra by vowel assimilation.
[THALABI:v1p109/r4] THALABI, d. 427 · إبراهيم بن أبي عبلة الشامي | reports | Ibrāhīm ibn Abī ʿAbla reads both dāl and lām with ḍamma, assimilating one ḍamma to the next.
[THALABI:v1p109/r5] THALABI, d. 427 · زيد بن علي | reports | Zayd ibn ʿAlī reads rabb al-ʿālamīn in the accusative as praise; Abū Saʿīd ibn Aws explains the reading as an implied “I praise the Lord of the worlds.”
[THALABI:v1p109/r6] THALABI, d. 427 · author | holds | The usual genitive reading means creator, originator, owner, and manager of all creation.
[THALABI:v1p109/r7] THALABI, d. 427 · author | holds | Rabb can mean master or lord, as in Joseph’s use of rabb for one’s master; poetry calls leaders of tribes rabb. | mentions 12:42
[THALABI:v1p109/r8] THALABI, d. 427 · النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم | reports | A Prophetic question uses rabb for an owner: “Are you owner of camels or owner of sheep?”; poetry likewise calls someone the owner of a bridge or herds.
[THALABI:v1p109/r9] THALABI, d. 427 · author | holds | Rabb can also mean companion, pasture or nourisher, and one who repairs something, each supported by Arabic poetry.
[THALABI:v1p110/r1] THALABI, d. 427 · author | prefers | The author prefers the sense of abiding because theologians agree God has always been Lord.
[THALABI:v1p110/r2] THALABI, d. 427 · أبو بكر محمد بن موسى الواسطي | reports | Al-Wāsiṭī defines the Lord as creator at the beginning, nourisher through sustenance, and forgiver at the end.
[THALABI:v1p110/r3] THALABI, d. 427 · author | holds | A creature cannot be called al-rabb with the definite article; only an annexed “lord of X” is allowed, since only God owns all and the article is universal.
[THALABI:v1p110/r4] THALABI, d. 427 · author | holds | Al-ʿālamīn is a plural of ʿālam without a singular of the same form, like anām, rahṭ, and jaysh.
[THALABI:v1p110/r5] THALABI, d. 427 · أبي بن كعب | reports | Ubayy ibn Kaʿb’s report says the worlds are angels, enumerating four groups of 4,500 and vast angelic hosts, including spirit beings whose praise reaches the Throne-bearers.
[THALABI:v1p110/r6] THALABI, d. 427 · أبو معاذ النحوي | reports | Abū Muʿādh al-Naḥwī says the worlds are the children of Adam.
[THALABI:v1p110/r7] THALABI, d. 427 · أبو هيثم خالد بن يزيد، ابن عباس | reports | Abū Haytham says the worlds are jinn and humans, citing “a warner to the worlds”; this interpretation is also transmitted from Ibn ʿAbbās by ʿAṭiyya and Saʿīd ibn Jubayr. | mentions 25:1
[THALABI:v1p110/r8] THALABI, d. 427 · الحسين بن الفضل | reports | Al-Ḥusayn ibn al-Faḍl says the worlds are people, citing the address “Do you approach males among the worlds?” | mentions 26:165
[THALABI:v1p110/r9] THALABI, d. 427 · العجاج | reports | The poet al-ʿAjjāj gives a different interpretation of the worlds; the source does not spell it out here.
[THALABI:v1p111/r1] THALABI, d. 427 · الفراء وأبو عبيدة | reports | Al-Farrāʾ and Abū ʿUbayda say the worlds are four kinds of rational beings—angels, jinn, humans, and devils—excluding animals, and derive the term from knowledge.
[THALABI:v1p111/r10] THALABI, d. 427 · سعيد بن المسيب | reports | Saʿīd ibn al-Musayyib counts one thousand worlds, six hundred in the sea and four hundred on land.
[THALABI:v1p111/r11] THALABI, d. 427 · الضحاك | reports | Al-Ḍaḥḥāk counts 420 worlds: 360 barefoot and unclothed, unaware of their Creator, and sixty that wear clothes.
[THALABI:v1p111/r12] THALABI, d. 427 · وهب | reports | Wahb counts 18,000 worlds and likens the inhabited portion of this world amid wasteland to a tent in a desert.
[THALABI:v1p111/r13] THALABI, d. 427 · أبو سعيد الخدري | reports | Abū Saʿīd al-Khudrī counts 40,000 worlds, with the known world from east to west being only one.
[THALABI:v1p111/r14] THALABI, d. 427 · مقاتل بن حيان | reports | Muqātil ibn Ḥayyān counts 80,000 worlds, divided equally between land and sea.
[THALABI:v1p111/r15] THALABI, d. 427 · مقاتل بن سليمان | reports | Muqātil ibn Sulaymān says fully explaining the worlds would require a thousand volumes of a thousand pages each.
[THALABI:v1p111/r16] THALABI, d. 427 · كعب الأحبار | reports | Kaʿb al-Aḥbār says only God can count the worlds, citing the verse that none knows His hosts but He. | mentions 74:31
[THALABI:v1p111/r2] THALABI, d. 427 · عبد العزيز بن يحيى الكناني | reports | ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz al-Kinānī says the worlds are the purified among creation.
[THALABI:v1p111/r3] THALABI, d. 427 · عبد الرحمن بن زيد بن أسلم | reports | ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn Zayd says the worlds are those who receive sustenance.
[THALABI:v1p111/r4] THALABI, d. 427 · الخضر بن إسماعيل | reports | Al-Khiḍr ibn Ismāʿīl treats al-ʿālamīn as a collective noun for a large multitude.
[THALABI:v1p111/r5] THALABI, d. 427 · أبو عمرو بن العلاء، ابن عباس | reports | Abū ʿAmr says the worlds are spiritual beings; the source links this with Ibn ʿAbbās’s gloss “every living thing that walks on earth.”
[THALABI:v1p111/r6] THALABI, d. 427 · سفيان بن عيينة | reports | Sufyān ibn ʿUyayna says al-ʿālamīn is a collective plural for different kinds of things.
[THALABI:v1p111/r7] THALABI, d. 427 · جعفر بن محمد الصادق | reports | Jaʿfar al-Ṣādiq says the worlds are the people of Paradise and the people of Hell.
[THALABI:v1p111/r8] THALABI, d. 427 · الحسن وقتادة ومجاهد | reports | Al-Ḥasan, Qatāda, and Mujāhid say the worlds comprise all created beings, citing Pharaoh’s question and God’s answer that He is Lord of the heavens, earth, and all between them. | mentions 26:23, 26:24
[THALABI:v1p111/r9] THALABI, d. 427 · author | holds | On the all-creatures interpretation, ʿālamīn derives from knowledge or sign, because creatures are visible and display the mark of their maker.
[THALABI:v1p90/r1] THALABI, d. 427 · بعض العلماء | reports | Some scholars reconcile reports that the Fatiha is Meccan and Medinan by saying Gabriel revealed it twice, once in each place, to honor its status; this explains its name “Mathani.”
[THALABI:v1p90/r2] THALABI, d. 427 · النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم | reports | Abu Said al-Khudri reports the Prophet saying that the Opening of the Book is a cure for poison.
[THALABI:v1p90/r3] THALABI, d. 427 · النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم | reports | Hudhayfa ibn al-Yaman reports that recitation of “Praise belongs to God, Lord of the worlds” by a child at school can avert a destined punishment for forty years.
[THALABI:v1p90/r4] THALABI, d. 427 · الحسن | reports | Al-Hasan says knowledge of all revealed books is gathered in the Quran, then in its muṣḥaf section, then in the Fatiha; knowing its interpretation is like knowing all revealed books.
[MAWARDI:1:2/r1] MAWARDI, d. 450 · author | holds | Hamd is praise of the praised one’s beautiful attributes and actions, while shukr is praise for a favor; every shukr is hamd but not every hamd is shukr, so God may praise Himself but not thank Himself.
[MAWARDI:1:2/r10] MAWARDI, d. 450 · author | holds | Al-alamin is the plural of alam, with no singular of the same form, like raht and qawm; each age or community is an alam, as the cited al-A‘raj verse illustrates.
[MAWARDI:1:2/r11] MAWARDI, d. 450 · ابن عباس | reports | Ibn Abbas takes the worlds to mean rational beings: angels, humans, and jinn.
[MAWARDI:1:2/r12] MAWARDI, d. 450 · unattributed | reports | Another view takes the worlds to mean the present world and all it contains.
[MAWARDI:1:2/r13] MAWARDI, d. 450 · أبو إسحاق الزجاج | reports | Al-Zajjaj takes the worlds to include everything God created in this world and the afterlife.
[MAWARDI:1:2/r14] MAWARDI, d. 450 · unattributed | reports | The derivation from knowledge fits the interpretation that alam means rational beings.
[MAWARDI:1:2/r15] MAWARDI, d. 450 · unattributed | reports | The alternative derivation is from sign, since the worlds are signs pointing to their creator; this fits the interpretation that alam means all created things.
[MAWARDI:1:2/r2] MAWARDI, d. 450 · author | holds | Hamd differs from madh: hamd is deserved only for a good act, while madh may praise an act or a non-action; all hamd is madh, but not vice versa.
[MAWARDI:1:2/r3] MAWARDI, d. 450 · author | holds | God may be praised for knowledge and power but not hamd for them, since they are attributes of essence; He may be praised and hamd for creating and providing, attributes of action.
[MAWARDI:1:2/r4] MAWARDI, d. 450 · unattributed | reports

 | One derivation of rabb is owner, as in the owner of a house.
[MAWARDI:1:2/r5] MAWARDI, d. 450 · unattributed | reports | Another derivation is master; 12:41 calls a human master rabb. | mentions 12:41
[MAWARDI:1:2/r6] MAWARDI, d. 450 · unattributed | reports | A third meaning is manager; rabbani scholars are so called for managing people through knowledge, and a housewife is called rabbat al-bayt for managing the home. | mentions 5:44
[MAWARDI:1:2/r7] MAWARDI, d. 450 · unattributed | reports | A fourth derivation connects rabb to nurturing; stepchildren are named rabائب because the husband raises them, as in 4:23. | mentions 4:23
[MAWARDI:1:2/r8] MAWARDI, d. 450 · author | holds | If rabb means owner or master, it describes God’s essence; if it means manager or nurturer, it describes His action.
[MAWARDI:1:2/r9] MAWARDI, d. 450 · author | holds | With the definite article, rabb is exclusive to God; without it, the word is shared by God and His servants.
[MAWARDI-FULL:v1p53/r1] MAWARDI-FULL, d. 450 · author | holds | Hamd praises a person for fine attributes and acts, while shukr praises for a blessing; every thanks is praise but not every praise is thanks, so God may praise Himself but not thank Himself.
[MAWARDI-FULL:v1p53/r10] MAWARDI-FULL, d. 450 · العجاج | reports | The cited line using ʿālam witnesses the word's poetic use.
[MAWARDI-FULL:v1p53/r2] MAWARDI-FULL, d. 450 · author | holds | Hamd is deserved only for a good act, while madh may concern an act or a non-act; thus God may be praised for knowledge and power but not hamd for these essential attributes, while creation and provision merit both.
[MAWARDI-FULL:v1p53/r3] MAWARDI-FULL, d. 450 · author | reports | One derivation of Rabb is owner, as in the owner of a house.
[MAWARDI-FULL:v1p53/r4] MAWARDI-FULL, d. 450 · author | reports | Another derives Rabb from master; in 12:41 the word refers to a person's master. | mentions 12:41
[MAWARDI-FULL:v1p53/r5] MAWARDI-FULL, d. 450 · author | reports | A third meaning of Rabb is manager, as scholars are called rabbaniyyun for managing people through knowledge.
[MAWARDI-FULL:v1p53/r6] MAWARDI-FULL, d. 450 · author | reports | A fourth derivation is from nurturing or raising, as in the word for a wife's daughter raised in the household.
[MAWARDI-FULL:v1p53/r7] MAWARDI-FULL, d. 450 · author | holds | Calling God Rabb as owner or master describes an essential attribute; calling Him Rabb as manager and nurturer describes action.
[MAWARDI-FULL:v1p53/r8] MAWARDI-FULL, d. 450 · author | holds | With the definite article al-Rabb is exclusive to God; without it the word is shared by God and creatures.
[MAWARDI-FULL:v1p53/r9] MAWARDI-FULL, d. 450 · author | holds | ʿĀlamīn is a plural with no singular of the same form, like raht and qawm; people of each era form an ʿālam.
[MAWARDI-FULL:v1p54/r1] MAWARDI-FULL, d. 450 · ابن عباس | reports | He defines the worlds as rational beings: angels, humans, and jinn.
[MAWARDI-FULL:v1p54/r2] MAWARDI-FULL, d. 450 · author | reports | A second interpretation makes the worlds this world and all that it contains.
[MAWARDI-FULL:v1p54/r3] MAWARDI-FULL, d. 450 · أبو إسحاق الزجاج | reports | He defines the worlds as everything God created in this world and the next.
[MAWARDI-FULL:v1p54/r4] MAWARDI-FULL, d. 450 · author | reports | If ʿālam means rational beings, the word derives from knowledge.
[MAWARDI-FULL:v1p54/r5] MAWARDI-FULL, d. 450 · author | reports | If ʿālam means every creature, the word derives from sign because creation points to its Creator.
[QUSHAYRI:v1p10/r1] QUSHAYRI, d. 465 · author | holds | One group praises God for the subtle wonders disclosed to their hearts, hidden kindness in their innermost selves, and sudden inspirations of His encounters.
[QUSHAYRI:v1p10/r10] QUSHAYRI, d. 465 · author | holds | If mercy is the will of blessing or blessing itself, blessings differ in rank: some benefit bodies and outward life, others spirits and inner life.
[QUSHAYRI:v1p10/r2] QUSHAYRI, d. 465 · author | holds | Another group praises Him while witnessing the eternal attributes and does not turn from majesty and generosity to count blessings; praising majesty differs from thanking for favors.
[QUSHAYRI:v1p10/r3] QUSHAYRI, d. 465 · author | holds | A further group is consumed by divine unity: God speaks through them, from Himself and toward Himself, while outwardly they remain in differentiation and inwardly are held by the gathering of union.
[QUSHAYRI:v1p10/r4] QUSHAYRI, d. 465 · author | holds | The name Lord means master; “the worlds” includes every creature, rational and inanimate, whose entities God owns and whose forms and dwellings He brings into being.
[QUSHAYRI:v1p10/r5] QUSHAYRI, d. 465 · author | holds | Lord also means nurturer: He supports worshippers' souls, guides seekers' hearts, unifies knowers' spirits, provides for bodies, and lets spirits witness generosity.
[QUSHAYRI:v1p10/r6] QUSHAYRI, d. 465 · author | holds | Lord also means one who sets affairs right: He cares for ascetics, suffices worshippers, and gives knowers His ancient care, leading some to contentment, others to longing, and others to readiness for meeting Him.
[QUSHAYRI:v1p10/r7] QUSHAYRI, d. 465 · author | holds | Al-Rahman and al-Rahim derive from mercy, an eternal attribute meaning the will of blessing; as emphatic forms they do not differ for those who verify spiritual realities.
[QUSHAYRI:v1p10/r8] QUSHAYRI, d. 465 · قيل | reports | An alternative view makes al-Rahman more emphatic and complete; only God is called al-Rahman absolutely, while al-Rahim can describe others.
[QUSHAYRI:v1p10/r9] QUSHAYRI, d. 465 · author | holds | The servant recognizes God as al-Rahman through His mercy; without that mercy no one would know Him by this name.
[QUSHAYRI:v1p11/r1] QUSHAYRI, d. 465 · author | reports | On the view that distinguishes the names, al-Rahman has a specific name but broad meaning, giving everyone outward comfort, while al-Rahim has a broad name but specific meaning, giving believers inward life.
[QUSHAYRI:v1p11/r2] QUSHAYRI, d. 465 · author | reports | The paired names are also read as outward refreshment from al-Rahman and inward illumination from al-Rahim.
[QUSHAYRI:v1p11/r3] QUSHAYRI, d. 465 · author | reports | Al-Rahman discloses His manifestation, while al-Rahim gently takes charge of the servant.
[QUSHAYRI:v1p11/r4] QUSHAYRI, d. 465 · author | reports | Al-Rahman grants faith, while al-Rahim bestows recognition; another pairing assigns recognition to al-Rahman and forgiveness to al-Rahim.
[QUSHAYRI:v1p11/r5] QUSHAYRI, d. 465 · author | reports | Further distinctions pair al-Rahman with granting forgiveness and al-Rahim with bestowing divine satisfaction, then pair them with veiling and the bliss of vision.
[QUSHAYRI:v1p11/r6] QUSHAYRI, d. 465 · author | reports | Al-Rahman enables spiritual practice, while al-Rahim brings realization; practice belongs to seekers and realized communion to those who have found.
[QUSHAYRI:v1p11/r7] QUSHAYRI, d. 465 · author | reports | Al-Rahman makes things for the servants through gracious care, and al-Rahim wards things off through gracious solicitude.
[QUSHAYRI:v1p9/r1] QUSHAYRI, d. 465 · author | holds | Hamd is praise of the praised one by naming noble attributes and beautiful acts; the definite article denotes the whole, so every praise, whether for attribute or act, belongs to God.
[QUSHAYRI:v1p9/r2] QUSHAYRI, d. 465 · author | holds | God is praised for the manifestation of His sovereignty and thanked for the abundance of His beneficence.
[QUSHAYRI:v1p9/r3] QUSHAYRI, d. 465 · author | holds | Praise is due to God's majesty and beauty, while thanks answer His abundant gifts and gracious favors.
[QUSHAYRI:v1p9/r4] QUSHAYRI, d. 465 · author | holds | God's self-praise is a perfection of His attributes and power; creatures praise Him for His beneficence, generosity, majesty, and beauty.
[QUSHAYRI:v1p9/r5] QUSHAYRI, d. 465 · author | holds | Qushayri enumerates God's eternal existence, generosity, oneness, everlastingness, hearing, sight, decree, speech, might, mercy, and beauty as aspects of His exalted perfection.
[QUSHAYRI:v1p9/r6] QUSHAYRI, d. 465 · author | holds | The passage expresses divine unity through paired identities: His being is His essence, eternity His endlessness, decree His destiny, majesty His beauty, and command and anger are inseparable from their counterparts.
[QUSHAYRI:v1p9/r7] QUSHAYRI, d. 465 · author | holds | Knowing that His friends long to praise Him but cannot do justice to His glory, God praises Himself in the Fatiha; hearing God's praise of Himself revives and honors their secrets.
[QUSHAYRI:v1p9/r8] QUSHAYRI, d. 465 · author | holds | On hearing God's self-praise, the Prophet recognized that restraint was fitting and said he could not enumerate God's praise, for God is as He praised Himself.
[QUSHAYRI:v1p9/r9] QUSHAYRI, d. 465 · author | holds | Those at one level praise God for gifts that benefit or avert harm, but recognize only a portion of His kindness and favors.

[WAHIDI-BASIT:v1p466/r1] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · author | reports | The opening fragment questions what thanks mean for a giver acting to obtain pleasure and answer compassion; its antecedent lies outside this segment.
[WAHIDI-BASIT:v1p466/r2] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · أبو بكر | reports | Abū Bakr suggests that God praises Himself at the start of Scripture to teach people praise and thanks, earning them greater reward through their recitation as a kindness to them.

[WAHIDI-BASIT:v1p466/r4] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · author | holds | Anyone who praises God thereby exposes himself to God's favor and reward.
[WAHIDI-BASIT:v1p466/r5] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · بعض العلماء | reports | Asked how the best-formula hadith counts as supplication, a scholar answers that praise itself suffices: a servant need not state requests after praising God, just as a creature may be won by praise.
[WAHIDI-BASIT:v1p466/r6] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · أبو بكر | holds | Ḥamd is broader than shukr: thanks follow a prior favor and do not praise someone's inherent good qualities, whereas praise can precede a gift and commend qualities.
[WAHIDI-BASIT:v1p466/r7] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · author | holds | A poet's indirect reference to praise as glorification and exaltation supports the breadth of ḥamd.
[WAHIDI-BASIT:v1p485/r1] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · author | holds | Rabb can derive from nurturing: al-Aṣmaʿī defines rabb al-ṣanīʿa as completing and improving a craft, and rabb al-skin as filling it with butter.
[WAHIDI-BASIT:v1p485/r10] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · author | rejects | The author rejects the theologians' proposed root as unattested to linguists: rabb does not mean remain, though arrabba can mean remain and could support their derivation.
[WAHIDI-BASIT:v1p485/r2] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · author | holds | Poetry about fat ripening in a skin and good deeds increasing supports the sense of completing and improving.
[WAHIDI-BASIT:v1p485/r3] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · author | holds | With the nurturing sense, God raises creatures and nourishes them through His blessings.
[WAHIDI-BASIT:v1p485/r4] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · author | holds | Rabb can also mean owner: a person who owns a thing, or stands above someone as a master.
[WAHIDI-BASIT:v1p485/r5] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · صفوان بن أمية | reports | Ṣafwān ibn Umayya uses rabb for a superior or master, preferring a Qurashī master to a Hawāzin one.
[WAHIDI-BASIT:v1p485/r6] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · author | holds | Anyone who owns something is its rabb; Arabic usage calls a person owner of a house or estate and includes the Prophet's question about owning camels or sheep.
[WAHIDI-BASIT:v1p485/r7] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · author | holds | The word rabb may mean master without literal ownership, as in 12:42 and al-Aʿshā's reference to the lord of Kindah; God is owner and master in truth. | mentions 12:42
[WAHIDI-BASIT:v1p485/r8] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · some linguists | reports | Some linguists derive the owner sense from nurturing: an owner raises and brings up what he owns, while a master is an owner.
[WAHIDI-BASIT:v1p485/r9] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · theologians | reports | Some theologians say rabb has eternally described God as an essential attribute and derive it as abiding, from rabb bi-al-makān, to remain in a place.
[WAHIDI-BASIT:v1p489/r1] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · author | holds | Al-ʿālamīn is the plural of ʿālam on the faʿil pattern, and its derivation has two reported explanations.
[WAHIDI-BASIT:v1p489/r10] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · أبو إسحاق | prefers | Abū Isḥāq chooses the all-creatures derivation and equates Lord of the worlds with Lord of everything in 6:164. | mentions 6:164
[WAHIDI-BASIT:v1p489/r2] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · author | reports | One derivation connects ʿālam with knowledge or signs: every creature is a sign pointing to its maker, and ordinary speech uses al-ʿālam to mean all created things.
[WAHIDI-BASIT:v1p489/r3] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · الحسن ومجاهد وقتادة | reports | Al-Ḥasan, Mujāhid, and Qatāda understand the worlds as all creatures, supported by Pharaoh's question and Moses' reply in 26:23–24. | mentions 26:23, 26:24
[WAHIDI-BASIT:v1p489/r4] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · ابن عباس | reports | In Saʿīd ibn Jubayr's transmission, Ibn ʿAbbās says that when ʿālamīn derives from knowledge it means rational beings, namely jinn and humans.
[WAHIDI-BASIT:v1p489/r5] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · أبو الهيثم والأزهري | reports | Abū al-Haytham and al-Azharī choose the jinn-and-human interpretation, since 25:1 calls the Qur'an a warning to the worlds and Muḥammad warned those two groups. | mentions 25:1
[WAHIDI-BASIT:v1p489/r6] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · الحسين بن الفضل وأبو معاذ | reports | Al-Ḥusayn ibn al-Faḍl and Abū Muʿādh say the worlds here are the children of Adam, citing 26:165. | mentions 26:165
[WAHIDI-BASIT:v1p489/r7] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · الفراء وأبو عبيدة | reports | Al-Farrāʾ and Abū ʿUbayda define ʿālamīn as rational beings in four communities: angels, humans, jinn, and devils; beasts are not called a world.
[WAHIDI-BASIT:v1p489/r8] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · author | holds | The word can denote the people of a single era: God's favoring the Children of Israel above the worlds in 2:47 means their contemporaries. | mentions 2:47
[WAHIDI-BASIT:v1p489/r9] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · author | holds | All rational-creature readings are compatible with the knowledge derivation; those who hold them say Moses answered Pharaoh with a clearer description to confound him, not with a lexical definition.

[JISHUMI:v1p205/r10] JISHUMI, d. 494 · author | holds | All reciters agree on kasra for the bāʾ in rabb.
[JISHUMI:v1p205/r11] JISHUMI, d. 494 · author | holds | Ḥamd, praise, and gratitude are near-synonyms, but praise may answer to blessing or other good, whereas gratitude is only for a blessing; their opposites are blame and ingratitude respectively.
[JISHUMI:v1p205/r12] JISHUMI, d. 494 · author | reports | Another gloss defines praise and gratitude as acknowledging a benefactor’s blessings while believing in His greatness; gratitude is primarily of the heart, and may be required verbally when denial is suspected.

[JISHUMI:v1p205/r14] JISHUMI, d. 494 · author | reports | Rabb can mean master, owner, or nurturer/reformer, from the idea of upbringing.
[JISHUMI:v1p205/r15] JISHUMI, d. 494 · ابن عباس وأبي علي | reports | Al-ʿālamīn may derive from knowledge, from a sign of its maker, or denote the rational kinds—angels, jinn, and humans—according to Ibn ʿAbbās and Abū ʿAlī.
[JISHUMI:v1p205/r16] JISHUMI, d. 494 · author | reports | Other explanations make al-ʿālamīn the people of each age or everything contained by the celestial sphere; it has no singular from the same word-form, like qawm and rahṭ.
[JISHUMI:v1p205/r7] JISHUMI, d. 494 · author | holds | The standard reading has ḥamd with a nominative dāl and li-llāh with kasra on lām; al-Ḥasan reads dāl with kasra, while Ibrāhīm b. Abī ʿAbla reads both letters with ḍamma by vowel-following.

[IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p10#2/r12] IBNJAWZI-ZAD, d. 597 · author | holds | Rabb has three uses: owner, one who sets something right, and an obeyed master; the last is illustrated by Joseph 12:41. | mentions 12:41
[IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p10#2/r13] IBNJAWZI-ZAD, d. 597 · الجمهور | reports | Most readers put rabb in the genitive; Abū al-Ghāliya, Ibn al-Sumayfa, and ʿĪsā ibn ʿUmar read it in the accusative; several others use nominative.
[IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p10#2/r14] IBNJAWZI-ZAD, d. 597 · أبو رزين العقيلي والربيع بن خيثم وأبو عمران الجوني | reports | These readers pronounce the bāʾ of rabb in the nominative.
[IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p10#2/r15] IBNJAWZI-ZAD, d. 597 · أهل العربية | reports | For Arab grammarians, ʿālamīn is the plural of ʿālam and names all created beings from beginning to end; people also call their present age a world.
[IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p10#2/r16] IBNJAWZI-ZAD, d. 597 · الحطيئة | reports | Al-Ḥuṭayʾa's line uses al-ʿālamīn for people of the present age, as evidence for that usage.
[IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p10#2/r17] IBNJAWZI-ZAD, d. 597 · أهل النظر | reports | The speculative theologians use ʿālam for the created cosmos as a whole: the celestial sphere, heavens, earth, and what lies between.
[IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p10#2/r2] IBNJAWZI-ZAD, d. 597 · الجمهور | reports | Most readers pronounce the lām of lillāh with kasra; Ibn ʿAbla uses ḍamma, a dialect of some Rabīʿa according to al-Farrāʾ.
[IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p10#2/r3] IBNJAWZI-ZAD, d. 597 · ابن السميفع | reports | Ibn al-Sumayfa reads al-ḥamda with fatḥa on dāl and kasra on lām.
[IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p10#2/r4] IBNJAWZI-ZAD, d. 597 · أبو نهيك | reports | Abū Nuhayk reads both dāl and lām in al-ḥamd lillāh with kasra.
[IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p10#2/r5] IBNJAWZI-ZAD, d. 597 · author | holds | Praise and gratitude overlap, but praise may be offered initially whereas gratitude is only in response to a blessing.
[IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p10#2/r6] IBNJAWZI-ZAD, d. 597 · قيل | reports | Another grammatical account takes the wording as a declarative form whose intended force is a command: say, “Praise belongs to God.”
[IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p10#2/r7] IBNJAWZI-ZAD, d. 597 · ابن قتيبة | reports | Ibn Qutayba defines praise as commending a person's inherent virtues, while gratitude is praise for a favor or kindness received.
[IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p10#2/r8] IBNJAWZI-ZAD, d. 597 · ابن قتيبة | reports | Ibn Qutayba notes that ḥamd can stand for shukr, as in praising someone for a kindness, just as one thanks him for courage.
[IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p10#2/r9] IBNJAWZI-ZAD, d. 597 · author | holds | Rabb means owner; for a created being the title is used only in a construct phrase such as owner of the house or servant.
[IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p12/r1] IBNJAWZI-ZAD, d. 597 · أهل النظر | reports | The derivation of ʿālam from ʿalāma, “sign,” supports the speculative theologians' view: the world is named as a sign pointing to its Creator.
[IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p12/r2] IBNJAWZI-ZAD, d. 597 · الضحاك عن ابن عباس | reports | One reported interpretation takes “the worlds” to mean all creation: heavens and earths, what they contain, and what lies between them.
[IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p12/r3] IBNJAWZI-ZAD, d. 597 · أبو صالح عن ابن عباس | reports | Another report interprets the worlds as every living creature that moves on the surface of the earth.
[IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p12/r4] IBNJAWZI-ZAD, d. 597 · ابن عباس ومجاهد ومقاتل | reports | A third interpretation identifies the worlds as jinn and humans; it is reported from Ibn ʿAbbās and held by Mujāhid and Muqātil.
[IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p12/r5] IBNJAWZI-ZAD, d. 597 · ابن عباس، واختاره ابن قتيبة | reports | A fourth view includes jinn, humans, and angels; it is also transmitted from Ibn ʿAbbās and chosen by Ibn Qutayba.
[IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p12/r6] IBNJAWZI-ZAD, d. 597 · ابن عباس | reports | A fifth interpretation, also transmitted from Ibn ʿAbbās, says the worlds here are the angels.
[RAZI:1:1/r1] RAZI, d. 606 · author | holds | Razi sketches the sūra’s sequence: seek refuge from sins, begin good works in God’s name, praise and recognize his lordship and mercy, heed judgment, worship and seek help, ask guidance, and avoid ignorance and error.
[RAZI:1:2/r1] RAZI, d. 606 · author | holds | Praise is praise for a blessing, and praise for a blessing requires knowing it; God’s blessings cannot be counted, as the Qur’an says. | mentions 14:34, 16:18
[RAZI:1:2/r10] RAZI, d. 606 · author | holds | One cannot know God as Lord of the worlds without first understanding what “Lord” and “the worlds” mean.
[RAZI:1:2/r11] RAZI, d. 606 · author | holds | The worlds comprise every existent other than God: spatial bodies, incorporeal entities, and attributes; bodies divide into simple entities and composites.
[RAZI:1:2/r12] RAZI, d. 606 · author | holds | Razi lists spheres, stars and elemental “mothers” among simple bodies, and the three generated kinds—minerals, plants and animals—among composites.
[RAZI:1:2/r13] RAZI, d. 606 · author | holds | Razi says there is no proof that bodies are limited to the familiar cosmic categories: since an infinite void lies beyond the world and God can do all possible things, He can create countless external worlds, each larger than this one and containing analogous heavens, earths and celestial bodies.
[RAZI:1:2/r14] RAZI, d. 606 · author | rejects | Razi rejects philosophers’ arguments that there is only one world as weak and based on unsound premises; he cites Abū al-ʿAlāʾ al-Maʿarrī’s verses about God’s many heavens and the smallness of our past and future.
[RAZI:1:2/r15] RAZI, d. 606 · author | holds | Even a lifetime devoted to mineral wonders, plants’ flowers and fruits, or the varieties of beasts, wild animals, birds and insects would not reach the depths of these topics.
[RAZI:1:2/r16] RAZI, d. 606 · author | holds | Razi links the inexhaustibility of created wonders and divine wisdom to the Qur’anic image of earthly trees as pens and seas as ink, which would not exhaust God’s words. | mentions 31:27
[RAZI:1:2/r2] RAZI, d. 606 · author | holds | A rational person should examine the self, composed of soul and body; the body is the less excellent and less beneficial of the two parts.
[RAZI:1:2/r3] RAZI, d. 606 · author | holds | Anatomists have identified nearly five thousand benefits and interests that God wisely arranged in the creation of the human body.
[RAZI:1:2/r4] RAZI, d. 606 · author | holds | Known bodily benefits are only a drop in the ocean of the unknown; understanding divine wisdom in creating the human being involves ten thousand questions or more.
[RAZI:1:2/r5] RAZI, d. 606 · author | holds | Adding the wisdom evident in the Throne, Footstool, heavens, fixed and moving stars, and the varied measures and colors of created things expands the inquiry to roughly a million questions.
[RAZI:1:2/r6] RAZI, d. 606 · author | holds | The same inquiry includes the wisdom in minerals, plants, animals, their kinds and states; God has made most of creation serve human benefit. | mentions 45:13
[RAZI:1:2/r7] RAZI, d. 606 · author | holds | Razi links the statement that God subjected what is in the heavens and earth for people to the vast created benefits contained in praise. | mentions 45:13
[RAZI:1:2/r8] RAZI, d. 606 · author | holds | Because all these innumerable blessings and their wisdom fall under praise to God, the phrase “Praise belongs to God” encompasses about a million questions, more or less.
[RAZI:1:2/r9] RAZI, d. 606 · author | holds | “Lord” is in a genitive construction with “the worlds” as its genitive complement; understanding this relation requires knowing both terms.
[RAZI-FULL:v1p144/r1] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | Many names indicate the honor of the named; Fātiḥat al-Kitāb is so called because it opens codices, teaching, recitation, and prayer, or because praise opens speech, or because it was the first sura sent down.
[RAZI-FULL:v1p144/r2] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | It is called Sūrat al-Ḥamd because its opening word is praise.
[RAZI-FULL:v1p144/r3] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | It is called the Mother of the Qur’an because its verses encompass the Qur’an’s four central aims: theology, resurrection, prophethood, and divine decree.
[RAZI-FULL:v1p144/r4] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | A second reason for calling it the Mother of the Book is that all revelation comprises praise, worshipful service, and requests for unveiling; the sura includes each in that order.
[RAZI-FULL:v1p144/r5] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | A third reason is that all knowledge concerns either divine lordship or human servitude: the opening praises God’s mastery, while the remainder shows the servant’s dependence on His aid and guidance.
[RAZI-FULL:v1p144/r6] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | A fourth reason is that the sura gathers theology, religious duties, and spiritual purification: praise and lordship establish divine existence and attributes, worship presents duties, and

[RAZI-FULL:v1p144/r7] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | In the mystical reading, guidance brings light to the heart, the blessed become polished mirrors reflecting sanctity, and the final plea seeks protection from desire and doubt.
[RAZI-FULL:v1p149/r1] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | The phrase al-ḥamdu lillāh raises questions about God’s existence and right to praise; Rabb al-ʿālamīn answers the first, while al-Raḥmān, al-Raḥīm, and Mālik yawm al-dīn answer the second.
[RAZI-FULL:v1p149/r2] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | Knowledge of God’s existence is theoretical, not immediate; the world of heavens, earth, seas, minerals, plants, and animals needs a governing, originating, nurturing, and sustaining cause.
[RAZI-FULL:v1p149/r3] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | Al-ʿālamīn includes everything besides God, which depends on Him for existence and continuance; every indivisible particle and individual accident proves the wise, powerful God. | mentions 17:44
[RAZI-FULL:v1p149/r4] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | Rāzī prefers Rabb al-ʿālamīn to Creator of the worlds because sustaining creatures after their beginning is disputed, and the phrase stresses their dependence on God at every moment.
[RAZI-FULL:v1p15/r2] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | Praise is due to the one who possesses everything in the heavens.
[RAZI-FULL:v1p150#2/r1] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | Razi reads Lord of the worlds as an argument for the ancient God's existence; the created lights, darkness, and angels are kinds within that all-encompassing world-order. | mentions 6:1, 35:1
[RAZI-FULL:v1p150#2/r2] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | Because worlds include everything besides God, including space and time, their Lord created them and existed before them; this proves His transcendence beyond place, direction, and spatial extension.
[RAZI-FULL:v1p150#2/r3] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | The same lordship excludes indwelling: the creator precedes every created locus and therefore never depends on a place, against Christians and adherents of indwelling.
[RAZI-FULL:v1p150#2/r4] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | Deserving praise shows God acts by choice, not by necessity: fire and ice are not praised for natural effects, while changing effects prove a voluntary, powerful agent.
[RAZI-FULL:v1p150/r1] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | As the Mother of the Qur’an, the Fātiḥa is the source from which other suras branch; every being besides God is evidence of His divinity.
[RAZI-FULL:v1p150/r2] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | Al-Anʿām’s praise for creating the heavens, earth, darkness, and light is one subset of Rabb al-ʿālamīn; dependence on God for preservation entails dependence for origination. | mentions 6:1
[RAZI-FULL:v1p150/r3] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | Al-Kahf’s praise for the revealed Book concerns spiritual nurture through knowledge and unveiling, one kind of the Fātiḥa’s universal nurturing. | mentions 18:1
[RAZI-FULL:v1p150/r4] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | Saba’s statement that everything in the heavens and earth belongs to God is another subset within the universal lordship named in the Fātiḥa. | mentions 34:1
[RAZI-FULL:v1p150/r5] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | Fāṭir describes bringing the heavens and earth into existence, distinct from creation as determination yet also included within Rabb al-ʿālamīn. | mentions 35:1
[RAZI-FULL:v1p151/r1] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | The world's evident order and its fitness for human interests show that its maker knows; praise thus implies God's existence, transcendence from place and indwelling, and utmost power, knowledge, and wisdom.
[RAZI-FULL:v1p151/r3] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | The sequence Lord of the worlds, Merciful, Compassionate, Master of Judgment is, in Razi's view, a rationally unsurpassable ordering of God's attributes.
[RAZI-FULL:v1p153#2/r1] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | All worlds share the contingency, need, and change that make a person depend on God; their common cause of need establishes God's lordship over every creature and heaven.
[RAZI-FULL:v1p153#2/r2] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | The one able to create the immense worlds, Throne, heavens, and stars can destroy them and is independent of them.
[RAZI-FULL:v1p153/r1] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | Although the world contains evil, good predominates: health over illness, satiety over hunger, and ease and joy over painful states.
[RAZI-FULL:v1p153/r2] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | Changing states arise after nonexistence and therefore point to a capable creator; a necessary-by-nature cause would produce effects eternally without change.
[RAZI-FULL:v1p153/r3] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | Since beneficial ease and safety predominate, the agent is merciful and beneficent and deserves praise; these familiar facts make the reason for praising God apparent to every rational person.
[RAZI-FULL:v1p154/r3] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | Because worldly benefits and protection from harm usually require visible causes, people love those causes, and repeated action and imitation make this attachment deeply rooted.
[RAZI-FULL:v1p154/r4] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | Razi frames the needed reflection as asking whether a ruler's worldly sovereignty came from his own strength and wisdom.
[RAZI-FULL:v1p155/r1] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | A ruler may be weak and unintelligent, so his authority comes from the allotment of a wise determiner, not his own strength or wisdom.
[RAZI-FULL:v1p155/r2] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | Recognizing the true cause detaches the heart from apparent means: every benefit comes from God and every harm is attributed to Him, so praise and requests belong to God alone.
[RAZI-FULL:v1p155/r3] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | Reflection scales from the small world to the greater one: no condition in either world is ordered except by God's decree.
[RAZI-FULL:v1p156/r1] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | Most scholars require recitation in prayer, while al-Asamm and al-Hasan b. Salih deny that recitation is obligatory.
[RAZI-FULL:v1p156/r2] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | The command to perform the dawn recitation in Quran 17:78 is a command to read and therefore makes recitation obligatory. | mentions 17:78
[RAZI-FULL:v1p156/r3] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · أبو الدرداء عن النبي | reports | A man asked the Prophet whether prayer includes recitation; when the man concluded that it was obligatory, the Prophet approved him.
[RAZI-FULL:v1p156/r4] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · ابن مسعود عن النبي | reports | In another report, the Prophet answers a question about reciting in prayer by asking whether there can be prayer without recitation.
[RAZI-FULL:v1p156/r5] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · الأصم | reports | Al-Asamm argues that the Prophet described prayer as things seen, whereas recitation is not visible and must therefore fall outside prayer; Razi answers that seeing with two objects means knowing.
[RAZI-FULL:v1p156/r6] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | Al-Shafi'i and most scholars require al-Fatiha itself; omitting even one letter knowingly invalidates prayer, whereas Abu Hanifa says it is not required.
[RAZI-FULL:v1p156/r7] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | The Prophet's lifelong practice of reciting al-Fatiha obligates imitation, supported by Quranic commands to follow him. | mentions 7:158, 24:63, 3:31
[RAZI-FULL:v1p156/r8] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | Razi charges Abu Hanifa with inconsistency for requiring forehead wiping from one report while denying al-Fatiha's requirement despite its mass-transmitted practice.
[RAZI-FULL:v1p157#2/r1] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | The prayer's two halves arise through the verses of al-Fatiha; since prayer entails this division and it entails this surah, al-Fatiha is necessary for valid prayer.
[RAZI-FULL:v1p157#2/r2] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | Against the objection that the negation in no prayer except with al-Fatiha must mean incompleteness rather than invalidity, Razi cites a version explicitly denying prayer's occurrence for one who omits it.
[RAZI-FULL:v1p157#2/r3] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | If al-Fatiha is a constituent of prayer, omitting it means the prayer's very essence does not exist, so the hadith's negation can remain literal.
[RAZI-FULL:v1p157#2/r4] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | prefers | If the hadith must be figurative, invalidity is nearer than mere incompleteness because a nonexistent act resembles an invalid act more than a valid but imperfect one; presumption, prohibition, and caution reinforce this reading.
[RAZI-FULL:v1p157/r1] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | Because the established form of the Prophet's prayer included al-Fatiha, the command to establish prayer requires it; the command recurs over a hundred times in the Quran. | mentions 2:43
[RAZI-FULL:v1p157/r2] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | The rightly guided caliphs consistently recited al-Fatiha; reports in both Sahihs say the Prophet, Abu Bakr, and Umar began recitation with al-Hamd, so their practice should be followed.
[RAZI-FULL:v1p157/r3] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | Razi criticizes Abu Hanifa for relying on Uthman's report in the fugitive-divorce issue despite contrary Companions and Quran, but not following all Companions' practice on al-Fatiha.
[RAZI-FULL:v1p157/r4] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | Muslims everywhere recite al-Fatiha in prayer; even if some regard it as recommended rather than obligatory, abandoning the unanimous practice leaves the believers' path and incurs Quran 4:115's warning. | mentions 4:115
[RAZI-FULL:v1p158#2/r1] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | The Prophet identifies al-Fatiha as a surah unmatched in the Torah, Gospel, or Psalms; the Companions' answer about what they recite in prayer indicates a known universal practice.

r2] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | Razi argues that Quran 73:20 requires al-Fatiha: the options are al-Fatiha, another surah, or a choice; the latter two fail because another is not universally required and al-Fatiha is agreed better and more complete. | mentions 73:20
[RAZI-FULL:v1p158#2/r3] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | Al-Fatiha is the recitation made accessible to all because every Muslim has it memorized, whereas other surahs may not be memorized by each person.
[RAZI-FULL:v1p158#2/r4] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | The original duty to pray remains until evidence shows discharge; al-Fatiha is superior and makes prayer more complete, so omitting it does not establish discharge.
[RAZI-FULL:v1p158/r1] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · أبو هريرة عن النبي | reports | The Prophet says a prayer without al-Fatiha is deficient and incomplete; Razi argues that a deficient performance does not discharge the continuing obligation.
[RAZI-FULL:v1p158/r2] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | Razi compares Abu Hanifa's ruling that an Eid fast cannot make up Ramadan because it is incomplete and asks why the same reasoning does not invalidate prayer without al-Fatiha.
[RAZI-FULL:v1p158/r3] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · ابن المنذر عن أبي هريرة عن النبي | reports | Ibn al-Mundhir transmits from Abu Huraira that the Prophet said a prayer without al-Fatiha does not suffice.
[RAZI-FULL:v1p158/r4] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · رفاعة بن مالك عن النبي | reports | A man who asks the Prophet to teach him prayer is told to face the qibla, say takbir, and recite al-Fatiha; Razi treats this imperative as obligation and recitation as part of prayer.
[RAZI-FULL:v1p159/r1] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | Although belief in obligation may itself leave theoretical doubt, actual recitation creates no danger while omission creates fear of failing the duty; therefore action is the safer course.
[RAZI-FULL:v1p159/r2] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | If prayers with and without al-Fatiha were both valid, habitual recitation would make other surahs abandoned; because the community agrees al-Fatiha is preferable, Razi concludes omission is invalid.
[RAZI-FULL:v1p159/r3] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | Just as bowing and prostration cannot be replaced, al-Fatiha cannot be replaced by another reading, with caution as the common rationale.
[RAZI-FULL:v1p159/r4] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | The duty to pray persists; neither Quran 73:20 nor analogy proves discharge without al-Fatiha, and ritual worship is a domain where analogy should be set aside. | mentions 73:20
[RAZI-FULL:v1p159/r5] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | Since the Prophet recited al-Fatiha throughout his life, replacing it with another recitation is innovation and abandonment of the required prophetic example.
[RAZI-FULL:v1p159/r6] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | Prayer without al-Fatiha loses an agreed extra virtue without compensation, which Razi regards as improper and therefore impermissible.
[RAZI-FULL:v1p160/r1] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · أبو هريرة عن النبي | reports | Abu Huraira reports that the Prophet ordered him to announce that there is no prayer without recitation, even if by al-Fatiha.
[RAZI-FULL:v1p160/r2] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | Razi answers Quran 73:20 by the same three options: al-Fatiha itself, another passage, or a choice; the latter two fail, and al-Fatiha is accessible to all. | mentions 73:20
[RAZI-FULL:v1p160/r3] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | prefers | Razi counters the opposing report with Abu Huraira's version no prayer except by al-Fatiha; if reports conflict, the stronger and safer view is his.
[RAZI-FULL:v1p160/r4] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | reports | Razi reports disagreement over the minimum recitation for Hanafis: Abu Hanifa accepts one verse, even isolated letters, while Abu Yusuf and Muhammad require three short verses or one long verse.
[RAZI-FULL:v1p161/r2] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · أم سلمة عن النبي | reports | Umm Salama reports that the Prophet recited al-Fatiha while counting the basmala as its first verse, followed by the rest of its verses.
[RAZI-FULL:v1p162/r2] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · أبو هريرة عن النبي | reports | In the divided-prayer report, God calls the basmala glorification, al-Hamd praise, the two mercy names extolling, the Master of Judgment entrustment, and the remaining response a sharing and a request granted.
[RAZI-FULL:v1p17/r10] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | Al-Rāzī says there is no proof that only the familiar kinds of bodies exist: an infinite void lies beyond this world, and God can create innumerable greater worlds containing counterparts of its cosmic features; philosophers’ arguments for one world rely on weak premises.
[RAZI-FULL:v1p17/r5] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | Praise is praise for blessing, and praising a blessing presupposes knowing it; God’s blessings cannot be counted, as the cited verse says. | mentions 14:34
[RAZI-FULL:v1p17/r6] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | Al-Rāzī illustrates the scale of the inquiry through the human body: anatomists found nearly five thousand benefits, and known examples are only a drop beside the unknown; understanding divine wisdom in human creation entails ten thousand or more questions.
[RAZI-FULL:v1p17/r7] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | Considering divine wisdom in the throne, heavens, luminaries, elements, minerals, plants, and animals adds vast further questions; most of creation is made for human benefit, and al-hamd lillah thus encompasses roughly a million issues. | mentions 45:13
[RAZI-FULL:v1p17/r8] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | The construction rabb al-ʿālamīn is an iḍāfa, whose relation cannot be known without first knowing both correlated terms.
[RAZI-FULL:v1p17/r9] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | Al-ʿālamīn means every existent other than God; these beings comprise extended bodies, separate entities, and attributes, with bodies divided into simple and composite kinds.
[RAZI-FULL:v1p178#2/r1] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | Madḥ is broader than hamd: one may praise a living or inanimate thing such as a pearl, but cannot give it hamd.
[RAZI-FULL:v1p178#2/r2] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | Madḥ can precede or follow a benefaction, whereas hamd is only after beneficence.
[RAZI-FULL:v1p178#2/r3] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | Madḥ can be condemned, as in the warning to throw dust in flatterers’ faces, whereas hamd is generally commanded.
[RAZI-FULL:v1p178#3/r1] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | Madḥ denotes a general kind of excellence, while hamd denotes the specific virtue of benefaction; this completes the distinction that madḥ is broader.
[RAZI-FULL:v1p178#3/r2] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | Hamd applies whether a benefaction reaches the speaker or someone else, while shukr is limited to a benefit received by the thankful person.
[RAZI-FULL:v1p178#3/r3] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | Saying al-hamdu lillah rather than al-madhu lillah acknowledges God as a freely choosing agent, not a necessary emanation as philosophers claim.
[RAZI-FULL:v1p178#3/r4] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | Al-hamdu lillah is better than ash-shukru lillah because it praises God for every benefit to the worlds, even one not received by the speaker; shukr is personal gratitude.
[RAZI-FULL:v1p178#3/r5] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · المخالف | reports | One reported distinction says hamd thanks God for warding off calamity, while shukr thanks Him for gifts; an objection asks why the lesser benefit is named first.
[RAZI-FULL:v1p178#3/r6] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | Razi offers three answers: thanking for the lesser implies gratitude for the greater; warded-off harm is unbounded while gifts are finite; and preventing harm matters more than adding benefit.
[RAZI-FULL:v1p178#3/r7] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | The formula says al-hamdu lillah rather than ahmadu Allah so it declares God worthy of praise before any creature praises Him, from eternity to eternity.
[RAZI-FULL:v1p178#3/r8] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | Al-hamdu lillah also means praise and thanks are God’s due and property, because His abundant favors make Him inherently deserving of them.
[RAZI-FULL:v1p179/r1] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | prefers | The declarative al-ḥamdu lillāh is preferable to ahmadu Allāh: it establishes praise as God’s right instead of reporting one speaker’s act.
[RAZI-FULL:v1p179/r2] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | The lām in lillāh can signify fitting اختصاص, ownership, or power and dominion; each makes all praise belong to God.
[RAZI-FULL:v1p179/r3] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | Al-ḥamdu lillāh has eight letters corresponding to Paradise’s eight gates; saying it with a pure heart merits those gates.
[RAZI-FULL:v1p179/r4] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | reports | One grammatical view makes definite al-ḥamd refer to a prior known instance, or otherwise to all praise to avoid ambiguity.
[RAZI-FULL:v1p179/r5] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | reports | A second grammatical view says the definite noun denotes only the essence or nature of praise, not universal scope.
[RAZI-FULL:v1p179/r6] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | On either grammatical analysis, the phrase denies that anyone besides God is independently entitled to praise.
[RAZI-FULL:v1p180/r1] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · Prophet | reports | The Prophet is cited as saying that whoever does not thank people does not thank God; al-Rāzī answers that God is the true source of every human benefit.
[RAZI-FULL:v1p180/r10] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | Because full gratitude is beyond human capacity, the verse states that all praise belongs to God rather than commanding people to praise Him.
[RAZI-FULL:v1p180/r2] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | A human benefactor acts only because God creates the motive, the blessing, and the recipient’s capacity to benefit, so God is the true benefactor.
[RAZI-FULL:v1p180/r3] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | A giver who seeks

 reward, praise, repayment, or release from stinginess seeks compensation and is not the true benefactor; God gives from intrinsic fullness.
[RAZI-FULL:v1p180/r4] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | Every blessing is a possible existent brought into being by God, directly or through means; therefore praise for blessing belongs to God. | mentions 16:53
