[RAZI-FULL:v1p180/r8] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | Human conceptions of perfection never reach God’s greater perfection, so people cannot praise Him as He deserves.
[RAZI-FULL:v1p180/r9] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · الواسطي | reports | Al-Wāsiṭī calls gratitude shirk when a person imagines that his thanks can equal God’s blessings.
[RAZI-FULL:v1p182#2/r1] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | The report’s expanded wording contrasts one immeasurable blessing with the servant’s boundless thanks in saying al-ḥamdu lillāh.
[RAZI-FULL:v1p182#2/r2] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | Worldly blessings are finite, but the praise phrase is infinite; what remains after accounting for a finite blessing is endless, warranting eternal reward.
[RAZI-FULL:v1p182#2/r3] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | Existence is better than nonexistence, and every possible existent receives its existence from God; hence every creature receives His blessing and mercy.
[RAZI-FULL:v1p182#2/r4] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | Praise precedes tasbīḥ because it includes transcendence and adds God’s beneficence, making Him beyond mere completeness.
[RAZI-FULL:v1p182#2/r5] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | Rationally, beneficence requires knowing every need, power to meet it, and freedom from need; divine beneficence therefore presupposes perfection without deficiency.
[RAZI-FULL:v1p182/r1] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · داود | reports | David asks how he can thank God when even the ability to thank depends on God’s gift; God says recognizing that incapacity is gratitude according to one’s capacity.
[RAZI-FULL:v1p182/r2] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · Prophet | reports | A report says that when a blessed servant says al-ḥamdu lillāh, God tells the angels that the servant returned something priceless for an unvalued gift.
[RAZI-FULL:v1p182/r3] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | Al-ḥamdu lillāh encompasses every praise uttered or possible from all creatures, prophets, angels, saints, scholars, and future inhabitants of Paradise. | mentions 10:10
[RAZI-FULL:v1p183#2/r1] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | reports | A report says Adam’s first words were al-ḥamdu lillāh after he sneezed; the people of Paradise end with the same praise, so the world begins and ends with it. | mentions 10:10
[RAZI-FULL:v1p183#2/r2] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | rejects | Al-Rāzī rejects supplying an unspoken command ‘say’: the phrase is already a complete assertion that praise belongs to God.
[RAZI-FULL:v1p183#2/r3] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | The assertion makes God intrinsically deserving of praise through His essence and acts, whether people praise Him or not; what is essential exceeds what depends on another.
[RAZI-FULL:v1p183#2/r4] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | Stating that praise is due, rather than directly commanding it, lets the obedient praise God while leaving the disobedient with a lesser offense than rejecting an order.
[RAZI-FULL:v1p183#2/r5] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | reports | The Jabriyya argue that if humans created faith, the human would deserve more praise for this noblest act than God; therefore God creates faith.
[RAZI-FULL:v1p183#2/r6] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | reports | The Jabriyya argue that Muslims praise God for the blessing of faith; if faith were a human act, praising God for it would wrongly credit Him with another’s act. | mentions 3:188
[RAZI-FULL:v1p183/r1] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | Praise thanks God for past blessings and brings future increase, as promised in the Qur’an; it closes barriers and opens the way to knowledge of God, hence the name al-Fātiḥa. | mentions 14:7
[RAZI-FULL:v1p183/r2] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · السري السقطي | reports | Al-Sarī al-Saqaṭī spent thirty years seeking forgiveness for thanking God that his shop survived Baghdad’s fire while others’ homes and shops burned, since his happiness showed disregard for others.
[RAZI-FULL:v1p183/r3] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | The phrase should be reserved for the best blessings: religious benefits outrank worldly ones, inner acts outrank bodily acts, and seeing a worldly benefit as the giver’s gift is nobler than treating it merely as a benefit.
[RAZI-FULL:v1p184/r1] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | reports | The Jabriyya argue that obligatory acts only avert blame and cannot earn praise, while voluntary grace would make God gain praise and thus be perfected by another.
[RAZI-FULL:v1p184/r2] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | reports | They further argue that if God is praised intrinsically, no act causes that entitlement, so no duty, compensation, or reward is owed; if it is not intrinsic, God would depend on another.
[RAZI-FULL:v1p184/r3] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · الجبرية | reports | The Jabriyya infer that faith too comes from God: all praise belongs to Him, praise follows blessing, and faith is the greatest blessing.
[RAZI-FULL:v1p184/r4] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · الجبرية | reports | They argue that God’s self-praise, though blameworthy among people, shows divine acts cannot be judged by human standards and challenges Muʿtazilī principles.
[RAZI-FULL:v1p185/r1] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · المعتزلة | reports | The Muʿtazila say absolute praise is deserved by one whose acts contain no evil, rulings no injustice, and judgments no oppression; they reject the Jabriyya picture of God creating disbelief then punishing it.
[RAZI-FULL:v1p185/r2] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · المعتزلة | reports | They argue that if a servant deserves God’s praise, the servant must be capable of action, contrary to determinism; if God praises Himself, that is also invalid, so the phrase only works on their doctrine.
[RAZI-FULL:v1p185/r3] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | reports | Scholars disagree whether gratitude is owed by reason or only by revealed law; the latter cite the rule that punishment awaits a messenger and the removal of excuses by messengers. | mentions 17:15, 4:165
[RAZI-FULL:v1p185/r4] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | prefers | Al-Rāzī argues that gratitude is due at all times, even before revelation: the verse makes praise God’s right without qualification and grounds it in His nurturing and mercy.
[RAZI-FULL:v1p185/r5] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | True praise is any act expressing reverence for a benefactor: inward belief in perfection, spoken words of praise, or bodily deeds that express it; saying al-ḥamdu lillāh merely reports praise.
[RAZI-FULL:v1p185/r6] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | reports | One group says God cannot command praise: if it repays a blessing, the command makes generosity transactional; if not, it is needless toil imposed on another.
[RAZI-FULL:v1p185/r7] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | reports | The same group says praise is useless to a God complete in Himself and that punishing people eternally for omitting a useless act would not befit the generous Lord.
[RAZI-FULL:v1p185/r8] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | reports | A second group calls praise bad manners: the tiny thanks cannot match immeasurable blessings, recalling blessings distracts from knowing the giver, and praise for benefits seems self-interested.
[RAZI-FULL:v1p186/r1] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | Only God is necessary in Himself; everything else is possible and is called the world because its existence points to God.
[RAZI-FULL:v1p186/r2] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | Possible existents divide into spatial bodies, attributes of bodies, and things neither; bodies include celestial spheres and scriptural entities, earthly elements and composites, while attributes comprise about forty genera.
[RAZI-FULL:v1p186/r3] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | The third class is spirits: lower spirits include good jinn and evil demons; higher ones are attached to celestial bodies or are holy, disembodied spirits.
[RAZI-FULL:v1p186/r4] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | Since possible beings need God to bring them into existence and preserve them, He is their deity as creator and their Lord as sustainer.
[RAZI-FULL:v1p186/r5] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | Created nurturers seek their own profit, such as reward or praise, while God nurtures for the creatures’ benefit rather than His own.

[RAZI-FULL:v1p187/r3] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | Unlike human benefaction, God’s care never ends and reaches everyone. | mentions 7:156

[RAZI-FULL:v1p214#2/r5] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | The seven Fatiha verses remove seven vices: praise dispels desire, Lord of the worlds greed, Judgment Day anger, worship and aid pride and vanity, guidance caprice, the favored path unbelief and doubt, and the final phrase innovation.

[RAZI-FULL:v1p217/r1] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · الله تعالى | reports | In a divine report transmitted by the Prophet, God responds to each Fatiha phrase: the opening remembers Him, praise praises Him, the mercy names magnify Him, Judgment Day glorifies Him or is entrusted to Him, worship belongs to Him, aid relies on Him, and guidance is the servant's request.

[QURTUBI:1:2/r17] QURTUBI, d. 671 · author | holds | The cited verse uses the word aḥmadī as a plural of ḥamd, supporting the linguistic discussion of the word’s forms.
[QURTUBI:1:2/r18] QURTUBI, d. 671 · author | holds | Ḥamd is the opposite of blame; ḥamīd and maḥmūd describe one praised, and taḥmīd is more emphatic than ḥamd.
[QURTUBI:1:2/r19] QURTUBI, d. 671 · author | holds | The poet’s use of muḥammad for a person rich in praiseworthy qualities explains the name Muhammad; another verse says the Throne’s Lord is Maḥmūd and the Prophet is Muhammad.
[QURTUBI:1:2/r2] QURTUBI, d. 671 · رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم | reports | Anas reports that God is pleased when a servant eats or drinks and praises Him for it; Qurtubi cites this from Muslim.
[QURTUBI:1:2/r20] QURTUBI, d. 671 · author | holds | Maḥmada means the opposite of blame; aḥmada can mean one’s affairs turned praiseworthy or that one found a place pleasing, while a ḥamada is someone who overpraises things and ḥamadat al-nār is the sound of its flames.
[QURTUBI:1:2/r21] QURTUBI, d. 671 · الطبري والمبرد | reports | Al-Ṭabarī and al-Mubarrad hold that ḥamd and shukr have the same meaning; Qurtubi says this view is not sound.
[QURTUBI:1:2/r22] QURTUBI, d. 671 · ابن عطاء | reports | Al-Sulami transmits from Jaʿfar al-Ṣādiq and Ibn ʿAṭāʾ the synonymy view; Ibn ʿAṭāʾ explains praise as gratitude for God enabling people to learn and praise Him.
[QURTUBI:1:2/r23] QURTUBI, d. 671 · الطبري | reports | Al-Ṭabarī argues the terms are synonymous because Arabic permits the phrase al-ḥamdu lillāhi shukran, praise to God in gratitude.
[QURTUBI:1:2/r24] QURTUBI, d. 671 · ابن عطية | reports | Ibn ʿAṭiyya counters that adding shukran narrows the praise to gratitude for a particular blessing, which shows the words are not identical.
[QURTUBI:1:2/r25] QURTUBI, d. 671 · بعض العلماء | reports | Some scholars say gratitude is broader because it can be expressed by tongue, limbs, and heart, while praise is verbal alone.
[QURTUBI:1:2/r26] QURTUBI, d. 671 · بعض العلماء | reports | Another view makes praise broader because it includes both gratitude and commendation, can stand in place of gratitude, and is not itself replaced by gratitude.
[QURTUBI:1:2/r27] QURTUBI, d. 671 · ابن عباس | reports | Ibn ʿAbbās calls praise the word of every grateful person and illustrates its use by Adam, Noah, Abraham, David and Solomon, Muhammad, and the people of Paradise. | mentions 23:28, 14:39, 27:15, 17:111, 35:34, 10:10
[QURTUBI:1:2/r28] QURTUBI, d. 671 · author | prefers | Qurtubi’s preferred distinction is that praise commends attributes without requiring prior kindness, whereas gratitude praises a benefactor for a favor; praise is broader because it includes commendation as well as thanks.
[QURTUBI:1:2/r29] QURTUBI, d. 671 · author | holds | Ḥamd can also mean satisfaction: one says I tested him and praised him to mean I was pleased with him; Qurtubi links this usage to maqāman maḥmūdan and a prophetic phrase about approving washing the urethra. | mentions 17:79
[QURTUBI:1:2/r3] QURTUBI, d. 671 · الحسن | reports | Al-Hasan says that no blessing exists for which praise of God is not better than the blessing itself.
[QURTUBI:1:2/r30] QURTUBI, d. 671 · جعفر الصادق | reports | Jaʿfar al-Ṣādiq gives a symbolic reading of the letters: ḥāʾ signifies unity, mīm dominion, and dāl permanence; knowing these is knowing God.
[QURTUBI:1:2/r31] QURTUBI, d. 671 · شقيق بن إبراهيم | reports | Shafīq ibn Ibrāhīm says gratitude has three conditions: recognizing the giver, being content with what was given, and not disobeying God while one retains strength.
[QURTUBI:1:2/r32] QURTUBI, d. 671 · author | holds | God praises Himself and opens His Book with praise, while people are forbidden to claim purity for themselves; Qurtubi cites the command not to praise yourselves and the report to throw dust in flatterers’ faces. | mentions 53:32
[QURTUBI:1:2/r33] QURTUBI, d. 671 · author | holds | God’s self-praise precedes any creature’s praise and is without cause, while created praise is mixed with ulterior causes.
[QURTUBI:1:2/r34] QURTUBI, d. 671 · علماؤنا | reports | Qurtubi’s scholars say an imperfect creature should not praise himself to attract benefits or repel harm.
[QURTUBI:1:2/r35] QURTUBI, d. 671 · قيل | reports | One explanation says God praised Himself eternally because His servants cannot fulfill the duty of praising Him; even the Messenger declared that he could not enumerate praise to God.
[QURTUBI:1:2/r36] QURTUBI, d. 671 · النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم | reports | The Prophet’s confession that he cannot enumerate praise to God illustrates the limits of human praise.
[QURTUBI:1:2/r37] QURTUBI, d. 671 · author | reports | A poet says that when people praise God rightly, He is as they praise Him and greater than their praise can express.
[QURTUBI:1:2/r38] QURTUBI, d. 671 · قيل | reports | Another explanation says God praised Himself eternally because He knew His blessings would overwhelm servants’ ability to repay them, thereby easing the burden of indebtedness and making the blessing more enjoyable.
[QURTUBI:1:2/r39] QURTUBI, d. 671 · سفيان بن عيينة ورؤبة بن العجاج | reports | The seven readers and most people read the dāl in al-ḥamdu with nominative ḍamma; Sufyān ibn ʿUyayna and Ruʾba ibn al-ʿAjjāj are reported to read it accusative, with an implied verb.
[QURTUBI:1:2/r4] QURTUBI, d. 671 · رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم | reports | Anas reports from the Prophet that when God gives a servant a blessing and the servant praises Him, the praise is better than what was received.
[QURTUBI:1:2/r40] QURTUBI, d. 671 · سيبويه | reports | Sībawayh says nominative al-ḥamdu lillāh conveys that praise from the speaker and all creatures belongs to God, while the accusative reports only the speaker’s own praise.
[QURTUBI:1:2/r41] QURTUBI, d. 671 · غير سيبويه | reports | Another explanation takes the nominative as an appeal for pardon and as exaltation and glorification, so it functions as supplication rather than a plain report.
[QURTUBI:1:2/r42] QURTUBI, d. 671 · الطبري | reports | Al-Ṭabarī says God’s praise of Himself implicitly commands His servants to praise Him, as though the wording said, Say praise belongs to God.
[QURTUBI:1:2/r43] QURTUBI, d. 671 · author | holds | Qurtubi treats the implied command to say as a common Arabic ellipsis whose context supplies the omitted words, and says the same construction applies to the later address, as though it said, Say, You alone we worship. | mentions 1:5
[QURTUBI:1:2/r44] QURTUBI, d. 671 · ابن أبي عبلة | reports | Ibn Abī ʿAbla reads the dāl and lām with ḍamma by vowel assimilation for phonetic harmony, a common pattern illustrated by other words and a poetic line.
[QURTUBI:1:2/r45] QURTUBI, d. 671 · الحسن بن أبي الحسن وزيد بن علي | reports | Al-Ḥasan ibn Abī al-Ḥasan and Zayd ibn ʿAlī read the dāl of al-ḥamd with kasra by assimilation of the first vowel to the second.
[QURTUBI:1:2/r46] QURTUBI, d. 671 · author | holds | Rabb means owner; al-Ṣiḥāḥ says it is a divine name used of others only in an annexed construction, though pre-Islamic Arabs also used it for a king.
[QURTUBI:1:2/r47] QURTUBI, d. 671 · author | holds | Rabb also means master: Qurtubi cites the command to remember Joseph with his master and the report that a slave woman gives birth to her mistress. | mentions 12:42
[QURTUBI:1:2/r48] QURTUBI, d. 671 · الهروي وغيره | reports | Al-Harawī and others say rabb can mean one who rectifies, manages, mends, or tends something to completion; they connect rabbāniyyūn with tending the books.
[QURTUBI:1:2/r49] QURTUBI, d. 671 · رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم | reports | A prophetic question about a blessing one tends means taking responsibility for it and putting it right.
[QURTUBI:1:2/r5] QURTUBI, d. 671 · رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم | reports | A report in Nawādir al-uṣūl from Anas says that if someone possessed the whole world and then praised God, the praise would be better than it.
[QURTUBI:1:2/r50] QURTUBI, d. 671 · author | holds | Rabb can also mean the deity, as shown by a poet’s line about a lord upon whose head a fox urinates.
[QURTUBI:1:2/r51] QURTUBI, d. 671 · النحاس | reports | Al-Naḥḥās records the intensive forms rabbāhu, rabbabahu, and rabbatahu; al-Ṣiḥāḥ says rabbahu, rabbabahu, and tarabbabahu all mean he raised him, and marbūb means the one raised.
[QURTUBI:1:2/r52] QURTUBI, d. 671 · بعض العلماء | reports | Some scholars call Rabb the greatest name of God because callers frequently invoke Him by it and it conveys the bond of care, mercy, and need between Lord and servant.
[QURTUBI:1:2/r53] QURTUBI, d. 671 · author | reports | One derivation traces Rabb to tarbiya, since God manages and nurtures creation; the stepdaughter is called

 rabība because her mother’s husband raises her. In this sense it is an attribute of action, while owner or master denotes an attribute of essence. | mentions 4:23
[QURTUBI:1:2/r54] QURTUBI, d. 671 · author | holds | With the definite article, Rabb is specific to God; without it, the term can apply to God or a servant, but God alone owns owners and owned things, creates and provides, and cannot lose His dominion as human owners can.
[QURTUBI:1:2/r55] QURTUBI, d. 671 · قتادة | reports | Qatāda says al-ʿālamīn is the plural of ʿālam and means every existing thing other than God, with no singular on this pattern, like rahṭ or qawm.
[QURTUBI:1:2/r56] QURTUBI, d. 671 · الحسين بن الفضل | reports | Al-Ḥusayn ibn al-Faḍl says the worlds are the people of each era, citing the address about men among the worlds; al-ʿAjjāj and Jarīr also use ʿālam for human communities. | mentions 26:165
[QURTUBI:1:2/r57] QURTUBI, d. 671 · ابن عباس | reports | Ibn ʿAbbās says the worlds are jinn and humans, citing the Qur’an’s description of the Prophet as a warner to all worlds, since he was not sent as a warner to animals. | mentions 25:1
[QURTUBI:1:2/r58] QURTUBI, d. 671 · الفراء وأبو عبيدة | reports | Al-Farrāʾ and Abū ʿUbayda restrict the term to rational beings: humans, jinn, angels, and devils, excluding animals because the plural form is for rational beings; al-Aʿshā’s verse is cited.
[QURTUBI:1:2/r59] QURTUBI, d. 671 · زيد بن أسلم | reports | Zayd ibn Aslam says the worlds are the beings who receive sustenance.
[QURTUBI:1:2/r6] QURTUBI, d. 671 · author | holds | Abu ʿAbd Allah explains that the person first receives the world and then the enduring word of praise, which is better because the world perishes while the word remains among the righteous deeds. | mentions 18:46
[QURTUBI:1:2/r60] QURTUBI, d. 671 · أبو عمرو بن العلاء | reports | Abū ʿAmr ibn al-ʿAlāʾ says the worlds are spiritual beings; a similar Ibn ʿAbbās gloss includes every living creature moving on earth.
[QURTUBI:1:2/r61] QURTUBI, d. 671 · وهب بن منبه | reports | Wahb ibn Munabbih says God has eighteen thousand worlds, of which this world is one.
[QURTUBI:1:2/r62] QURTUBI, d. 671 · أبو سعيد الخدري | reports | Abū Saʿīd al-Khudrī says God has forty thousand worlds, with the inhabited world from east to west counting as one.
[QURTUBI:1:2/r63] QURTUBI, d. 671 · مقاتل | reports | Muqātil says there are eighty thousand worlds, forty thousand on land and forty thousand at sea.
[QURTUBI:1:2/r64] QURTUBI, d. 671 · الربيع بن أنس عن أبي العالية | reports | Al-Rabīʿ ibn Anas transmits from Abū al-ʿĀliya that jinn and humans are worlds and that each of earth’s four corners contains 1,500 worlds created to worship God.
[QURTUBI:1:2/r65] QURTUBI, d. 671 · author | prefers | Qurtubi prefers the first view, that the worlds include every creature and existent thing, supported by Pharaoh asking about the Lord of the worlds and Moses answering that He is Lord of the heavens, earth, and all between them. | mentions 26:23, 26:24
[QURTUBI:1:2/r66] QURTUBI, d. 671 · الزجاج والخليل | reports | Al-Zajjāj derives ʿālam from knowledge or a sign: it is everything God created in this life and the next and it points to its maker and planner; al-Khalīl likewise says a sign or marker indicates a thing.
[QURTUBI:1:2/r67] QURTUBI, d. 671 · الجنيد | reports | A man praised God before al-Junayd but stopped before saying Lord of the worlds; al-Junayd urged him to complete the verse, explaining that created things vanish when paired with the Eternal.
[QURTUBI:1:2/r68] QURTUBI, d. 671 · author | holds | Rabb may be read in the nominative by syntactic disconnection, meaning He is Lord of the worlds, or in the accusative as a word of praise.
[QURTUBI:1:2/r7] QURTUBI, d. 671 · author | reports | Another wording says that what the servant gave was more than what he received; this frames praise as the servant’s gift and the world as God’s gift, though both ultimately come from God.
[QURTUBI:1:2/r8] QURTUBI, d. 671 · رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم | reports | Ibn ʿUmar reports that angels could not record a servant’s praise fitting God’s majesty, so God told them to write it as the servant had said until He rewards him.
[QURTUBI:1:2/r9] QURTUBI, d. 671 · author | holds | The language note explains that aʿḍala means a matter became difficult and intractable; muʿaḍḍalāt are hardships, and the verb also describes obstructed childbirth.
[QURTUBI-FULL:1:1-7/r2] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · author | holds | The terms madhma and ahmada describe blame versus praise, finding something agreeable, and becoming worthy of praise; hamda can mean one who overpraises, while hamadat al-nar is its crackling.
[QURTUBI-FULL:1:1-7/r3] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · أبو جعفر الطبري | reports | Al-Tabari and al-Mubarrad treat hamd and shukr as synonymous; al-Sulami also attributes this position to Jaʿfar al-Sadiq and Ibn ʿAtaʾ, who says praise is thanks for God teaching it.
[QURTUBI-FULL:1:1-7/r4] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · ابن عطية | rejects | Ibn ʿAtiyya says “praise to God, in thanks” restricts praise to a blessing and therefore argues against equating praise and gratitude.
[QURTUBI-FULL:1:1-7/r5] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · بعض العلماء | reports | Some say gratitude is broader because it uses tongue, limbs, and heart, whereas praise is only verbal.
[QURTUBI-FULL:1:1-7/r6] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · بعض العلماء | reports | Others say praise is broader: it includes gratitude and commendation, can stand in place of gratitude, but gratitude cannot replace praise.
[QURTUBI-FULL:1:1-7/r7] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · ابن عباس | reports | Ibn ʿAbbas calls praise the expression of every grateful person, citing Adam’s praise at a sneeze and praise by Noah, Abraham, David and Solomon, the Prophet, and Paradise’s people. | mentions 23:28, 14:39, 27:15, 17:111, 35:34, 10:10
[QURTUBI-FULL:1:2#2/r1] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · author | holds | The expressions for a matter becoming difficult or blocked explain the report’s wording about the two angels; either verb form may be used without the extra yāʾ.
[QURTUBI-FULL:1:2#2/r2] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم | reports | Abu Malik al-Ashʿari reports that purification is half of faith, praise fills the balance, and glorification with praise fills the space between heaven and earth.
[QURTUBI-FULL:1:2#2/r3] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · طائفة من العلماء | reports | One group prefers alhamdulillah because it combines praise with the monotheism expressed by “There is no god but God.”
[QURTUBI-FULL:1:2#2/r4] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · طائفة من العلماء | reports | Another group prefers “There is no god but God” because it repels unbelief and shirk and is the profession for which people are fought.
[QURTUBI-FULL:1:2#2/r5] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · ابن عطية | prefers | Ibn ʿAtiyya chooses the monotheistic formula, citing the report that it is the best utterance of the Prophet and earlier prophets.
[QURTUBI-FULL:1:2#2/r6] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · author | holds | Muslims agree God is praised for all blessings; since faith is a blessing and belongs among all created things, faith is God’s act and creation, against the Qadariyya.
[QURTUBI-FULL:1:2#2/r7] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · author | holds | Hamd means complete praise; the definite article encompasses every kind of praise, all of which God deserves for His beautiful names and exalted attributes.
[QURTUBI-FULL:1:2#2/r8] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · author | reports | A poet uses hamd in a small-number plural form; hamd is the opposite of blame, tahmid is more emphatic, and Muhammad names one rich in praiseworthy qualities.
[QURTUBI-FULL:1:2#3/r1] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم | reports | The Prophet admitted that he could not enumerate praise of God, illustrating the creature’s inability to fulfill God’s due praise.
[QURTUBI-FULL:1:2#3/r2] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · author | reports | Other explanations say God praised Himself because servants cannot fully praise Him, or because abundant blessings exceed their capacity; divine praise removes the burden of gratitude.
[QURTUBI-FULL:1:2#3/r3] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · author | prefers | Hamd praises the praised one’s attributes without prior favor, while shukr praises a benefactor for a favor; thus hamd is broader and fits the verse’s scope.
[QURTUBI-FULL:1:2#3/r4] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · author | reports | Hamd can mean satisfaction, as in saying one was pleased with someone or in the “praised station”; a Prophetic expression likewise means “I approve for you.” | mentions 17:79
[QURTUBI-FULL:1:2#3/r5] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · جعفر الصادق | reports | Jaʿfar al-Sadiq offers an esoteric reading of the letters of hamd: unity, dominion, and permanence; knowing these attributes is the reality of praising God.
[QURTUBI-FULL:1:2#3/r6] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · شقيق بن إبراهيم | reports | Shafiq says gratitude requires recognizing the giver, accepting what is given, and not disobeying while one has strength.
[QURTUBI-FULL:1:2#3/r7] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · author | holds | God praises Himself and opens His Book with praise, while scripture and the Prophet forbid human self-praise; human praise is compromised by motives, unlike God’s eternal self-praise. | mentions 53:32
[QURTUBI-FULL:1:2#3/r8] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · علماؤنا | reports | The scholars say an imperfect creature should not praise himself to attract benefits or ward off harms.
[QURTUBI-FULL:1:2#4/r1] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · القراء السبعة | reports | The seven readers and most people read alhamdu with the dāl in the nominative; Sufyan ibn ʿUyayna and Ruʾba report an accusative reading with an implied verb.
[QURTUBI-FULL:1:2#4/r2] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · سيبويه | reports | Sibawayh says the nominative attributes praise to the speaker and all creation, while the accusative attributes it to the speaker alone.
[QURTUBI-FULL:1:2#4/r3] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · author | reports | Other grammarians take the phrase as an appeal for pardon and mercy, magnification, or a request rather than a plain report; anot

[QURTUBI-FULL:1:2#4/r4] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · الطبري | reports | Al-Tabari says God’s praise of Himself implicitly commands people to praise Him; Arabic can omit the understood imperative, as in the cited poem.
[QURTUBI-FULL:1:2#4/r5] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · ابن أبي عبلة | reports | Ibn Abi ʿAbla reads the dāl and lām with ḍamma for vowel harmony, a common Arabic tendency also illustrated by other readings and poetic examples.
[QURTUBI-FULL:1:2#5/r1] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · الحسن بن أبي الحسن | reports | Hasan al-Basri and Zayd ibn ʿAli read the dāl with kasra by vowel assimilation.
[QURTUBI-FULL:1:2#5/r10] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · author | reports | Rabb may derive from nurture: God manages and raises creation; stepdaughters are called rabāʾib because a husband raises them, making Rabb an attribute of action, while owner or master is an attribute of essence. | mentions 4:23
[QURTUBI-FULL:1:2#5/r11] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · author | holds | With the definite article, Rabb belongs exclusively to God; without it, people may be called a household’s lord. God alone creates and provides, owns both owners and owned things, and cannot lose His dominion.
[QURTUBI-FULL:1:2#5/r2] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · author | reports | A poem’s “wayl ummiha” derives from “waylun li-ummiha”: the first lām was dropped and the hamza’s ḍamma shifted after kasra proved heavy.
[QURTUBI-FULL:1:2#5/r3] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · author | holds | Rabb means owner; lexically it is a divine name, used of others only in a possessive construction, though pre-Islamic Arabs also used it for a king.
[QURTUBI-FULL:1:2#5/r4] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · author | reports | Rabb can mean master, as in Joseph’s “your lord,” and the hadith that a slave woman gives birth to her mistress. | mentions 12:42
[QURTUBI-FULL:1:2#5/r5] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · الهروي | reports | Rabb also means one who repairs, manages, restores, or takes care of something; rabbani scholars are named for tending to scripture.
[QURTUBI-FULL:1:2#5/r6] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · author | reports | A hadith asks whether someone has a blessing he tends for another, using rabbaha for tending and improving it.
[QURTUBI-FULL:1:2#5/r7] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · author | reports | Rabb can also mean the one worshipped; the cited poet mocks a fox worshipped after it soils an idol’s head.
[QURTUBI-FULL:1:2#5/r8] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · author | reports | The verb has intensive forms and can mean raising a child; al-Nahhas records rabbahu, rabbabahu, and rabbatahu as forms.
[QURTUBI-FULL:1:2#5/r9] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · بعض العلماء | reports | Some consider Rabb God’s greatest name because supplicants frequently call upon Him by it and the name conveys the relation of care, mercy, and dependence.
[QURTUBI-FULL:1:2/r1] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم | reports | Abu Hurayra and Abu Saʿid report that when a servant says “Praise belongs to God,” God affirms the servant and says the praise belongs to Him.
[QURTUBI-FULL:1:2/r2] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم | reports | Anas reports that God is pleased when a servant praises Him after eating a meal or drinking.
[QURTUBI-FULL:1:2/r3] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · الحسن | reports | Hasan says that no blessing is better than saying “Praise belongs to God.”
[QURTUBI-FULL:1:2/r4] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم | reports | Anas reports that praising God for a blessing is met with a gift greater than what the servant received.
[QURTUBI-FULL:1:2/r5] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم | reports | A report from Anas says that if someone owned the whole world and then said alhamdulillah, the praise would be better than it.
[QURTUBI-FULL:1:2/r6] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · أبو عبد الله | reports | Abu ʿAbd Allah explains that the enduring word is better because the world perishes, while praise remains among the righteous deeds; both world and praise ultimately come from God. | mentions 18:46
[QURTUBI-FULL:1:2/r7] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · author | reports | A variant says the gift was greater than what was received; this treats praise as the servant’s gift and the world as God’s, though both are from God, who enriches with the world and honors with praise in the afterlife.
[QURTUBI-FULL:1:2/r8] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم | reports | Ibn ʿUmar reports that angels could not record a servant’s praise “as befits” God’s majesty, so God told them to write it as spoken and reward him when they meet.
[BAYDAWI:1:2/r1] BAYDAWI, d. 685 · author | holds | Ḥamd praises chosen goodness, whether a blessing or otherwise; madh praises goodness without qualification, so one praises knowledge and generosity but only commends beauty.
[BAYDAWI:1:2/r10] BAYDAWI, d. 685 · author | holds | If the article is exhaustive, all praise belongs to God because He bestows every good directly or indirectly; this implies He is living, powerful, willing, and knowing. | mentions 16:53
[BAYDAWI:1:2/r11] BAYDAWI, d. 685 · author | reports | Readings assimilate dāl and lām in opposite directions, treating the letters as one word because they are used together.
[BAYDAWI:1:2/r12] BAYDAWI, d. 685 · author | reports | Rabb originally means tarbiya, bringing something to perfection little by little, then became an intensive description like ṣawm and ʿadl.
[BAYDAWI:1:2/r13] BAYDAWI, d. 685 · author | reports | Another derivation makes rabb a descriptive form from rabba-yarubbuhu; it then means owner because an owner preserves and nurtures what is owned.
[BAYDAWI:1:2/r14] BAYDAWI, d. 685 · author | holds | Rabb is unqualified for God alone, though it can be qualified for others, as in “return to your lord.” | mentions 12:50
[BAYDAWI:1:2/r15] BAYDAWI, d. 685 · author | holds | ʿĀlam means what makes something known, like a signet or mold; it came to denote all besides God, substances and accidents, whose contingency indicates the necessary Creator.
[BAYDAWI:1:2/r16] BAYDAWI, d. 685 · author | holds | The plural encompasses diverse classes and uses the masculine rational plural because rational beings predominate among them.
[BAYDAWI:1:2/r17] BAYDAWI, d. 685 · author | reports | Another view restricts al-ʿālamīn to rational beings—angels and the human and jinn races—with others included secondarily.
[BAYDAWI:1:2/r18] BAYDAWI, d. 685 · author | reports | A further view takes it here to mean people: each person contains counterparts of the cosmos that reveal the Creator, as in the verse about looking within oneself. | mentions 51:21
[BAYDAWI:1:2/r19] BAYDAWI, d. 685 · author | reports | The accusative rabb al-ʿālamīn is analyzed as praise, a vocative, or an implied verb indicated by “praise.”
[BAYDAWI:1:2/r2] BAYDAWI, d. 685 · author | reports | Some consider ḥamd and madh synonymous or close companions.
[BAYDAWI:1:2/r20] BAYDAWI, d. 685 · author | holds | Contingent things need an originator at coming-to-be and a sustainer for as long as they exist.
[BAYDAWI:1:2/r3] BAYDAWI, d. 685 · author | holds | Shukr responds to a blessing through speech, action, and belief; a poem names hand, tongue, and hidden heart as the three responses.
[BAYDAWI:1:2/r4] BAYDAWI, d. 685 · author | holds | Shukr is broader than ḥamd and madh in one respect and narrower in another; praise is a branch of gratitude and better signals blessings than hidden belief or ambiguous bodily acts, so it is gratitude's chief element.
[BAYDAWI:1:2/r5] BAYDAWI, d. 685 · النبي | reports | The Prophet is quoted saying praise is the head of gratitude and that whoever does not praise God has not thanked Him.
[BAYDAWI:1:2/r6] BAYDAWI, d. 685 · author | holds | Blame is the opposite of praise, and ingratitude the opposite of shukr.
[BAYDAWI:1:2/r7] BAYDAWI, d. 685 · author | holds | Al-ḥamdu is nominative as subject with “to God” as predicate, though an accusative reading is also reported.
[BAYDAWI:1:2/r8] BAYDAWI, d. 685 · author | holds | The nominative conveys universal and permanent praise belonging to God rather than newly arising praise.
[BAYDAWI:1:2/r9] BAYDAWI, d. 685 · author | holds | Ḥamd is a verbal noun normally governed by an implicit, rarely used verb; its article may denote the genus or point to the familiar idea of praise.
[BAYDAWI-FULL:1:2#2/r1] BAYDAWI-FULL, d. 685 · author | holds | Rabb originally means gradual nurturing toward completion, then became an intensive description; another derivation treats it as a noun for the owner who preserves and develops what he owns.
[BAYDAWI-FULL:1:2#2/r2] BAYDAWI-FULL, d. 685 · author | holds | Rabb is used of others only in a qualified phrase, whereas al-ʿālam names what makes something known and came to mean everything besides God.
[BAYDAWI-FULL:1:2#2/r3] BAYDAWI-FULL, d. 685 · author | holds | The worlds comprise all substances and accidents, whose possibility and need for a necessary cause show God's existence; the plural gathers different genera, with rational beings predominant in its form.
[BAYDAWI-FULL:1:2#2/r4] BAYDAWI-FULL, d. 685 · author | reports | An alternative restricts the term to knowledgeable beings—angels, humans, and jinn—with other creatures included only secondarily.
[BAYDAWI-FULL:1:2#2/r5] BAYDAWI-FULL, d. 685 · author | reports | Another view means human beings here: each person contains counterparts of the greater world's substances and accidents, through which the Creator is known, as 51:21 invites people to observe themselves. | mentions 51:21
[BAYDAWI-FULL:1:2#2/r6] BAYDAWI-FULL, d. 685 · author | reports | An accusative reading treats رب العالمين as praise, direct address, or an implied action indicated by الحمد.
[BAYDAWI-FULL:1:2#2/r7] BAYDAWI-FULL, d. 685 · author | holds | Possible things need God not only to originate them but also to keep them in existence.
[BAYDAWI-FULL:1:2/r1] BAYDAWI-FULL, d. 685 · author | holds | Ḥamd is praise for chosen excellence, including a blessing, while madḥ is praise for any excellence; one praises knowledge but merely commends beauty.

2/r2] BAYDAWI-FULL, d. 685 · author | reports | Some regard ḥamd and madḥ as equivalent; shukr is gratitude for a blessing expressed in speech, action, and belief.
[BAYDAWI-FULL:1:2/r3] BAYDAWI-FULL, d. 685 · author | holds | Gratitude is broader than praise and commendation in one respect but narrower in another; praise is its chief expression because it displays blessings and makes gratitude audible.
[BAYDAWI-FULL:1:2/r4] BAYDAWI-FULL, d. 685 · النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم | reports | A report calls praise the head of gratitude and says one who does not praise God has not thanked Him.
[BAYDAWI-FULL:1:2/r5] BAYDAWI-FULL, d. 685 · author | holds | The word is nominative as a subject with لله as predicate, though an accusative reading exists; nominative signals praise as universal and enduring rather than newly arising.
[BAYDAWI-FULL:1:2/r6] BAYDAWI-FULL, d. 685 · author | holds | The definite article can mark the genus or all praise: in reality every good comes from God, directly or through an intermediary, as 16:53 says. | mentions 16:53
[BAYDAWI-FULL:1:2/r7] BAYDAWI-FULL, d. 685 · author | holds | The entitlement to praise implies that God is living, powerful, willing, and knowing.
[BAYDAWI-FULL:1:2/r8] BAYDAWI-FULL, d. 685 · author | reports | Two recitations assimilate the dāl and lām in either direction, treating them as one word because the terms are used together.
[NASAFI:1:1/r12] NASAFI, d. 710 · أبو هريرة عن النبي | reports | Abu Hurayra reports God’s dialogue dividing the Fatiha between Himself and the servant: praise, glorification, and exaltation belong to God; the worshipper’s request for guidance and the response to it belong to the servant, while worship and aid are shared.
[NASAFI:1:2/r1] NASAFI, d. 710 · author | holds | Hamd is describing someone with praise and excellence, giving preference to the praiseworthy quality.
[NASAFI:1:2/r10] NASAFI, d. 710 · author | holds | Rabb is used absolutely only of God, while for human masters it is restricted by a possessive phrase, as in Joseph’s story; al-Wasiti explains God as creator at the beginning, sustainer, and forgiver at the end. | mentions 12:23, 12:50
[NASAFI:1:2/r11] NASAFI, d. 710 · الواسطي | reports | Al-Wasiti describes God as creator at the beginning, nourisher through provision, and forgiver at the end.
[NASAFI:1:2/r12] NASAFI, d. 710 · author | holds | Rabb is one of God’s greatest names.
[NASAFI:1:2/r13] NASAFI, d. 710 · author | reports | Al-‘alamin may mean everything the Creator knows of bodies, substances, and accidents, or every existing thing besides God, named for being evidence of His existence.
[NASAFI:1:2/r14] NASAFI, d. 710 · author | holds | The plural ending -in is used although normally associated with rational beings or their equivalent because ‘alamin has an adjectival sense, indicating knowledge.
[NASAFI:1:2/r2] NASAFI, d. 710 · author | holds | Al-hamdu is nominative as a subject, though it can be read accusative with an implied verb as an explanatory verbal noun, like ‘thanks’ or ‘ingratitude’; nominative wording conveys a settled, enduring meaning.
[NASAFI:1:2/r3] NASAFI, d. 710 · author | holds | The lām in lillah attaches to an omitted predicate, understood as ‘due’ or ‘established.’
[NASAFI:1:2/r4] NASAFI, d. 710 · قيل | reports | One view treats hamd and madh as near-synonyms: both are praise and notice of beauty, whether for a blessing, courage, or noble lineage.
[NASAFI:1:2/r5] NASAFI, d. 710 · author | holds | Unlike hamd, shukr is only for a blessing and can be expressed by heart, tongue, and limbs; the cited poet names hand, tongue, and the veiled heart as its three forms.
[NASAFI:1:2/r6] NASAFI, d. 710 · النبي | reports | A Prophetic report calls praise the head of gratitude and says a servant has not thanked God without praising Him; praise leads because the tongue makes gratitude more public than the hidden heart or ambiguous bodily acts.
[NASAFI:1:2/r7] NASAFI, d. 710 · قيل | reports | Another distinction makes madh praise inherent perfections, shukr praise for beneficence, and hamd broad enough to cover both.
[NASAFI:1:2/r8] NASAFI, d. 710 · author | holds | For Nasafi, the definite article in al-hamd is comprehensive, against the Mu‘tazila; its attachment to Allah, the name of the divine essence, gathers all perfections and reflects the doctrine of created acts.
[NASAFI:1:2/r9] NASAFI, d. 710 · author | holds | Rabb means owner; the cited exchange has Safwan tell Abu Sufyan that being owned by a Qurayshi is preferable to being owned by a Hawazini. Rabb can also be a verbal noun used intensively as an adjective.
[NASAFI-FULL:v1p4#2/r5] NASAFI-FULL, d. 710 · author | prefers | The report begins God's response when the servant says “Praise belongs to God,” which indicates the basmala is not part of al-Fatiha; if it is outside al-Fatiha, consensus excludes it from other surahs too.
[NASAFI-FULL:v1p6#2/r1] NASAFI-FULL, d. 710 · author | holds | Al-hamd is beautiful praise given preferentially; syntactically it is a nominative subject with an implied predicate such as “due” or “established,” while a reading with an implicit verb makes it an accusative verbal noun.
[NASAFI-FULL:v1p6#2/r10] NASAFI-FULL, d. 710 · author | holds | Rabb is used without qualification only for God; human use requires a restriction, as in the cited accounts of Joseph. | mentions 12:23, 12:50
[NASAFI-FULL:v1p6#2/r11] NASAFI-FULL, d. 710 · author | holds | Al-ʿālamīn denotes what makes the Creator known—bodies, substances, and accidents—or every existent apart from God; its sound masculine plural reflects a descriptive quality associated with rational beings.
[NASAFI-FULL:v1p6#2/r2] NASAFI-FULL, d. 710 · author | holds | The shift from accusative to nominative indicates that praise is settled and enduring.
[NASAFI-FULL:v1p6#2/r3] NASAFI-FULL, d. 710 · author | holds | Hamd and madḥ may both mean praising what is beautiful, whether a favor or an inherent quality; shukr is specifically for a favor and uses heart, tongue, and limbs, whereas hamd is praise by tongue alone.
[NASAFI-FULL:v1p6#2/r4] NASAFI-FULL, d. 710 · author | reports | The cited poet says favors elicited three forms of gratitude: hand, tongue, and the veiled heart.
[NASAFI-FULL:v1p6#2/r5] NASAFI-FULL, d. 710 · author | reports | A report calls praise the head of gratitude and says a servant has not thanked God without praising Him; verbal mention spreads notice of a favor more than inward belief or ambiguous bodily acts.
[NASAFI-FULL:v1p6#2/r6] NASAFI-FULL, d. 710 · author | reports | An alternative distinction makes madḥ praise inherent perfections, such as power and knowledge, and shukr praise for benefactions; hamd covers both.
[NASAFI-FULL:v1p6#2/r7] NASAFI-FULL, d. 710 · author | holds | The definite article in al-hamd is exhaustive according to the author's school, against the Mu'tazila; joining it to Allah's proper name gathers every perfection and rests on the doctrine of created acts.
[NASAFI-FULL:v1p6#2/r8] NASAFI-FULL, d. 710 · author | holds | Rabb means owner or master; the source cites Safwan telling Abu Sufyan that being ruled by a Quraysh man is preferable to being ruled by a Hawazin man, and allows “rabb” as an intensive verbal noun.
[NASAFI-FULL:v1p6#2/r9] NASAFI-FULL, d. 710 · الواسطى | reports | Al-Wasiti explains Rabb as creator at the beginning, sustainer through nourishment, and forgiver at the end, and calls it God's greatest name.
[QASHANI:1:2/r1] QASHANI, d. 736 · author | holds | Praise in action and in the tongue of each thing’s state is the appearance of its perfections and attainment of its ends, a fitting opening tribute to its Lord.
[QASHANI:1:2/r2] QASHANI, d. 736 · author | holds | All beings praise and glorify God through their particular properties, orientation toward ends, and actualization of potential; their dependence on Him alone denies partners and deficiency and manifests His majesty and beauty. The Qur’an says every thing glorifies Him. | mentions 17:44
[QASHANI:1:2/r3] QASHANI, d. 736 · author | holds | God is Lord of the worlds as origin, preserver, and manager of all; worlds means everything known to God, and the sound masculine plural reflects encompassing knowledge or predominance.
[QASHANI:1:2/r4] QASHANI, d. 736 · author | holds | Divine provision includes general and particular good: outward blessings such as health and livelihood, and inward blessings such as knowledge and recognition.
[QASHANI:1:2/r5] QASHANI, d. 736 · author | holds | God is owner at the final return and recompense; only the worshipped one to whom sovereignty returns can reward enduring blessing for perishable life, as servants shed acts and attributes and receive true existence after annihilation.
[QASHANI:1:2/r6] QASHANI, d. 736 · author | holds | All praise belongs to God eternally according to His due, at beginning, end, and everything between; He is both praiser and praised, worshipper and worshipped, in detail and in unity.
[QASHANI:1:2/r7] QASHANI, d. 736 · author | holds | Seeing God’s attributes in His speech leads servants to address Him by worship and ask His aid, since they see no other object of worship or independent power; every motion becomes worship and love seeks His beauty everywhere.
[ABUHAYYAN:1:2/r1] ABUHAYYAN, d. 745 · author | holds | Ḥamd is verbal praise of beauty, for a blessing or otherwise, and its opposite is blame; it is not a reversal of madḥ, since madḥ can apply to inanimate things.
[ABUHAYYAN:1:2/r10] ABUHAYYAN, d. 745 · أبو عبيدة والفراء | reports | Abū ʿUbayda and al-Farrāʾ include humans, jinn, angels, and devils among al-ʿālamīn.
[ABUHAYYAN:1:2/r11] ABUHAYYAN, d. 745 · ابن عطية | reports | Ibn ʿAṭiyya says al-ʿālamīn means the two classes of moral beings, humans and jinn.
[ABUHAYYAN:1:2/r12] ABUHAYYAN, d. 745 · أبو معاذ | reports | Abū Muʿādh restricts al-ʿālamīn to the children of Adam.
[ABUHAYYAN:1:2/r13] ABUHAYYAN, d. 745 · الصادق | reports | Al-Ṣādiq defines al-ʿālamīn as the people of Paradise and the Fire.

[ABUHAYYAN:1:2/r14] ABUHAYYAN, d. 745 · عبد الرحمن بن زيد | reports | ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn Zayd says al-ʿālamīn means those who receive provision.
[ABUHAYYAN:1:2/r15] ABUHAYYAN, d. 745 · الحسن وقتادة | reports | Al-Ḥasan and Qatāda define al-ʿālamīn as every created thing.
[ABUHAYYAN:1:2/r16] ABUHAYYAN, d. 745 · بعضهم | reports | Another reported interpretation restricts al-ʿālamīn to spiritual beings.
[ABUHAYYAN:1:2/r17] ABUHAYYAN, d. 745 · الجمهور | reports | The majority read al-ḥamdu with ḍamma on the dāl. Ibrāhīm ibn Abī ʿAbla assimilates its mīm to the following lām; al-Ḥasan and Zayd ibn ʿAlī assimilate the dāl's kasra to the lām's, a stranger assimilation.
[ABUHAYYAN:1:2/r18] ABUHAYYAN, d. 745 · الحسن وزيد بن علي | reports | Al-Ḥasan and Zayd ibn ʿAlī assimilate the dāl's kasra to the lām's kasra; the author calls this stranger because a case vowel follows a non-case vowel.
[ABUHAYYAN:1:2/r19] ABUHAYYAN, d. 745 · هارون العتكي ورؤبة وسفيان بن عيينة | reports | Hārūn al-ʿAtakī, Ruʾba, and Sufyān ibn ʿUyayna read al-ḥamda in the accusative.
[ABUHAYYAN:1:2/r2] ABUHAYYAN, d. 745 · ابن الأنباري | rejects | Ibn al-Anbārī treats ḥamd as an inversion of madḥ; Abū Ḥayyān rejects this because a jewel may be praised but not thanked.
[ABUHAYYAN:1:2/r20] ABUHAYYAN, d. 745 · author | holds | The article in al-ḥamd may be anaphoric, defining the familiar praise; essential, defining the nature; or generic, encompassing all praises. A verbal noun is ordinarily not pluralized.
[ABUHAYYAN:1:2/r21] ABUHAYYAN, d. 745 · ابن الأعرابي | reports | Ibn al-Aʿrābī records the plural aḥmad for ḥamd, apparently treating its different kinds as distinct, and cites a poem using aḥmadī.
[ABUHAYYAN:1:2/r22] ABUHAYYAN, d. 745 · القراء السبعة | prefers | The nominative reading is stronger and agreed upon by the seven canonical readers: it states that praise is established and enduringly belongs to God, including praise by God and others.
[ABUHAYYAN:1:2/r23] ABUHAYYAN, d. 745 · author | holds | With nominative al-ḥamdu the lām marks entitlement; with accusative al-ḥamda a verb such as “I praise God” must be supplied, conveying renewed action.
[ABUHAYYAN:1:2/r24] ABUHAYYAN, d. 745 · author | prefers | For the accusative reading, Abū Ḥayyān prefers an omitted verb directly indicated by the wording, such as “I praise God,” over “I say” or “adhere to praise.”
[ABUHAYYAN:1:2/r25] ABUHAYYAN, d. 745 · author | holds | In the accusative reading the lām is explanatory, not a strengthening of transitivity, since the verbal noun cannot govern this phrase as its object.
[ABUHAYYAN:1:2/r26] ABUHAYYAN, d. 745 · زيد بن علي وطائفة | reports | Zayd ibn ʿAlī and a group read rabb al-ʿālamīn in the accusative as praise; the reading weakens if the following adjectives remain genitive.
[ABUHAYYAN:1:2/r27] ABUHAYYAN, d. 745 · الأهوازي | reports | Al-Ahwāzī reports Zayd ibn ʿAlī reading rabb, raḥmān, and raḥīm all in the accusative, avoiding the mismatch in case. | mentions 1:3
[ABUHAYYAN:1:2/r28] ABUHAYYAN, d. 745 · author | rejects | Abū Ḥayyān rejects parsing accusative rabb as an implied verb of praise or as apposition: one rests on imagined syntax, the other is interrupted by raḥmān raḥīm. | mentions 1:3
[ABUHAYYAN:1:2/r29] ABUHAYYAN, d. 745 · author | holds | Rabb may be a verbal noun used adjectivally or an active participle with deleted alif; as a title it is exclusive to God, while others require a possessive complement.
[ABUHAYYAN:1:2/r3] ABUHAYYAN, d. 745 · author | prefers | Views say ḥamd and shukr are synonymous, ḥamd is broader, or shukr praises God's acts while ḥamd praises His attributes; Abū Ḥayyān prefers ḥamd as broader.
[ABUHAYYAN:1:2/r30] ABUHAYYAN, d. 745 · author | holds | The article in al-ʿālamīn is exhaustive; ʿālam is an irregular collective and its sound masculine plural is even more irregular because it violates some conditions of that pattern.
[ABUHAYYAN:1:2/r31] ABUHAYYAN, d. 745 · author | prefers | Abū Ḥayyān prefers that al-ʿālamīn denote morally responsible beings, supported by the verse about signs for the knowledgeable; Ḥafṣ's kasra on the lām clarifies the sense. | mentions 30:22
[ABUHAYYAN:1:2/r4] ABUHAYYAN, d. 745 · author | holds | The lām can express possession, transfer of ownership, entitlement, relation, cause, communication, exclamation, specification, result, location, endpoint, and superiority; Qur'anic and Arabic examples illustrate these functions. | mentions 16:72, 4:105, 28:8, 21:47, 17:78, 7:57, 17:107
[ABUHAYYAN:1:2/r5] ABUHAYYAN, d. 745 · author | holds | Rabb can mean master, owner, constant one, deity, or reformer; some add “companion,” supported by a poem about the master of the dogs.
[ABUHAYYAN:1:2/r6] ABUHAYYAN, d. 745 · بعضهم | reports | Some lexicographers allow rabb to mean “companion,” adducing a poem in which a man approaches as master of the dogs.
[ABUHAYYAN:1:2/r7] ABUHAYYAN, d. 745 · ابن عباس | reports | One report from Ibn ʿAbbās defines al-ʿālamīn as every being with a soul.
[ABUHAYYAN:1:2/r8] ABUHAYYAN, d. 745 · البجلي | reports | Al-Bajalī says al-ʿālamīn means people.
[ABUHAYYAN:1:2/r9] ABUHAYYAN, d. 745 · ابن عباس | reports | Another report from Ibn ʿAbbās specifies humans, jinn, and angels.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p32/r1] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | holds | Ḥamd is verbal praise for beauty, whether based on a blessing or not, spoken with the tongue; it is the opposite of blame.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p32/r10] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | reports | Other reported scopes include Adam's children, the people of Paradise and Hell, all recipients of provision, every made thing, and spiritual beings; Abū Ḥayyān leaves the correct count to God.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p32/r11] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · الجمهور | reports | The majority pronounce the dāl of al-ḥamdu with ḍamma.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p32/r12] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · إبراهيم بن أبي عبلة | reports | Ibrāhīm ibn Abī ʿAbla harmonizes the mīm's vowel with the following lām's ḍamma.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p32/r13] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · الحسن وزيد بن علي | reports | Al-Ḥasan and Zayd ibn ʿAlī harmonize the dāl's kasra with the lām's kasra, a stranger kind of agreement between inflectional and non-inflectional vowels.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p32/r2] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · ابن الأنباري | reports | Ibn al-Anbārī says ḥamd is a metathesized form of madḥ; Abū Ḥayyān rejects this despite their parallel inflection.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p32/r3] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | prefers | Three positions equate praise and thanks, make ḥamd broader, or distinguish thanks for deeds from praise for attributes; Abū Ḥayyān prefers ḥamd as broader.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p32/r4] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | holds | The lām in lillāh has numerous possible relations, including ownership, entitlement, relation, cause, communication, specification, outcome, time, endpoint, and elevation.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p32/r5] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | holds | Rabb may mean master, owner, abiding one, worshipped one, or reformer; some also understand companion or creator.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p32/r6] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · ابن عباس | reports | Ibn ʿAbbās is cited for two scopes of al-ʿālamīn: every living being, or humans, jinn, and angels.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p32/r7] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · البجلي | reports | Al-Bajalī says al-ʿālamīn means people.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p32/r8] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · ابن عطية | reports | Ibn ʿAṭiyya restricts al-ʿālamīn to the two responsible kinds, humans and jinn.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p32/r9] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · أبو عبيدة والفراء | reports | Abū ʿUbayda and al-Farrāʾ include humans, jinn, angels, and devils in al-ʿālamīn.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p34/r1] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · هارون العتكي، ورؤبة، وسفيان بن عيينة | reports | Hārūn al-ʿAtakī, Ruʾba, and Sufyān ibn ʿUyayna read al-ḥamda in the accusative.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p34/r10] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | rejects | Abū Ḥayyān rejects deriving the accusative rabb from a prior implied verb such as We praise God, since this analogy to ellipsis in coordination is not productive.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p34/r2] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | reports | The definite article on ḥamd may indicate a known instance, the abstract quality, or the entire genus of praise; the last implies exhaustive praise.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p34/r3] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · ابن الأعرابي | reports | Ibn al-Aʿrābī records the plural aḥmad for ḥamd, as if accounting for its varied kinds, and Abū Ḥayyān quotes a poetic example.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p34/r4] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | prefers | The nominative reading is semantically stronger and unanimously adopted by the Seven because it states that praise is established for God.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p34/r5] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | reports | The accusative reading needs an implied governor such as I praise God or I praised God; it presents praise as newly occurring and names its agent.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p34/r6] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | prefers | Among proposed governors for the accusative, Abū Ḥayyān prefers the explicit-sense verb ahmadu over a command or other unexpressed verb.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p34/r7] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | holds | With the accusative, lillāh is an explanatory lām; it cannot be governed by the verbal noun, as the Arabic construction saqyan li-Zayd shows.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p34/r8] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · زيد بن علي وطائفة | reports | Zayd ibn ʿAlī and a group read rabb al-ʿālamīn in the accusative as praise, though lowering the following epithets weakens the construction.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p34/r9] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · الأهوازي | reports | Al-Ahwāzī records Zayd ibn ʿAlī reading rabb, raḥmān, and raḥīm all in the accusative, which removes the syntactic weakness.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p35/r1] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | holds | Rabb is a verbal noun used adjectivally in one analysis, or an active participle with its alif omitted, like barr from bārr.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p35/r2] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | holds | Rabb is used

[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p35/r3] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | prefers | Although al-ʿālamīn is an irregular plural, Abū Ḥayyān favors the responsible creatures because a cited verse and Ḥafṣ's lām-kasra reading support that scope. | mentions 29:44
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p35/r4] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | holds | God's lordship and mercy make Him worthy of praise; lordship as mastery or ownership is followed fittingly by mercy, which sustains servants' hope after failure.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p35/r5] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · أبو العالية وابن السميفع وعيسى بن عمرو | reports | Abū al-ʿĀliya, Ibn al-Sumayfaʿ, and ʿĪsā ibn ʿAmr read raḥmān and raḥīm in the accusative, as detached epithets.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p35/r6] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · أبو رزين العقيلي والربيع بن خيثم وأبو عمران الجوني | reports | Abū Razīn, al-Rabīʿ ibn Khuthaym, and Abū ʿImrān al-Jūnī read both epithets in the nominative as detached clauses.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p35/r9] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | rejects | Parsing rabb as apposition is weak because raḥmān and raḥīm intervene.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p53/r2] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | holds | The definite article in al-ḥamd intensifies praise by making it comprehensive.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p53/r3] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | reports | Some rhetoricians call “Praise be to God” a statement whose intended force is command, like “no doubt in it” meaning “do not doubt.” | mentions 2:2
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p53/r4] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | holds | The lām in “to God” restricts all praise to Him, and the annexation “Master of the Day of Judgment” underscores His sole dominion when other dominions vanish. | mentions 40:16
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p53/r5] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | reports | The accusative reading of “al-ḥamd” involves ellipsis; grammarians differ over whether its omitted governing word repeats the noun or is another word.
[SAMIN-DURR:1:2#2/r1] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | reports | The article in al-hamd is analyzed as universal, generic, or referring to known praise; al-Zamakhshari chooses the generic reading.
[SAMIN-DURR:1:2#2/r2] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · الزمخشري | rejects | Al-Zamakhshari rejects the universal reading; the author infers that praise here is performed by the servant, who cannot produce every praise by himself and others.
[SAMIN-DURR:1:2#2/r3] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | holds | Hamd is fundamentally a verbal noun and therefore normally has no dual or plural; Ibn al-A'rabi nevertheless reports an af'al plural with poetic evidence.
[SAMIN-DURR:1:2#2/r4] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | holds | The common reading raises al-hamd as subject with a deleted nominal predicate, the preferred estimate, though a verb can also be supplied.
[SAMIN-DURR:1:2#2/r5] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | prefers | The author prefers a nominal estimate because it is mandatory in fa-idha and amma clauses; the relative clause al-ladhi fi al-dar instead requires a verb but is not structurally comparable.
[SAMIN-DURR:1:2#2/r6] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | holds | A prepositional phrase or adverb functioning as clause predicate, relative clause, adjective, or circumstantial phrase has an omitted governor; a generic kā'in cannot be overt except in a poetic anomaly. | mentions 27:40
[SAMIN-DURR:1:2#3/r1] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | holds | The omitted governor can generally be a noun or verb, but relative clauses require a verb and the fa-idha and amma constructions require a noun; grammarians differ over the default elsewhere.
[SAMIN-DURR:1:2#3/r2] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | reports | A rare accusative al-hamda is parsed either as a verbal noun replacing I praise, or as an imperative-like source meaning say praise; al-Tabari favors the command interpretation, but the author prefers declarative force.
[SAMIN-DURR:1:2#3/r3] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | prefers | The accusative may alternatively be a direct object of recite or read, but the verbal-noun analysis is better because the wording itself supports it.
[SAMIN-DURR:1:2#3/r4] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | prefers | Raising al-hamd is stronger and more expressive of stable praise, while accusative signals renewal; Abraham's salām is better than the angels' salāman by the verse's instruction to answer more beautifully. | mentions 11:69, 4:86
[SAMIN-DURR:1:2#3/r5] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | holds | On the accusative reading, li-llah is attached to an omitted explanatory verb such as I mean; source nouns do not normally govern this lām phrase, though it may strengthen a derivative verb. | mentions 47:8
[SAMIN-DURR:1:2#4/r1] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | holds | The kasra in a variant al-hamdi may be vowel harmony with the following lām, a Tamim and some Ghatafan dialect feature; another possibility is hidden nominative or accusative inflection.
[SAMIN-DURR:1:2#4/r2] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | holds | A variant with damma on the lām of li-llah follows the preceding dāl; al-Zamakhshari prefers harmony from inflection to building, citing a Qays dialect and Qur'anic murdifin. | mentions 8:9
[SAMIN-DURR:1:2#4/r3] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | holds | The lām in li-llah expresses entitlement here; other senses include ownership, transfer, kinship, cause, address, oath exclamation, clarification, result, location, endpoint, elevation, and augmentation. | mentions 16:72, 4:105, 12:23, 28:8, 21:47, 17:78, 35:13, 17:109, 12:43, 11:107, 43:29, 16:1, 27:72, 8:9
[SAMIN-DURR:1:2#5/r1] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | holds | The lām may be explanatory, resultative, locative meaning in, at, or after, terminative, or superposition; the source gives examples for each. | mentions 12:23, 28:8, 21:47, 17:78, 35:13, 17:109
[SAMIN-DURR:1:2#5/r2] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | reports | The lām is regularly extra with a preposed complement of a verb or with a derivative governor, and elsewhere only irregularly. | mentions 12:43, 11:107
[SAMIN-DURR:1:2#5/r3] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | reports | For raddafa lakum, some explain the lām by semantic inclusion and others regard it as extra. | mentions 27:72
[SAMIN-DURR:1:2#6/r1] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | holds | The common reading makes rabb genitive as an adjective or appositive to Allah; accusative allows an implied I praise, a detached praise, or vocative, with vocative weakest because it separates adjective from noun; nominative is detached predicate huwa rabb.
[SAMIN-DURR:1:2#6/r2] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | holds | Rabb can mean lord, owner, enduring, worshipped, or reformer; some add companion, supported by two poems, but here the author prefers owner and says no extra sense is needed; creator is another proposal.
[SAMIN-DURR:1:2#6/r3] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | reports | One view treats rabb as an adjective, either fa'l or fa'il from rāb with a shortened long vowel; the author objects that bār and barr may simply be separate forms.
[SAMIN-DURR:1:2#6/r4] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | reports | Others treat rabb as the verbal noun rabba yarubbu, meaning owned or governed, functioning as an agent noun like a just or fasting man.
[SAMIN-DURR:1:2#6/r5] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | holds | Rabb is normally reserved for God unless annexed to a noun, though pre-Islamic Arabs used it without qualification for a human king, which the author calls unbelief. | mentions 12:50
[SAMIN-DURR:1:2#6/r6] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · الحارث بن حلزة | reports | Al-Harith ibn Hilliza's line calls a human king al-rabb without qualification, exemplifying pre-Islamic usage.
[SAMIN-DURR:1:2#6/r7] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | holds | When a known noun is described by praise, blame, or compassion, its adjective may follow or detach with an implicit verb or subject; no explicit governor is allowed.
[SAMIN-DURR:1:2#7/r1] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | holds | With several such adjectives one may follow all, detach all, or mix them, but must follow first and detach later to avoid splitting adjective from noun.
[SAMIN-DURR:1:2#7/r2] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | holds | Al-alamin is an annexed sound masculine plural in form but an ism-jam because its singular differs; it cannot be plural of alam if that covers all non-divine beings while al-alamin means rational beings only.
[SAMIN-DURR:1:2#7/r3] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | reports | Sibawayh similarly says a'rab is not plural of arab because the former is narrower; an objection that al-alamin could mean only rational alam is answered by comparison with the unavailable form shay'un.
[SAMIN-DURR:1:2#7/r4] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · الراغب | reports | Al-Raghib transmits Ibn Abbas's explanation that al-alamin means angels, jinn, and humans, and says the word was formed as an instrument of knowing the Creator.
[SAMIN-DURR:1:2#7/r5] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | prefers | The author prefers al-Raghib's account that the sound plural includes all creation, with human usage prevailing when humans share the label.
[SAMIN-DURR:1:2/r1] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | holds | Hamd praises beauty whether or not a favor was bestowed and is expressed only by the tongue; shukr is for a received favor and may be by heart, tongue, or limbs. | mentions 34:13
[SAMIN-DURR:1:2/r2] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | holds | A poem listing hand, tongue, and hidden conscience as three gifts illustrates that gratitude includes bodily action as well as speech.
[SAMIN-DURR:1:2/r3] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | reports | Views range from treating hamd and shukr as synonymous, to making hamd absolutely broader, to distinguishing praise of attributes from thanks for acts.
[SAMIN-DURR:1:2/r4] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | rejects | Tha'lab's derivation of hamd as a reversal of madh is unsound: both forms are equally common, and hamd applies to God where madh does not; a possible prohibition is acknowledged.
[SAMIN-DURR:1:2/r5] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · الراغب | reports | Al-Raghib defines hamd as praise for excellence, narrower than m

[IBNKATHIR:1:1/r44] IBNKATHIR, d. 774 · author | holds | In the divine hadith, “prayer” means recitation, as in 17:110; because the Fatiha details the division, its recitation is a major pillar of prayer. | mentions 17:110

[IBNKATHIR:1:2/r1] IBNKATHIR, d. 774 · القراء السبعة | reports | The seven canonical readers vocalize the dāl of al-ḥamdu with ḍamma, making al-ḥamdu a subject and li-llāhi its predicate.
[IBNKATHIR:1:2/r10] IBNKATHIR, d. 774 · author | holds | Ibn Kathir questions Ibn Jarir's equation: praise is verbal commendation for necessary or bestowed qualities, while thanks applies only to bestowed qualities and may be inward, spoken, or enacted.
[IBNKATHIR:1:2/r11] IBNKATHIR, d. 774 · author | holds | Ibn Kathir resolves the scope dispute by saying praise covers more kinds of objects but is speech-only, whereas thanks uses more kinds of means but concerns bestowed qualities alone.
[IBNKATHIR:1:2/r12] IBNKATHIR, d. 774 · الجوهري | reports | Al-Jawhari defines praise as the opposite of blame, says taḥmīd is more emphatic than ḥamd, and regards ḥamd as broader than thanks.
[IBNKATHIR:1:2/r13] IBNKATHIR, d. 774 · الجوهري | reports | Al-Jawhari defines thanks as praising a benefactor for what he bestowed and says using the preposition li- is more eloquent.
[IBNKATHIR:1:2/r14] IBNKATHIR, d. 774 · author | holds | Ibn Kathir distinguishes praise from eulogy: eulogy can concern living or dead people and even objects, precede or follow a favor, and address necessary or bestowed qualities.
[IBNKATHIR:1:2/r15] IBNKATHIR, d. 774 · علي بن أبي طالب | reports | When Umar asks what al-ḥamdu lillāh means after learning other formulas of glorification, Ali answers that it is a phrase God approves for Himself.
[IBNKATHIR:1:2/r16] IBNKATHIR, d. 774 · ابن عباس | reports | Ibn Abbas says al-ḥamdu lillāh is a word of thanks; when a servant says it, God says that His servant has thanked Him.
[IBNKATHIR:1:2/r17] IBNKATHIR, d. 774 · ابن عباس | reports | Ibn Abbas explains praise as thanks, humble submission, and acknowledgment of God's favors, guidance, and origination.
[IBNKATHIR:1:2/r18] IBNKATHIR, d. 774 · كعب الأحبار | reports | Ka'b al-Ahbar says al-ḥamdu lillāh is God's praise.
[IBNKATHIR:1:2/r19] IBNKATHIR, d. 774 · الضحاك | reports | Al-Dahhak calls al-ḥamdu lillāh the cloak of the Most Merciful and notes that a hadith has come with a similar meaning.
[IBNKATHIR:1:2/r2] IBNKATHIR, d. 774 · سفيان بن عيينة ورؤبة بن العجاج | reports | Sufyan ibn Uyaynah and Ru'bah ibn al-Ajjaj read al-ḥamda with fatḥa as an implied verbal object.
[IBNKATHIR:1:2/r20] IBNKATHIR, d. 774 · النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم | reports | A report attributed to the Prophet says that whoever says al-ḥamdu lillāhi rabbi l-ʿālamīn has thanked God, who then increases him.
[IBNKATHIR:1:2/r21] IBNKATHIR, d. 774 · النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم | reports | The Companion al-Aswad ibn Sari asks to recite praises of his Lord, and the Prophet replies that his Lord loves praise.
[IBNKATHIR:1:2/r22] IBNKATHIR, d. 774 · النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم | reports | The Prophet says the best remembrance is lā ilāha illā Allāh and the best supplication is al-ḥamdu lillāh; al-Tirmidhi grades this report ḥasan gharīb.
[IBNKATHIR:1:2/r23] IBNKATHIR, d. 774 · النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم | reports | Anas reports that when a servant praises God for a blessing, the reward for that praise is better than the blessing received.

[IBNKATHIR:1:2/r25] IBNKATHIR, d. 774 · النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم | reports | Ibn Umar reports that angels cannot calculate the full reward for a servant's praise fitting God's majesty, so God tells them to record it as said until He rewards him.
[IBNKATHIR:1:2/r26] IBNKATHIR, d. 774 · طائفة | reports | A group holds that al-ḥamdu lillāhi rabbi l-ʿālamīn is better than lā ilāha illā Allāh because it combines praise with monotheism.
[IBNKATHIR:1:2/r27] IBNKATHIR, d. 774 · آخرون | reports | Others hold that lā ilāha illā Allāh is superior because it distinguishes faith from unbelief and is the formula people must profess; reports also call it the best remembrance.
[IBNKATHIR:1:2/r28] IBNKATHIR, d. 774 · author | holds | The definite article in al-ḥamdu encompasses every kind and form of praise as belonging to God, as expressed in a transmitted prayer.
[IBNKATHIR:1:2/r29] IBNKATHIR, d. 774 · author | holds | Rabb means owner and disposer, and in Arabic also master or one who manages something toward its good; each meaning applies to God.
[IBNKATHIR:1:2/r3] IBNKATHIR, d. 774 · ابن أبي عبلة | reports | Ibn Abi Abla reads both dāl and lām with ḍamma by assimilating the second vowel to the first; Ibn Kathir calls the reading anomalous.
[IBNKATHIR:1:2/r30] IBNKATHIR, d. 774 · author | holds | The unqualified title al-Rabb is used only for God; for other possessors it must be annexed, and some say al-Rabb is the greatest name.
[IBNKATHIR:1:2/r31] IBNKATHIR, d. 774 · author | holds | Al-ʿālamīn is the plural of ʿālam, encompassing every created being besides God; created kinds in heavens, earth, land, and sea are worlds, as is each generation.
[IBNKATHIR:1:2/r32] IBNKATHIR, d. 774 · ابن عباس | reports | Ibn Abbas describes the worlds as all creation belonging to God: heavens, earths, their inhabitants and everything between them, known and unknown.
[IBNKATHIR:1:2/r33] IBNKATHIR, d. 774 · ابن عباس وسعيد بن جبير وعكرمة | reports | Ibn Abbas, through Sa'id ibn Jubayr and Ikrimah, and other early authorities interpret the worlds as jinn and humans; Ibn Abi Hatim's chain is said to be unreliable.
[IBNKATHIR:1:2/r34] IBNKATHIR, d. 774 · القرطبي | reports | Al-Qurtubi supports the interpretation of the worlds as jinn and humans by citing the description of the Qur'an as a warning to the worlds. | mentions 25:1
[IBNKATHIR:1:2/r35] IBNKATHIR, d. 774 · الفراء وأبو عبيدة | reports | Al-Farra and Abu Ubayda restrict the term worlds to rational beings—humans, jinn, angels, and devils—and exclude animals.
[IBNKATHIR:1:2/r36] IBNKATHIR, d. 774 · زيد بن أسلم وأبو عمرو بن العلاء | reports | Zayd ibn Aslam and Abu Amr ibn al-Ala define worlds as everything with a spirit that receives provision.
[IBNKATHIR:1:2/r37] IBNKATHIR, d. 774 · مروان بن محمد بن مروان بن الحكم | reports | Ibn Asakir reports Marwan's claim that God created seventeen thousand worlds, with the inhabitants of the heavens and earth forming one and God alone knowing the rest.
[IBNKATHIR:1:2/r38] IBNKATHIR, d. 774 · قتادة | reports | Qatadah says each kind or species is a world.

[IBNKATHIR:1:2/r4] IBNKATHIR, d. 774 · الحسن وزيد بن علي | reports | Al-Hasan and Zayd ibn Ali read the dāl with kasra by assimilating the first vowel to the second.

[IBNKATHIR:1:2/r41] IBNKATHIR, d. 774 · تبيع الحميري | reports | Tubyay al-Himyari says the worlds comprise one thousand nations, six hundred in the sea and four hundred on land.
[IBNKATHIR:1:2/r42] IBNKATHIR, d. 774 · سعيد بن المسيب | reports | A similar count of one thousand worlds, divided into six hundred sea and four hundred land worlds, is also attributed to Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab.
[IBNKATHIR:1:2/r43] IBNKATHIR, d. 774 · النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم | reports | A report through Jabir tells how locusts became scarce under Umar, then attributes to the Prophet a saying that there are one thousand nations and locusts are the first to perish; Ibn Kathir says Muhammad ibn Isa is weak.
[IBNKATHIR:1:2/r44] IBNKATHIR, d. 774 · سعيد بن المسيب | reports | Al-Baghawi reports Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab's view that God has one thousand worlds, six hundred in the sea and four hundred on land.
[IBNKATHIR:1:2/r45] IBNKATHIR, d. 774 · وهب بن منبه | reports | Wahb ibn Munabbih says God has eighteen thousand worlds and this world is one of them.
[IBNKATHIR:1:2/r46] IBNKATHIR, d. 774 · مقاتل | reports | Muqatil says there are eighty thousand worlds.
[IBNKATHIR:1:2/r47] IBNKATHIR, d. 774 · كعب الأحبار | reports | Ka'b al-Ahbar says that no one knows the number of worlds except God.
[IBNKATHIR:1:2/r48] IBNKATHIR, d. 774 · أبو سعيد الخدري | reports | Al-Qurtubi reports from Abu Sa'id al-Khudri that God has forty thousand worlds and the inhabited east-to-west world is only one.
[IBNKATHIR:1:2/r49] IBNKATHIR, d. 774 · الزجاج | reports | Al-Zajjaj defines a world as everything God created in this life and the next.

[IBNKATHIR:1:2/r51] IBNKATHIR, d. 774 · author | holds | Ibn Kathir says ʿālam derives from ʿalāmah, a sign, because every created thing points to its Maker, Creator, and oneness; he cites a poem by Ibn al-Mu'tazz.

[IBNKATHIR:1:2/r8] IBNKATHIR, d. 774 · جعفر الصادق وابن عطاء | reports | The Sufi authorities Ja'far al-Sadiq and Ibn Ata are reported to hold that praise and thanks are equivalent.
[IBNKATHIR:1:2/r9] IBNKATHIR, d. 774 · ابن عباس | reports | Ibn Abbas calls al-ḥamdu lillāh the expression used by every grateful person.
[IBNKATHIR:1:5/r11] IBNKATHIR, d. 774 · الله تعالى | reports | In a divine report, God divides the prayer between Himself and His servant, responds to each recited section, calls 1:5 shared between them, and grants the servant's request.
[BURHAN:v1p438/r3] BURHAN, d. 794 · ابن حبان | reports | Ibn Hibban reads the report comparing al-Fatiha with the Torah and Gospel as a difference in reward granted by God’s favor, not as intrinsic superiority within the Quran.
[BURHAN:v1p438/r4] BURHAN, d. 794 · ابن حبان | reports | Ibn Hibban says calling al-Fatiha the greatest surah means greatest in reward, not that one part of the Quran is intrinsically superior.

[BURHAN:v3p284/r1] BURHAN, d. 794 · author | holds | The Fātiḥa has the usual order الحمد لله; in al-Jāthiya فلله الحمد answers the implied question of who deserves praise, like the question about today's dominion and its answer. | mentions 40:16
[BURHAN:v3p326/r1] BURHAN, d. 794 · author | holds | The successive praises intensify the servant's attention: God's exclusive praise, universal lordship, gifts of mercy, and command of judgment prepare the worshipper to approach and seek help.
[BURHAN:v3p326/r2] BURHAN, d. 794 · قيل | reports | One explanation says praise uses third person because it ranks below worship, while direct address elevates the worshipper's encounter; similarly, blessing is explicitly attributed to God but anger is phrased obliquely as a matter of etiquette. | mentions 6:101
[BURHAN:v4p338/r13] BURHAN, d. 794 · author | holds | These three senses can coincide in praise of God: He deserves praise, has authority over it, and is the one to whom it belongs.
[NASHR:v1p227/r4] NASHR, d. 833 · author | holds | Stopping after these phrases is good because their sense is understood, but starting with attached phrases such as rabb al-ʿālamīn, ṣirāṭ alladhīna, or ghayr al-maghḍūb ʿalayhim is poor, except at verse ends per the Sunnah.

[NASHR:v1p47/r12] NASHR, d. 833 · author | holds | Maki deems these noncanonical-imam readings permissible when reliably transmitted, since each has a sound Arabic analysis and agrees with the codex spelling; Ibn al-Jazari says others also share some forms.
