[NASHR:v1p48/r1] NASHR, d. 833 · زيد بن علي بن الحسين، رؤبة بن العجاج، هارون بن موسى العتكي، الحسن | reports | These readers pronounce the dāl of al-ḥamdu with fatḥa; the accusative is treated as a verbal noun with its commonly understood verb omitted.
[NASHR:v1p48/r2] NASHR, d. 833 · الحسن | reports | Al-Hasan also reads the lām in Allāh with fatḥa, matching the preceding accusative; the source calls this a dialect of some Qays speakers.
[NASHR:v1p48/r3] NASHR, d. 833 · قتيبة عن الكسائي | reports | Qutayba transmits imāla of the alif in lillāh from al-Kisa'i, explained by the following kasra.
[NASHR:v1p48/r4] NASHR, d. 833 · أبو زيد سعيد بن أوس الأنصاري | reports | Abu Zayd reports rabb al-ʿālamīn in both nominative and accusative; successive adjectives may differ, with some governed by an implied verb and others by an implied subject, but not revert to genitive.
[NASHR:v1p49/r7] NASHR, d. 833 · قتيبة عن الكسائي، كردم عن نافع، ورش | reports | The author adds unlisted transmissions: Qutayba from al-Kisa'i has imāla in al-ʿālamīn and al-raḥmān; Kurram from Nafi and al-Ahwazi from Warsh lengthen vowels in mālik, naʿbudu, and iyyāka.
[BIQAI:1:2/r1] BIQAI, d. 885 · author | holds | Because the basmala is a kind of praise, it is naturally followed by the comprehensive name al-ḥamd; this implicitly calls people to praise God as the one deserving every praise.
[BIQAI:1:2/r2] BIQAI, d. 885 · author | holds | People should make this form of praise open their affairs, since it awakens hope and fear of God and leads to steadfastness on guidance.
[BIQAI:1:2/r3] BIQAI, d. 885 · author | holds | Al-ḥamd lillāh establishes that God deserves every praise by His essence and all perfections; Rabb adds that He deserves praise as Lord, Owner, and Benefactor.
[BIQAI:1:2/r4] BIQAI, d. 885 · author | holds | Al-ʿālamīn points to creation's beginning, inviting inference from the made thing to its Maker and from the beginning to resurrection, as the Torah also begins with creation for this reason.
[BIQAI:1:2/r5] BIQAI, d. 885 · أبو الحسن الحرالي | reports | Al-Ḥarālī defines ḥamd as complete praise encompassing every action and attribute: all are from God and all are praise untouched by blame.
[BIQAI:1:2/r6] BIQAI, d. 885 · أبو الحسن الحرالي | reports | Al-Ḥarālī says that when praise is understood to pervade everything, the definite form al-ḥamd signals its completion; al- marks the endpoint and perfection of what it qualifies.
[BIQAI:1:7/r27] BIQAI, d. 885 · العلامة سعد الدين مسعود ابن عمرو التفتازاني الشافعي | reports | The first preservation is signaled by the Merciful, the Compassionate, whose great and subtle gifts sustain life.
[BIQAI-FULL:v1p11#2/r2] BIQAI-FULL, d. 885 · أبو الفضل محمد المشدالي المغربي | reports | Al-Mashdali's method for Qur'anic coherence is to identify a surah's purpose, its prerequisites and their distance from the goal, then answer expectations raised as the discourse unfolds.
[BIQAI-FULL:v1p11#2/r3] BIQAI-FULL, d. 885 · author | holds | A surah's name summarizes its purpose, as a title signals the details within; Adam demonstrated this naming principle when he named things before the angels.
[BIQAI-FULL:v1p11#2/r4] BIQAI-FULL, d. 885 · author | holds | The Fatiha's many titles converge on مراقبة: it is the Mother of the Book, foundation, oft-repeated, treasure, healing, sufficing, complete, protecting, incantation, praise, thanks, supplication and prayer.
[BIQAI-FULL:v1p11#2/r5] BIQAI-FULL, d. 885 · author | holds | The Fatiha is a treasure, cure, sufficiency, fulfillment, protection and incantation; it gathers praise, gratitude and supplication, with prayer as their greatest assembly.
[BIQAI-FULL:v1p12/r1] BIQAI-FULL, d. 885 · author | holds | The Fatiha's purpose is to establish God's exclusive right to all praise and perfection, sovereignty over both worlds, worship and aid, and to ask for the path of the successful rather than the doomed; its center is مراقبة.
[BIQAI-FULL:v1p13/r2] BIQAI-FULL, d. 885 · الحرالي | reports | The basmala relates to the Fatiha as the Fatiha relates to the Qur'an: each is a compact synthesis of what the larger whole details.
[BIQAI-FULL:v1p13/r6] BIQAI-FULL, d. 885 · author | holds | Since the basmala is a kind of praise, it naturally leads to comprehensive al-hamd: begin affairs by praising God as the one deserving every praise, with hope and awe guiding the way.
[BIQAI-FULL:v1p13/r7] BIQAI-FULL, d. 885 · author | holds | Al-hamd lillah establishes that God deserves praise for His essence and perfection; Rabb al-alamin adds His lordship, sovereignty and beneficence, while the worlds point to creation's beginning and the inference to resurrection.
[BIQAI-FULL:v1p13/r8] BIQAI-FULL, d. 885 · الحرالي | reports | Al-Harali defines al-hamd as complete praise covering all actions and attributes, all from God and free of blame; its definite form signals praise reaching its full extent.
[BIQAI-FULL:v1p13/r9] BIQAI-FULL, d. 885 · author | holds | Lordship does not yield wellbeing without mercy, so Rahman and Rahim follow al-hamd and encourage people to persist in praising God.
[BIQAI-FULL:v1p16/r5] BIQAI-FULL, d. 885 · الحرالي | reports | Al-Harali says all Qur'an is God's speech, but some verses voice what creatures at different levels ought to say yet cannot express; God teaches them words that fulfill their duty.
[BIQAI-FULL:v1p16/r6] BIQAI-FULL, d. 885 · الحرالي | reports | Al-Harali explains the sound report that God divided prayer between Himself and His servant: the first three verses are God's praise, which He accepts from the reciting servant as praise and glorification.
[BIQAI-FULL:v1p18#2/r3] BIQAI-FULL, d. 885 · author | holds | The Qur'an's arrangement is miraculous, so the Fatiha must retain its required order in prayer; rearrangement or insertion of foreign material invalidates it. Al-Isfahani locates its clearest inimitability in order.

item.text: Several sources disagree on the scope of “the worlds,” and the numerical reports give different counts. I’m keeping those counts separate and recording objections where a source gives one.

[BIQAI-FULL:v1p18#2/r6] BIQAI-FULL, d. 885 · author | holds | The root and forms of al-hamd suggest reaching an end, extension, encompassing and circularity; these imply lowering the head and can lead to contentment and gratitude.

[BIQAI-FULL:v1p22/r6] BIQAI-FULL, d. 885 · أبو هريرة | reports | In the authentic report in Muslim and the four Sunan, God says the Fatiha is divided between Himself and His servant: He answers praise, glorification and worship, and grants the servant's final requests.
[BIQAI-FULL:v1p24/r1] BIQAI-FULL, d. 885 · author | holds | Al-Baqara aims to prove the Book is guidance to follow; belief in the unseen, especially resurrection and the afterlife, is its greatest guidance and organizing theme.

[BIQAI-FULL:v1p24/r4] BIQAI-FULL, d. 885 · author | holds | The Book functions like a caliph from the resolute messengers, guiding every matter to the right exit: rejecting it fails, hesitation nearly perishes, and accepting it brings piety and excellence.

[BIQAI-FULL:v1p28/r3] BIQAI-FULL, d. 885 · الحرالي | reports | Alternatively, and the author says this is likelier, Rahmaniyyah universally grants blessings and removes harms whether for felicity or misery, while Rahimiyyah specifically gives the blessings and protection that lead to felicity.

[BIQAI-FULL:v1p31/r3] BIQAI-FULL, d. 885 · author | holds | Baqara answers the Fatiha's plea for guidance by directing worshippers to the Book, describing the guided and denied groups as patterns to follow or avoid; its pious are the straight path and its others the path of ruin.

[ITQAN:v3p284/r1] ITQAN, d. 911 · author | holds | The Fatiha points to all major Qur’anic disciplines: knowledge of God and attributes, prophecy, resurrection, worship, ethical conduct and the straight path, and stories teaching the outcomes of obedience and disobedience. | mentions 1:2, 1:3, 1:4, 1:5, 1:6, 1:7

 · author | holds | One quality can be both what a person is praised by and what they are praised for, as when someone is seen giving generously or praying; the two roles arise under different aspects.

[ALUSI:1:2/r107] ALUSI, d. 1270 · author | holds | Every possible being remains under God’s nurture: without the continuing influx of divine support and the removal of every impediment, it would return to nonexistence.
[ALUSI:1:2/r108] ALUSI, d. 1270 · author | holds | Because contingent beings need a cause both to begin and to persist, continual divine preservation is itself tarbiya; keeping even indefinitely many possible obstacles absent sustains a thing.
[ALUSI:1:2/r109] ALUSI, d. 1270 · بعض العارفين | reports | A mystic observes that God has other servants, but each person has no lord but Him, while God nurtures each as though He had no servant but that person.
[ALUSI:1:2/r11] ALUSI, d. 1270 · author | holds | Praising God for essential attributes raises a problem if ḥamd requires voluntary acts, since those attributes may be identical with or additional to the divine essence.
[ALUSI:1:2/r110] ALUSI, d. 1270 · author | holds | Although the sound masculine plural often denotes a small number, the form here hints that all created worlds remain few beside God’s greatness; the plural can also denote many. | mentions 39:67
[ALUSI:1:2/r111] ALUSI, d. 1270 · author | holds | For the gnostics, the station of lordship comprises names that call for objects, such as knowing and power, including shared names and creative names directed toward creatures.
[ALUSI:1:2/r112] ALUSI, d. 1270 · author | holds | The Sufi hierarchy distinguishes Rabb, Rahmān, and Allāh: Rahmān encompasses more divine attributes, while Allāh names the highest, all-encompassing station of divinity.
[ALUSI:1:2/r113] ALUSI, d. 1270 · author | holds | In this hierarchy, the essence-only manifestation of aḥadiyya is not disclosed to creatures, whereas ulūhiyya manifests the divine in relation to others.
[ALUSI:1:2/r114] ALUSI, d. 1270 · أرباب الظاهر | reports | The outward scholars explain why petitioners say yā Rabb: a petitioner seeks what benefits and nurtures him, so calling on the nurturer is especially apt. | mentions 17:110, 7:180
[ALUSI:1:2/r115] ALUSI, d. 1270 · author | holds | Al-Ālūsī’s own Sufi reading is that souls invoke God by the first name through which they acknowledged Him in the primordial covenant. | mentions 7:172
[ALUSI:1:2/r116] ALUSI, d. 1270 · الشيخ الأكبر | reports | Ibn ʿArabī’s account says the universal spirit sought its source without knowing that the sought reality was already within it, then recognized God in the station of lordship. | mentions 50:16
[ALUSI:1:2/r117] ALUSI, d. 1270 · الشيخ الأكبر | reports | In Ibn ʿArabī’s account the spirit names God its Rabb; God gives it divine names and attributes to know through existence, while veiling the manner of that gift because the creature cannot bear it. | mentions 50:16
[ALUSI:1:2/r118] ALUSI, d. 1270 · author | holds | Opening the sūra’s descriptions with Rabb al-ʿālamīn suits the Prophet’s mission and asks for compassion toward all creatures, since God is their Lord.
[ALUSI:1:2/r119] ALUSI, d. 1270 · زيد بن علي | reports | Zayd b. ʿAlī is reported to read rabb al-ʿālamīn in the accusative; the author’s preferred parse is an accusative of detachment with an implied verb such as أمدح.
[ALUSI:1:2/r12] ALUSI, d. 1270 · بعضهم | reports | One solution treats praise of divine attributes as praise for what is effectively voluntary because God’s essence suffices for those attributes.
[ALUSI:1:2/r120] ALUSI, d. 1270 · بعضهم | reports | One analysis treats the accusative as detachment from the preceding construction, supplying a verb of praise or mention; another says the prior الحمد licenses the construction.
[ALUSI:1:2/r121] ALUSI, d. 1270 · بعضهم | reports | Other proposed governors are the expressed الحمد, a vocative, or a past-tense reading of rabb; al-Ālūsī objects to the first for its syntax and to the latter parses as awkward.
[ALUSI:1:2/r122] ALUSI, d. 1270 · author | prefers | Al-Ālūsī considers accusative detachment the strongest analysis, especially if al-Raḥmān al-Raḥīm is read in the accusative as a substitute rather than an adjective.
[ALUSI:1:2/r13] ALUSI, d. 1270 · بعضهم | reports | Another solution defines voluntary action as action attributable to a free agent, whether or not that agent chose it in this instance.
[ALUSI:1:2/r14] ALUSI, d. 1270 · بعضهم | reports | A further view says divine attributes issue by choice in the sense that God would bring them about if He willed and would not if He did not, without making them temporally originated.
[ALUSI:1:2/r15] ALUSI, d. 1270 · الفلاسفة | reports | Philosophers appeal to the distinction between a necessary conditional and the actuality of its antecedent, but al-Ālūsī argues that necessity leaves divine volition nominal or makes the world’s origin incompatible with their account.
[ALUSI:1:2/r16] ALUSI, d. 1270 · author | prefers | Al-Ālūsī concludes that lexical ḥamd is praise for voluntary acts; praise of essential attributes is either figurative through their voluntary effects or conventional praise, both unobjectionable.
[ALUSI:1:2/r17] ALUSI, d. 1270 · الصدر | reports | The praiser must exalt the praised one through praise both outwardly and inwardly.
[ALUSI:1:2/r18] ALUSI, d. 1270 · المحققون | reports | The discerning scholars do not require the praiser to believe the praised quality actually exists; it suffices that the description not accompany an assertion of contempt.
[ALUSI:1:2/r19] ALUSI, d. 1270 · الدواني | reports | Al-Dawwānī explains al-Sharīf’s requirement of inward and outward exaltation as intending the performative creation of esteem, not belief in a proposition.
[ALUSI:1:2/r2] ALUSI, d. 1270 · الجنيد | reports | Junayd was asked about the spiritual end and answered that it is returning to the beginning, an apt pattern for the sūra’s opening praise.
[ALUSI:1:2/r20] ALUSI, d. 1270 · author | rejects | Al-Ālūsī rejects the replies that a praiser must believe the literal description or must intend a metaphorical description; denial of a statement’s content does not prevent its rhetorical use.
[ALUSI:1:2/r21] ALUSI, d. 1270 · author | holds | The fifth element is an expression that manifests the praised one’s praiseworthiness; speech is conventionally singled out because the tongue is the usual instrument of speaking.
[ALUSI:1:2/r22] ALUSI, d. 1270 · author | holds | A person without a tongue can still praise through lip sounds or speech produced in another organ, as witnessed in a person lacking the whole tongue.

[ALUSI-FULL:v1p71#2/r4] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · author | reports | A third argument derives genus from verbal nouns’ basic, non-comprehensive meaning; the reply is that surrounding indications can still make a verbal noun comprehensive.

[ELMALILI:1:2#2/r9] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · author | holds | The basmala is the crown, the Qur’an a perfect body, Fatiha its head, and alhamdu lillah its face; mercy, guidance, worship, and divine unity express its spiritual life.
[ELMALILI:1:2#3/r1] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · author | holds | Hamd is beautiful verbal praise that honors an agent for a voluntary benefaction or its source, goodness; it combines aspects of praise and gratitude and lacks a single Turkish equivalent.
[ELMALILI:1:2#3/r10] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · Gustave Le Bon | reports | Le Bon and other thinkers conclude that imagination rules people more strongly than reality.

[ELMALILI:1:2#3/r2] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · author | holds | Medh can praise living or inanimate things and can precede or follow a favor; hamd is directed to a choosing benefactor after a favor, though the benefit need not reach the praiser.
[ELMALILI:1:2#3/r3] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · author | holds | Shukr responds in speech, action, or heart to a blessing actually received; spoken gratitude is also hamd and medh, while inward or bodily thanks need not be either.
[ELMALILI:1:2#3/r4] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · author | holds | Every hamd is medh but not every medh is hamd; hamd is broader than gratitude in one respect and narrower in another, and unlike empty flattery both hamd and shukr affirm truth.
[ELMALILI:1:2#3/r5] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · author | holds | Hamd springs from justified hope or experienced enjoyment and leans toward the future, whereas shukr celebrates an accomplished gift and its received fulfillment.
[ELMALILI:1:2#3/r6] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · Resûl-i Ekrem | reports | The Prophet commands that dust be thrown in the faces of professional eulogists, illustrating the moral danger of medh that can become flattery.
[ELMALILI:1:2#3/r7] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · Resûl-i Ekrem | reports | The Prophet says that one who does not praise people does not praise God, making hamd generally commendable.

[ELMALILI:1:2#4/r11] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · author | holds | Alhamdu lillah informs believers, implies reverent praise, and uses a timeless nominal sentence; the four following clauses explain it, making Fatiha one sentence in substance.
[ELMALILI:1:2#4/r2] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · author | holds | Human happiness depends on recognizing and tasting a blessing, not merely possessing it; the recipient’s expressed hamd lets the giver witness that the gift reached its fitting recipient.
[ELMALILI:1:2#4/r3] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · author | holds | Giving stands above receiving, so the station of the praised giver is the highest rank; the joy of this rank culminates in further hamd and increased gifts. | mentions 14:7
[ELMALILI:1:2#4/r4] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · author | holds | Hamd advances through four ranks: praising, being praised, uniting both, then receiving praise while praising.
[ELMALILI:1:2#4/r5] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · author | holds | The final rank manifests the divine names Hamid, Mahmud, and Hamid together; the Prophet also bears the related names Ahmed and Muhammad.
[ELMALILI:1:2#4/r6] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · author | holds | The promised station of praise belongs especially to the Seal of the Prophets and is the station of the great intercession, where he receives the banner of praise.
[ELMALILI:1:2#4/r7] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · author | holds | Through the Prophet’s intercession, the community gathered beneath the banner of praise shares in divine hamd, and the people of Paradise conclude their plea with this verse. | mentions 10:10
[ELMALILI:1:2#4/r8] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · author | holds | Hamd’s fullest nature speaks through the Prophet’s Ahmediyyah and Muhammadiyyah; its ultimate reality belongs at its beginning and end to God alone.
[ELMALILI:1:2#4/r9] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · author | holds | The definite article in alhamd can express a known instance, totality, kind, or essence; because no particular hamd is presupposed, it here gathers the entire genus and all its ranks.
[ELMALILI:1:2#5/r1] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · author | holds | The sound plural al-alamin foregrounds rational beings; a concise Turkish rendering is difficult, but it means God alone is Lord of all realms and especially their rational inhabitants.
[ELMALILI:1:2#5/r10] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · author | holds | The sign in al-alamin, later clarified by al-Baqara’s description of the Qur’an as guidance for the Godfearing, signals the wisdom of revelation. | mentions 2:2
[ELMALILI:1:2#5/r2] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · author | holds | The plural’s focus on rational consciousness, reinforced by the merciful and sovereign attributes, draws reason from unseen knowledge to witnessed presence and the direct covenant of worship.

[ELMALILI:1:2#5/r5] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · author | holds | Nurturing is gradual movement toward perfection, visibly at work throughout the universe; contemplating the realms reveals the law of divine nurturing, while the realms themselves are known through their relation to God.
[ELMALILI:1:2#5/r6] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · bir kısım felâsife | reports | Some philosophers say the whole cosmos came to be all at once, with or without causes, rather than through gradual development.
[ELMALILI:1:2#5/r7] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · bir kısım felâsife | reports | Another group denies origination by claiming that the present cosmic order has existed eternally; on this view there is no real progress, striving, or acquisition.
[ELMALILI:1:2#5/r8] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · author | rejects | Daily observation and inference show that things arise gradually and disappear gradually; examples from geology, plants, animals, and human development contradict those denials.
[ELMALILI:1:2#5/r9] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · author | holds | The changing stages of the cosmos and human life still disclose a continuous, powerful reality that binds them and gives the observer awareness of unity.
[ELMALILI:1:2#6/r1] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · author | holds | Observation, experience, and reason jointly establish origination and development; science may affirm evolution, but it must recognize God as its complete first cause.
[ELMALILI:1:2#6/r2] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · author | rejects | Some misuse evolutionary language by treating nature’s law as an uncaused absolute, displacing divine nurturing and making humanity the absolute summit of existence.
[ELMALILI:1:2#6/r3] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · author | holds | Science depends on causality: what comes into existence after not existing must have a cause, since nothing can arise from nothing.
[ELMALILI:1:2#6/r4] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · author | holds | Cause and effect must be proportionate: an effect cannot exceed its complete cause, and known effects disclose their cause; otherwise nonbeing would produce being.
[ELMALILI:1:2#6/r5] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · author | holds | Consciousness, knowledge, and reason cannot have a blind force or blind nature as their complete cause; natural laws require an intelligent necessary being.
[ELMALILI:1:2#6/r6] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · author | holds | The wheat seed’s multiplication illustrates that one cannot explain the many grains by the seed’s isolated capacity alone; each added stage receives perfection from beyond itself.

[ELMALILI:1:2#7/r3] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · author | holds | Without God’s perfect lordship and nurturing, neither existence nor development could be real; the world’s real share in these qualities reveals God as Lord of all realms.
[ELMALILI:1:2#8/r1] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · author | holds | The world is the collection of all things other than God that point to Him through causal relations; any part possessing an ordered relation can be called a realm.
[ELMALILI:1:2#8/r10] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · author | rejects | The soul cannot itself be the ultimate cause of all truth: it acknowledges its limitations and does not claim to create at will or to have existed eternally.
[ELMALILI:1:2#8/r11] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · author | holds | Even the basic judgment I exist depends on affirming a true relation between self-awareness and being, which rests on God’s encompassing truth; all limited knowledge is thereby God’s gift.
[ELMALILI:1:2#8/r2] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · author | holds | Alam derives from the idea of a means of knowledge and is a collective noun; it is not applied to a wholly isolated individual.
[ELMALILI:1:2#8/r3] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · author | holds | The sound rational plural and the definite article extend the meaning across all realms and foreground rational beings; understanding the Lord of the worlds requires conceiving rational agents.
[ELMALILI:1:2#8/r4] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · author | holds | True knowledge is not mere conception but assent to the real relation between what is conceived; the ordered events we perceive become signs through this truth-consciousness.
[ELMALILI:1:2#8/r5] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · author | holds | Every ordered community of things, from inner awareness to external objects, is named a realm because it serves as a sign and means of knowing God’s creation, lordship, and perfection.
[ELMALILI:1:2#8/r6] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · author | holds | For those who truly witness, nothing is seen without God also being seen behind, before, or with it; the world is other-than-God and God lies beyond it.
[ELMALILI:1:2#8/r7] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · author | holds | Signs of God’s unity may be immediate or detailed, sensory or imagined, and can be read through perception, memory, and reason; all require conscious attention.
[ELMALILI:1:2#8/r8] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · author | holds | We know things through conscious attention and the representations it produces, yet we also judge external entities to possess objective reality beyond those representations.
[ELMALILI:1:2#8/r9] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · author | holds | Judging the self, consciousness, and external objects as truly corresponding already presupposes an encompassing necessary truth that guarantees their relations; this tacit attribution to God grounds our judgments.
[ELMALILI:1:2#9/r1] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · author | holds | The certainty I exist requires consciousness, and the truth of that self-awareness is guaranteed by the necessary testimony of the sovereign God, the beginning and end of every certainty.
[ELMALILI:1:2#9/r2] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · bazıları; bazıları | reports | Some call the Creator’s existence self-evident in a clear way, others self-evident but hidden, and others demonstrative; its appearance depends on each person’s strength of self-awareness.
[ELMALILI:1:2#9/r3] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · author | holds | The world is a sign of God, while God is its witness and light; the cited verses describe Him as the light of heaven and earth, witness over all, and first and last. | mentions 24:35, 41:53, 57:3
[ELMALILI:1:2#9/r4] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · author | holds | Faith is assent to this light, and Islam is living out that assent and relation to God.

[ELMALILI:1:2/r12] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · author | holds | It then grants people speech to pledge exclusive worship and dependence, binding human will and the right to ask for guidance into an enduring covenant between God and humanity. | mentions 1:5
[ELMALILI:1:2/r13] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · author | holds | The hidden humanity of the basmala becomes a speaking subject in al-Fatiha, while God is present as interlocutor; the surah captures the full relation of life and existence.
[ELMALILI:1:2/r14] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · author | holds | A sacred hadith says al-Fatiha is divided equally between God and servant, with the servant entitled to what is asked; its opening praises and glorifies God, its middle is shared, and its ending is the servant's supplication.
[ELMALILI:1:2/r2] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · author | holds | The Quran has an exhaustive, subtle order among surahs, stories, verses, words, and letters; analyzing it involves innumerable sciences, beginning with grammar and rhetoric.
[ELMALILI:1:2/r3] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · author | holds | Quranic rhetoric includes composition, context, implication, modes of expression, logic, wisdom, and the verbal and semantic beauties that secure fluency, force, balance, and inimitability.
[ELMALILI:1:2/r4] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · author | holds | These relations combine linguistic convention, rational logic, and natural taste; translation loses much of the first and third and consequently affects logical signification too.
[ELMALILI:1:2/r5] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · author | holds | Because human power cannot detail every relation, he will sketch them in places and pause especially over al-Fatiha.

[ELMALILI:1:2/r7] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · author | holds | Nothing lies outside the basmala's attraction, so it relates generally to al-Fatiha as one recites, writes, praises, or begins the Quran in its name.

[QUTB-ZILAL:1:2/r13] QUTB-ZILAL, d. 1386 · author | holds | Comparing Islam's simple, coherent account of God with the inherited tangle of beliefs reveals this creed as mercy for heart and mind.
[QUTB-ZILAL:1:2/r2] QUTB-ZILAL, d. 1386 · author | holds | Praising God wells up in a believer's heart at His mention: existence itself and ceaseless blessings call forth praise.
[QUTB-ZILAL:1:2/r3] QUTB-ZILAL, d. 1386 · author | holds | Praise begins and ends the Islamic worldview; the Qur'an says God alone is deity and that praise belongs to Him in this world

[IBNASHUR:1:2/r1] IBNASHUR, d. 1393 · author | holds | Important unfamiliar teaching should be preceded by preparation that removes resistance and mental obstacles, so hearers can benefit from guidance.

[IBNASHUR:1:2/r12] IBNASHUR, d. 1393 · author | holds | A good opening hints at its subject, preparing receptive hearers and allowing advanced hearers to assess or complete the argument; this displays the speaker's command of it.
[IBNASHUR:1:2/r13] IBNASHUR, d. 1393 · author | holds | A preface should use concise, comprehensive expression, a principle discussed by rhetoricians for places requiring careful composition.
[IBNASHUR:1:2/r14] IBNASHUR, d. 1393 · author | holds | A fourth rule for a preface is to begin with praise of God.
[IBNASHUR:1:2/r15] IBNASHUR, d. 1393 · author | holds | The surah's preparation rejects atheism and materialism, polytheism, stubbornness, and errors corrupting sound knowledge or true law; this is why it is called the Mother of the Quran. | mentions 1:4, 1:5, 1:6, 1:7
[IBNASHUR:1:2/r16] IBNASHUR, d. 1393 · author | holds | Arabic dignitary address begins with praise before a request; Umayya ibn Abi al-Salt says that praise of the addressee can itself satisfy the petitioner.

[IBNASHUR:1:2/r27] IBNASHUR, d. 1393 · السيد الشريف | reports | Al-Sayyid al-Sharif, apparently also Sa'd al-Din, reads the synonyms as retaining the voluntary-quality restriction, citing al-Zamakhshari on 49:7. | mentions 49:7

[IBNASHUR:1:2/r29] IBNASHUR, d. 1393 · author | reports | To allow praise of God's essential attributes under the majority's definition, scholars offer three replies: the attributes count as voluntary by their perfection, by their effects, or because God acts freely even when the praised attribute is not voluntary.

[IBNASHUR:1:2/r31] IBNASHUR, d. 1393 · author | holds | Hamd is the strongest language available to people for praising God, though it cannot fully convey realities beyond ordinary human experience.
[IBNASHUR:1:2/r32] IBNASHUR, d. 1393 · author | holds | Al-hamdu is nominative as the subject in every transmitted reading, and li-llah is its predicate, related to the general existential predicate.
[IBNASHUR:1:2/r33] IBNASHUR, d. 1393 · سيبويه | reports | Sibawayhi explains that praise expressions originally use an omitted verb in the absolute accusative, as in 'we praise God with praise'; the verbal noun replaces the verb.
[IBNASHUR:1:2/r34] IBNASHUR, d. 1393 · author | holds | Sibawayhi distinguishes supplicatory accusative sources from declarative ones such as hamdan and shukran, whose omitted verbs mean 'I praise' or 'I thank'.
[IBNASHUR:1:2/r35] IBNASHUR, d. 1393 · author | holds | The cited grammar says a definite source such as al-hamdu can be raised as a subject because it is declarative and definite; the sense of the omitted verb remains.
[IBNASHUR:1:2/r36] IBNASHUR, d. 1393 · صاحب الكشاف | reports | Al-Zamakhshari also describes hamd's original accusative with an omitted verb and its shift to nominative as a means of indicating stability.
[IBNASHUR:1:2/r37] IBNASHUR, d. 1393 · author | holds | The nominative makes a nominal sentence for permanence, the generic article broadens it, and fronting highlights it; the accusative construction cannot convey all three effects.
[IBNASHUR:1:2/r38] IBNASHUR, d. 1393 · سيبويه | reports | A reading with al-hamda in the accusative and definite article is a Tamimi dialect form attested by Sibawayhi; its implied verb limits praise to the speaker or intended group.
[IBNASHUR:1:2/r39] IBNASHUR, d. 1393 · author | holds | Raising hamd announces praise from the speaker and all creation, whereas the accusative announces only the speaker's praise.
[IBNASHUR:1:2/r40] IBNASHUR, d. 1393 · author | holds | Although anomalous, the accusative reading documents an Arabic stage in this familiar construction, showing that some speakers retained its absolute-object origin even with the article.
[IBNASHUR:1:2/r41] IBNASHUR, d. 1393 · author | holds | The nominative is more eloquent than the accusative, and definite accusative is more expressive than indefinite accusative; raising marks permanence and stability.
[IBNASHUR:1:2/r42] IBNASHUR, d. 1393 · صاحب الكشاف | reports | Al-Zamakhshari compares the nominative 'peace' in 51:25 with the earlier accusative greeting: Abraham answers with a more enduring, better greeting. | mentions 51:25
[IBNASHUR:1:2/r43] IBNASHUR, d. 1393 · author | holds | Praise is foregrounded because revelation of the Quran is the immediate great blessing being acknowledged; its contextual importance can take precedence over God's name's intrinsic importance.
[IBNASHUR:1:2/r44] IBNASHUR, d. 1393 · author | holds | The subject is deliberately fronted because another familiar formula could place the predicate first; the choice itself signals emphasis. | mentions 45:36
[IBNASHUR:1:2/r45] IBNASHUR, d. 1393 · author | holds | The article in al-hamd marks a known genus: its referent is recognizable to speaker and hearer, making the expression emphatic rather than singling out one instance.
[IBNASHUR:1:2/r46] IBNASHUR, d. 1393 · صاحب الكشاف | reports | Al-Zamakhshari rejects treating the article as grammatically exhaustive; Ibn Ashur agrees that it marks genus, while the construction's combined effect entails all praise.
[IBNASHUR:1:2/r47] IBNASHUR, d. 1393 · author | holds | The genus article with the possessive l

am implies all praise belongs to God: if any instance belonged to another, exclusive possession of the genus would fail; this is hyperbolic restriction.
[IBNASHUR:1:2/r48] IBNASHUR, d. 1393 · author | holds | The lam in li-llah may mean figurative exclusive possession or strengthen the verbal noun's relation as a weak, derived construction; exclusivity is also conveyed by the two definite parts.
[IBNASHUR:1:2/r49] IBNASHUR, d. 1393 · author | reports | One group treats the sentence as a plain report that praise belongs to God, objecting that this leaves the speaker not actually praising Him.
[IBNASHUR:1:2/r50] IBNASHUR, d. 1393 · author | reports | Defenders of a purely declarative analysis answer that reporting praise recognizes God's beautiful attributes, that the speaker is included in the general report, or that inherited practice entails following it.
[IBNASHUR:1:2/r51] IBNASHUR, d. 1393 · author | reports | A response says literal report may serve its implied praise, as saying 'long sword-strap' to imply tall stature.
[IBNASHUR:1:2/r52] IBNASHUR, d. 1393 · author | reports | Another group says the wording remains a report but its intended purpose is performative praise, like declarative wording for grief in 3:36; report form permits permanence, universality, exclusivity, and emphasis. | mentions 3:36
[IBNASHUR:1:2/r53] IBNASHUR, d. 1393 · فريق ثان | reports | A contrasting position calls the sentence a pure performative, shifted from reporting into praise like contracts and verbs of praise or blame.
[IBNASHUR:1:2/r54] IBNASHUR, d. 1393 · author | prefers | Ibn Ashur's preferred account is a report used to perform praise: the intention is performative, while report form supplies duration, universality, exclusivity, and emphasis unavailable to direct performative wording.
[IBNASHUR:1:2/r55] IBNASHUR, d. 1393 · author | holds | Dhu al-Rumma's phrase 'we brought into being thanks for its Creator' confirms that Arabs described praise or thanks as something they create, treating it as performative expression.
[IBNASHUR:1:2/r56] IBNASHUR, d. 1393 · author | holds | Allah is the proper name of the necessarily existent essence, worthy of every praise.
[IBNASHUR:1:2/r57] IBNASHUR, d. 1393 · author | prefers | The name derives from al-ilah, definite form of ilah, a generic word for deity; ilah is linked to worship or states entailing humble reverence and follows a passive fa'al pattern like kitab.
[IBNASHUR:1:2/r58] IBNASHUR, d. 1393 · author | holds | Ibn Ashur thinks the name was established before Arab idolatry and originally signified the unique deity; it became a proper name through exclusive reference, not common usage.
[IBNASHUR:1:2/r59] IBNASHUR, d. 1393 · author | holds | Arabs do not appear to have used definite singular al-ilah for an idol: they used a possessive construction, another title, or the plural alihah.
[IBNASHUR:1:2/r60] IBNASHUR, d. 1393 · author | holds | The name's origin recalls God specifically as deity and signals that He alone deserves worship because He created all.
[IBNASHUR:1:2/r61] IBNASHUR, d. 1393 · author | holds | Frequent use led speakers to drop the hamza from al-ilah, as in al-nas from al-unas; Ba'ith ibn Hurayth preserves al-ilah and Ubayd ibn al-Abras preserves al-unas with hamza.
[IBNASHUR:1:2/r62] IBNASHUR, d. 1393 · author | holds | Proper-name formation can alter a word: Ibn Jinni's example Shums ibn Malik changes the usual vowel, and Zamakhshari cites fixed-case Abdullah; Allah's naming has no parallel among personal names.
[IBNASHUR:1:2/r63] IBNASHUR, d. 1393 · author | holds | Calling Allah with ya while retaining the definite article shows that speakers treat the article as part of the name, unlike ordinary nouns entered by al.
[IBNASHUR:1:2/r64] IBNASHUR, d. 1393 · صاحب الكشاف | reports | Al-Zamakhshari uses al-Ba'ith's 'ma'adh al-ilah' as evidence that Allah originated from al-ilah; Ibn Ashur says this is persuasive because ma'adh conventionally takes Allah as its complement.
[IBNASHUR:1:2/r65] IBNASHUR, d. 1393 · الجوهري عن سيبويه | reports | Another proposed derivation takes Allah from laah, a verbal noun meaning to be hidden; the article was added to suggest the original sense, as in fadl and majd used as names.
[IBNASHUR:1:2/r66] IBNASHUR, d. 1393 · author | reports | A second proposal derives the name from wilah, 'overwhelmed and bewildered'; initial waw became hamza after kasra, then the article was added and hamza dropped.
[IBNASHUR:1:2/r67] IBNASHUR, d. 1393 · author | reports | A further etymology borrows Syriac laaha as a divine name, Arabized by removing its final alif and adding the article.
[IBNASHUR:1:2/r68] IBNASHUR, d. 1393 · الزجاج ونسب إلى الخليل وسيبويه | reports | Another group says the name was coined directly for God without derivation from alaha; one rationale is that Arabs named everything and would not leave God unnamed.
[IBNASHUR:1:2/r69] IBNASHUR, d. 1393 · صاحب الكشاف | reports | Al-Zamakhshari says Arabs pronounce Allah's lam emphatically except where the preceding sound requires kasra, treating inherited consensus as evidence against speculative explanations.
[IBNASHUR:1:2/r70] IBNASHUR, d. 1393 · جمع من العلماء | reports | A group of scholars, cited by al-Tilimsani, says discussion of Allah's name should be avoided out of reverence and because it requires scriptural permission.
[IBNASHUR:1:2/r71] IBNASHUR, d. 1393 · author | holds | Rabb is an attribute of Allah: after praise is attached to His essence to show inherent entitlement, the attribute adds entitlement through His qualities; this is clearer than saying 'praise belongs to Lord of the worlds.' | mentions 83:6
[IBNASHUR:1:2/r72] IBNASHUR, d. 1393 · author | holds | The four descriptions—Lord of the worlds, Merciful, Compassionate, King of Judgment Day—show each divine name's meaning merits praise and distinguishes God from alleged deities. | mentions 1:3, 1:4
[IBNASHUR:1:2/r73] IBNASHUR, d. 1393 · author | holds | Rabb may be a verbal noun or adjective on fa'l from rabba-yarubbu, 'to nurture and govern,' or from 'to own'; a verbal noun is intensive.
[IBNASHUR:1:2/r74] IBNASHUR, d. 1393 · author | holds | Tarbiya means gradually bringing something to completion; the adjective pattern fa'l from fa'ala yaf'ulu is rare, as in namma-yunimmu, nammun.
[IBNASHUR:1:2/r75] IBNASHUR, d. 1393 · author | prefers | Ibn Ashur prefers 'nurturer and governor' over 'owner' because it fits God's management of creation toward perfection and avoids redundancy with 'King of Judgment Day'; the latter can specify the afterlife. | mentions 1:4
[IBNASHUR:1:2/r76] IBNASHUR, d. 1393 · صاحب الكشاف | reports | Al-Zamakhshari limits rabb to 'master and owner,' its frequent Arabic sense, while allowing verbal-noun or adjective analysis; Ibn Ashur says context can select a less frequent established sense.
[IBNASHUR:1:2/r77] IBNASHUR, d. 1393 · الحارث بن حلزة | reports | Al-Harith ibn Hilliza calls Amr ibn Hind al-rabb in a poem, evidence that Arabs applied the title to a human ruler.
[IBNASHUR:1:2/r78] IBNASHUR, d. 1393 · النابغة | reports | Al-Nabigha calls al-Nu'man ibn al-Harith rabb and uses rabb again of al-Nu'man when describing God's favor to him.
[IBNASHUR:1:2/r79] IBNASHUR, d. 1393 · غاوي بن ظالم أو عباس بن مرداس | reports | A pre-Islamic poet applies rabb to an idol, ridiculing a deity with a fox urinating on its head; al-Uzza was also called al-Rabba and the plural is ارباب.
[IBNASHUR:1:2/r8] IBNASHUR, d. 1393 · author | holds | The many requirements for successful guidance and reception gather around these six foundations of spiritual preparation.
[IBNASHUR:1:2/r80] IBNASHUR, d. 1393 · صاحب الكشاف ومن تابعه | rejects | Al-Zamakhshari and followers claim rabb was used for others only with a qualifier; Ibn Ashur rejects this on unqualified poetic usage and the plural أرباب.
[IBNASHUR:1:2/r81] IBNASHUR, d. 1393 · author | holds | The Quran uses rabb for the Egyptian official in 12:23 and for multiple false gods in 12:39, confirming that Arabic applies the term to beings other than God. | mentions 12:23, 12:39
[IBNASHUR:1:2/r82] IBNASHUR, d. 1393 · author | holds | A hadith discourages calling a human master 'my rabb' as etiquette to prevent implication of worship; 'master' is preferred, compounds for a house or animal are allowed, and unrestricted use for a king is more disliked.
[IBNASHUR:1:2/r83] IBNASHUR, d. 1393 · author | holds | Al-alamin is the plural of alam; few nouns on fa'il take this plural, with yasm (jasmine) the other example, whose plurals occur in al-A'sha's verse.
[IBNASHUR:1:2/r84] IBNASHUR, d. 1393 · author | holds | An alam is a genus among existing things; the word may derive from knowledge or sign because each genus is distinguishable and serves as a sign by which it is known.
[IBNASHUR:1:2/r85] IBNASHUR, d. 1393 · author | holds | The fa'il pattern usually marks an instrument; worlds are thus imaginatively instruments for knowing the Maker or truths, a subtle coinage by the Arabs.
[IBNASHUR:1:2/r86] IBNASHUR, d. 1393 · author | holds | The plural uses the rational masculine form even though some worlds are nonrational, by giving precedence to rational beings.
[IBNASHUR:1:2/r87] IBNASHUR, d. 1393 · التفتزاني | reports | Al-Taftazani says alam names knowledgeable beings or each genus through which the Creator is known; singular alam normally needs a qualifying genitive, while 'the entire cosmos' is later theological terminology.
[IBNASHUR:1:2/r88] IBNASHUR, d. 1393 · author | holds | In this rhetorical context the definite article is exhaustive: there is no external or mental antecedent and no suitable literal or generic reading, so all genera are included.
[IBNASHUR:1:2/r89] IBNASHUR, d. 1393 · author | holds | Exhausting all genera entails their individuals, since lordship over abstract essences makes no sense; the plural with the definite article explicitly signals comprehensive scope.
[IBNASHUR:1:2/r9] IBNASHUR, d. 1393 · author | holds | The prayer teaches believers to val

ue blessings properly by thanking their giver, praising the giver of reason and success.
[IBNASHUR:1:2/r90] IBNASHUR, d. 1393 · author | rejects | The plural prevents an antecedent or generic reading and explicitly indicates exhaustive scope; Ibn Ashur rejects the Sakaki school's claim that singular is more comprehensive, referring to 2:31 for discussion. | mentions 2:31
[IBNASHUR-FULL:v15p244/r3] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · author | holds | The surah begins with praise so the second half of the Qur'an opens with الحمد لله, echoing the opening of the first half in al-Fātiḥa and the approximate start of the fourth quarter in Q 35:1.
[IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p132#2/r1] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · author | holds | He reads the sura's annexation to Fatihat al-Kitab as descriptive: it means a sura characterized as the Book's opening, with no separate title needed.
[IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p132#2/r11] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · author | holds | The sura's three aims together represent the Qur'an's original purposes, while its remaining material elaborates them.
[IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p132#2/r12] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · author | holds | He also supports the sura's comprehensiveness by citing the sound report that al-Ikhlas counts as a third of the Qur'an because all its wording praises God. | mentions 112:1
[IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p132#2/r2] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · author | holds | By contrast, Fatihat al-Kitab is a true annexation: al-Kitab here means the remainder of the Book apart from the sura called the Opening.
[IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p132#2/r3] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · author | holds | The names Umm al-Qur'an and Umm al-Kitab are established in the Sunna; “mother” denotes a thing's origin and source.
[IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p132#2/r4] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · أبو سعيد الخدري | reports | A report in Sahih al-Bukhari says Abu Sa'id al-Khudri recited Umm al-Qur'an over a person suffering from a sting as a healing prayer.
[IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p132#2/r5] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · النبيء صلى الله عليه وسلم | reports | A sound hadith calls a prayer without Umm al-Qur'an deficient.
[IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p132#2/r6] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · author | reports | One explanation of Umm al-Qur'an is that it begins and opens the Qur'an, making it like its origin.
[IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p132#2/r7] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · author | holds | A second explanation is that the sura gathers the Qur'an's three main aims: praise, commands and prohibitions, and promise and warning.
[IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p132#2/r8] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · author | holds | The opening praise gathers God's praised attributes, declares His uniqueness in divinity, and affirms resurrection and recompense.
[IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p133/r1] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · author | holds | A third explanation of Umm al-Qur'an is that it contains the Qur'an's theoretical wisdom and practical rulings, including theology, prophecy, admonition, worship, transactions, morals, and law.
[IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p133/r11] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · author | holds | Taken explicitly and by implication, the sura gives a general outline of the Qur'an's aims and prompts readers to seek their fuller detail as able.
[IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p133/r12] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · author | holds | Requiring al-Fatiha in every rak'ah preserves recollection of the Qur'an's purposes contained within it.
[IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p133/r2] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · author | holds | Al-hamdu lillah implies all attributes of perfection that entitle God to exclusive praise.
[IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p133/r3] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · author | holds | Rabb al-alamin encompasses God's acts and creative attributes for those who affirm such attributes.
[IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p134/r1] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · النبيء صلى الله عليه وسلم | reports | A report in Sahih al-Bukhari from Abu Sa'id ibn al-Mu'alla says the Prophet identified al-Hamdu lillah as the seven oft-repeated verses and the great Qur'an given to him.
[IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p134/r10] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · author | reports | On this reading, mathani in al-Fatiha resembles the repeated narratives and themes in the Qur'an called mathani in al-Zumar. | mentions 39:23
[IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p134/r11] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · author | rejects | The claim that al-Fatiha was named for being revealed once in Mecca and again in Medina is very remote: repetition of revelation is not accepted, and the sura is agreed to be Meccan.
[IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p134/r2] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · author | holds | The sura has seven verses by agreement among reciters and commentators, with a few dissenting counts.
[IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p134/r3] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · الحسن البصري | reports | Hasan al-Basri counts the sura as eight verses.
[IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p134/r4] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · الحسين الجعفي | reports | Al-Husayn al-Ju'fi counts it as six verses; an unspecified view counts nine, which requires excluding the basmala, while counting it in seven merges two verses.
[IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p134/r5] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · author | holds | Mathani is a plural of muthanna, with alternative vocalized or lightened forms; al-Jurjani notes that each can also be feminine.
[IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p134/r6] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · author | reports | Al-Kashshaf explains the name as referring to verses repeated in each rak'ah; this is also said to be transmitted from Umar.
[IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p134/r7] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · author | prefers | Ibn Ashur accepts the explanation tied to each rak'ah because al-Fatiha is joined to another sura in every rak'ah.
[IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p134/r8] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · author | reports | Another account connects the name to the early form of prayer: prayers were first prescribed as two rak'ahs, travel prayer remained so, and residence prayer was lengthened; an opposite account is also mentioned.
[IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p134/r9] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · author | reports | A further view takes mathani to mean repeated in prayer, citing Arabic use of the dual for repeated action.
[IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p135/r10] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · النبيء صلى الله عليه وسلم | reports | A hadith in both Sahihs from Abu Hurayra has God divide prayer between Himself and the servant, answering each portion of al-Fatiha and granting the servant's request. | mentions 1:2, 1:3, 1:4, 1:5, 1:6, 1:7
[IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p135/r11] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · author | reports | The verse division differs by region: Medinans exclude the basmala and count “those You favored” as a verse; Meccans and Kufans include the basmala and combine that phrase with its verse; Hasan counts both separately.
[IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p140/r1] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · author | holds | Ibn Ashur says sound Sunna contains no evidence that the basmala is a verse at the beginnings of Qur'anic suras, and presents six proofs.
[IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p140/r2] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · أبو هريرة | reports | The first proof is Malik's report from Abu Hurayra: God's division of prayer begins with al-Hamdu lillah, without mentioning the basmala; prayer here means recitation in prayer.
[IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p140/r3] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · أبي بن كعب | reports | In the second proof, Ubayy ibn Ka'b recites the celebrated sura from al-Hamdu lillah to its end when asked how he opens prayer, without reciting the basmala.
[IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p140/r4] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · أنس بن مالك | reports | Anas reports in Muslim and other collections that the Prophet, Abu Bakr, and Umar began recitation with al-Hamdu lillah and did not mention the basmala at either end.
[IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p140/r5] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · عائشة | reports | Aisha reports that the Prophet opened prayer with the takbir and began recitation with al-Hamdu lillah.
[IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p140/r6] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · عبد الله بن مغفل | reports | Ibn Mughaffal says he prayed with the Prophet and the first three caliphs but never heard them say the basmala, and directs worshippers to recite al-Hamdu lillah.
[IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p140/r7] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · author | holds | The decisive sixth proof is Medina's continuous practice: across generations, its mosque did not recite the basmala aloud in congregational prayers, making the practice mutawatir evidence that it is not part of the sura.
[IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p150/r5] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · البيضاوي | reports | Al-Baydawi explains pairing God's proper name with al-Rahman and al-Rahim as invoking His entitlement to assistance and mercy: al-Rahman signals the gifts involved in righteous action, with al-Rahim explained later.
[IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p152/r1] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · author | holds | Important guidance requires preparing listeners, stirring their attention, and removing stubbornness, false assumptions, and satanic impulses that block learning.
[IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p152/r10] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · author | holds | As a Qur'anic preface, al-Fatiha models an Arabic literary opening that improves understanding and attentive reception.
[IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p152/r9] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · author | holds | The sura also teaches gratitude by crowning supplication with praise of the giver of intellect and guidance; opening important speech with praise is therefore Qur'anic practice.
[IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p153/r1] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · author | holds | Al-Fatiha models four rules for introductions: keep them brief, foreshadow the subject, use concise comprehensive wording, and begin with praise of God.
[IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p153/r10] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · author | holds | These aims help explain why al-Fatiha is called Umm al-Qur'an.
[IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p153/r2] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · author | holds | A short introduction avoids tiring listeners while they await the main subject; the sura's brevity also explains placing it before longer chapters.
[IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p153/r3] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · author | holds | A prologue should display rhetorical aptness by signaling the purpose, preparing listeners either to receive its details or to assess and complete them, and showing the speaker's command of the subject.
[IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p153/r4] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · author | holds | A p

rologue should also be made of concise, comprehensive expressions and should open by praising God.
[IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p153/r5] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · author | holds | Because the Qur'an guides people and reforms both worldly and future life, listeners must prepare by removing stubbornness, error, and low impulses before receiving its wisdom.
[IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p154/r1] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · author | holds | God placed praise before the supplication, following Arabic eloquence in which requests to great people begin with commendation.
[IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p154/r2] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · أمية ابن أبي الصلت | reports | Umayya ibn Abi al-Salt's praise of Abd Allah ibn Jud'an says the addressee's modesty and praise can make a request unnecessary.
[IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p154/r3] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · author | holds | Opening weighty speech with praise became Qur'anic practice; Muslims call an important speech without such an opening “cut off,” following a hadith from Abu Hurayra.
[IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p154/r4] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · author | reports | Ziyad ibn Abi Sufyan's Basra sermon was nicknamed al-Batra because it did not begin with praise.
[IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p154/r5] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · author | holds | Hamd is praise for a chosen beautiful quality, whether an action such as generosity or another quality such as courage; thana' is its broader genus.
[IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p154/r6] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · author | rejects | Ibn al-Qatta' and others wrongly infer from a hadith that thana' can praise or blame; the negative usage is verbal symmetry and hints that one should praise a Muslim or stay silent.
[IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p154/r7] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · author | holds | Natha' with an initial n is the term used for good or bad mention, especially bad mention.
[IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p155/r1] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · الجمهور | reports | The majority hold that madh is broader than hamd because it can concern voluntary or involuntary qualities.
[IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p155/r2] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · الزمخشري | reports | Al-Zamakhshari calls hamd and madh “siblings”; Ibn Ashur rejects the interpretation that he means only a remote derivational relationship and reads him as calling them synonymous.
[IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p155/r3] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · السيد الشريف | reports | Al-Sayyid al-Sharif takes al-Zamakhshari to mean that both words remain restricted to chosen beautiful qualities, supported by his discussion of praise for beauty and noble character at 49:7. | mentions 49:7
[IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p155/r4] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · author | holds | Ibn Ashur notes that reliable scholars of rhetoric restrict praise to core virtues such as eloquence, courage, justice, and chastity, even where people praise attractive appearance. | mentions 49:7
[IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p155/r5] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · عبد الحكيم السلكوتي | reports | Abd al-Hakim al-Salkuti takes the two terms as synonymous without a voluntary-quality restriction, but Ibn Ashur presents this as an assumption or report rather than a preference.
[IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p156#2/r1] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · سيبويه | reports | Sibawayh explains conventional verbal nouns such as “beware” or “thanks” as accusatives governed by verbs suppressed from use, and distinguishes supplicatory formulas from other expressions.
[IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p156#2/r2] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · سيبويه | reports | For hamdan or shukran, an understood verb such as “I praise” is omitted because the source itself stands in its place, as in the established supplicatory formulas.
[IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p156#2/r3] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · سيبويه | reports | Sibawayh says some such source expressions can be made nominative topics, as in al-hamdu lillah; the definite form favors this declarative use.
[IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p156#2/r4] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · سيبويه | reports | Not every source phrase permits the nominative pattern; Sibawayh says expressions such as al-saqyu laka or al-raʿyu laka are not licensed.
[IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p156#2/r5] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · author | holds | Ibn Ashur cites Sibawayh to explain the Arabic stages of this verbal noun construction and the rationale for the nominative al-hamdu lillah.
[IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p156/r1] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · author | reports | A difficulty for defining hamd by voluntary qualities is that it would exclude God's essential attributes such as knowledge and power; proponents offer several answers.
[IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p156/r2] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · الجمهور | reports | One answer treats God's sublime attributes as voluntary because their possessor is independent; another says their voluntary effects make them equivalent to voluntary qualities.
[IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p156/r3] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · الجمهور | reports | A third answer reads “voluntary” as describing the praised agent, not the particular attribute for which praise is given.
[IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p156/r4] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · author | prefers | Ibn Ashur says the voluntary condition only excludes traits that are not perfections in human beings; God's necessary eternal attributes are perfections, so no workaround is needed.
[IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p156/r5] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · author | holds | Language can express transcendent realities only through the closest available terms from familiar human meanings.
[IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p156/r6] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · author | holds | Al-hamdu is nominative in all transmitted readings; its predicate is lillah, while an underlying analysis treats hamd as an accusative verbal noun replacing an omitted verb meaning “we praise God.”
[IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p157/r1] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · author | holds | Raising hamd creates a nominal sentence for permanence, generic al for comprehensive praise, and fronting for emphasis; these effects are unavailable in the ordinary accusative construction.
[IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p157/r2] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · author | holds | Accusative hamd can take al in the Tamim reading, but an implicit “I praise” limits praise to the speaker and “we praise” to believers or monotheists; generic hamd instead includes every praise.
[IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p157/r3] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · سيبويه | reports | Sibawayh's distinction is that nominative hamd reports praise from the speaker and all creatures, while accusative hamd reports the speaker's praise alone.
[IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p157/r4] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · author | holds | Ibn Ashur says the nominative definite wording is most eloquent, conveys enduring and comprehensive praise, and cites al-Kashshaf's comparison with Abraham's greeting at 51:25. | mentions 51:25
[IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p158/r1] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · author | holds | Praise precedes God's name because this occasion is the beginning of Qur'anic revelation, the great blessing that brings success in both worlds and evokes the Revealer's beautiful attributes.
[IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p158/r2] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · author | holds | Situational importance can warrant foregrounding praise despite God's name being inherently more important; rhetoric follows the occasion and highlights what might otherwise go unnoticed.
[IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p158/r3] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · author | holds | Hamd can be fronted deliberately even though it is the grammatical subject, since Arabic eloquent usage offers both al-hamdu lillah and lillah al-hamd. | mentions 45:36
[IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p159/r1] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · author | holds | The al in al-hamd is generic: because the verbal noun stands in place of an action, the definite form presents the kind of praise as familiar and makes it prominent, rather than identifying one instance.
[IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p159/r2] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · author | rejects | Although the generic article is not itself exhaustive, its combination with the lām of divine specification implies that every instance of praise belongs to God; the restriction is rhetorical and emphatic.
[IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p160/r1] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · author | holds | The lām in lillah can indicate rhetorical specification or strengthen the relation of the verbal-noun subject to its predicate; specification remains conveyed by the definiteness of both parts.
[IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p160/r2] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · author | holds | To decide whether al-hamdu lillah is report or performance, Ibn Ashur first explains that Arabic can turn statements into speech acts, as with sale formulas and words of praise or hope.
[IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p160/r3] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · author | reports | One camp treats the sentence as a plain report: reporting that God has praise acknowledges His beautiful qualities, and some say the speaker is included among those praising Him.
[IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p160/r4] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · author | reports | Other report-only explanations say the speaker's own praise follows conventionally from the statement or that its literal content serves an intended implication, though this can make the speaker's praise secondary.
[IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p160/r5] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · author | holds | He explains the indirect reading as analogous to saying “long sword-belt” to convey tall stature: a literal expression can serve an intended implication.
[IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p161/r1] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · author | reports | A second view treats the line as an informative sentence deliberately used to perform praise, as a report can enact sorrow in “I bore her as a female” at 3:36. | mentions 3:36
[IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p161/r2] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · author | reports | A separate view says the sentence is a pure performative transferred from reporting, like formulas for contracts and praise; the original report sense remains possible with contextual support.
[IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p161/r3] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · author | prefers | Ibn Ashur's conclusion is that al-hamdu lillah reports praise while functioning as its performance; declarative form adds permanence, comprehensiveness, exclusivity, and emphasis.
[IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p161/r4] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · author | holds | He says these effects cannot be achieved throug

h a purely performative wording such as hamdan lillah or ahmadu Allah hamdan.
[IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p162/r1] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · ذي الرمة | reports | Dhu al-Rumma's line about a flame says that it produced gratitude to its Creator, showing Arabs could describe praise or thanks as something brought into being.
[IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p162/r2] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · author | holds | Allah is the proper name of the necessarily existent divine essence, the one deserving every praise.
[IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p162/r3] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · author | holds | Ibn Ashur derives Allah from al-ilah, a common noun for deity; its root may mean worship or states such as bewilderment, stillness, fear, or ardor, all associated with submission and reverence.
[IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p162/r4] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · author | holds | The form is faʿal with passive meaning, like kitab; Arabs applied it to their objects of worship and pluralized it as alihah, easing the second hamza into a long vowel.
[IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p162/r5] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · author | holds | He conjectures that the name was established before Arab idolatry as the unique true deity, becoming a proper name by exclusive reference rather than predominance; it then marked the Creator as uniquely deserving worship.
[IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p162/r6] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · author | holds | Ibn Ashur finds no evidence that Arabs used the definite singular al-ilah for an idol; they used a possessive phrase, often rabb, or a plural, and a conquest report speaks of idols in the Kaaba.
[IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p162/r7] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · author | holds | He says frequent use led Arabs to drop the hamza in al-ilah when referring to God, as in al-nas from al-unas, though they retained it in some speech.
[IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p163/r1] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · author | holds | The divine name became a unique proper form whose article is treated as part of the word, as the vocative يا الله shows; its formation has no parallel among ordinary names.
[IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p163/r2] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · author | prefers | Al-Kashshaf's derivation of Allah from al-ilah is well supported: the poet's fixed expression معاذ الإلاه shows speakers treated al-ilah as the name's source, with variation only in the form's letters.
[IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p165/r1] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · author | holds | A poet's use of لاه and fixed expressions such as لله أبوك support treating لاه as a shortened form of Allah.
[IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p165/r2] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · الجوهري عن سيبويه | reports | One proposed origin is لاه, a verbal noun meaning that God is hidden, with the definite article added to suggest the original sense.
[IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p165/r3] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · author | reports | Another proposal derives the name from ولاه, meaning one overcome by bewilderment; its initial wāw became hamza and the hamza was later dropped.
[IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p165/r4] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · author | reports | A further proposal takes the divine name from Syriac لاها, adapted by dropping its final alif and adding Arabic ال.
[IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p165/r5] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · الزجاج | reports | Al-Zajjaj, with the view also attributed to al-Khalil and Sibawayh, holds that Allah was coined directly as God's name rather than derived from أله.
[IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p165/r6] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · صاحب الكشاف | reports | Al-Kashshaf says all Arabs pronounce the divine lām emphatically, and their agreement shows the practice was inherited.
[IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p165/r7] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · author | holds | The verse puts الحمد before لله because praise for revelation and Islam frames the opening recitation; contextual importance can precede God's intrinsic priority, while praising Him still attends to His affairs.
[IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p166#2/r1] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · author | prefers | Ibn Ashur prefers deriving رب from nurturing and directing: it suits God's governance and gradual completion of creatures, and avoids redundancy with ملك يوم الدين; one could answer that the worlds here mean only this world. | mentions 1:4
[IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p166#2/r2] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · صاحب الكشاف | reports | Al-Kashshaf limits رب here to master or king, allowing either a verbal noun or adjective, because the word most commonly carries those meanings.
[IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p166#2/r3] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · author | rejects | The claim that Arabs reserved رب for God is false: they used it for human rulers and masters, idols, and particular possessions; الربّة was a name for al-ʿUzza and أرباب is plural.
[IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p166/r1] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · التلمساني | reports | Al-Tilimsani reports a group of scholars who refrain from explaining the divine name out of reverence and because discussion requires scriptural permission; Ibn Ashur calls this an astonishing opinion.
[IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p166/r2] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · author | holds | رب العالمين apposes God's name: praise first recognizes His intrinsic worth, then this description adds His descriptive worthiness for praise. | mentions 83:6
[IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p166/r3] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · author | holds | The four descriptions that follow signal that each attribute also merits praise and distinguish God from the idols, objects, and elements other peoples worship.
[IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p166/r4] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · author | holds | رب may be a verbal noun or an adjective from upbringing, meaning one who nurtures and directs; tarbiya gradually brings something to its perfection. It may also derive from ownership, with an intensive or rare adjectival form.
[IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p167/r1] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · author | holds | Quranic expressions about Joseph's master and the rival lords show that رب can refer to someone besides God; the term remained available in Arabic usage. | mentions 12:23, 12:39
[IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p167/r2] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · author | holds | The hadith discouraging a person from calling a human master ربي is an etiquette rule to prevent suspected association; possessive phrases such as رب الدار remain permissible.
[IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p167/r3] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · author | holds | عالم names a class of beings, perhaps because each class marks itself out or enables knowledge of its maker; the form suggests an instrument, and its rational plural gives rational beings precedence over other classes.
[IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p167/r4] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · التفتزاني | reports | Al-Taftazani defines عالم as knowledgeable beings or any species by which the Creator is known, not a singular name for everything besides God; Ibn Ashur endorses this as accurate Arabic usage.
[IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p168/r1] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · author | holds | The article in العالمين is exhaustive because the context supplies neither an external nor mental referent; it therefore covers every relevant species and, by implication, its individuals.
[IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p168/r2] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · author | rejects | The plural العالمين makes exhaustive scope explicit and removes a possible generic or familiar reading; Ibn Ashur rejects the claim among al-Sakkaki's followers that an exhaustive singular is broader than an exhaustive plural. | mentions 2:31
[TABATABAI:10:10#2/r3] TABATABAI, d. 1402 · author | holds | Praise is description of God’s beautiful acts; only God’s sincere servants, whom He draws near without intermediary, can properly describe Him, as 37:159 says. | mentions 1:2, 37:159
[TABATABAI:1:1-5#3/r1] TABATABAI, d. 1402 · author | holds | God directly relates praise from selected prophets, Muhammad, and the purified inhabitants of Paradise; other creatures' praise is paired with glorification because they cannot encompass divine perfection. | mentions 23:28, 14:39, 17:111, 27:15, 10:10
[TABATABAI:1:1-5#3/r2] TABATABAI, d. 1402 · author | holds | Creatures cannot comprehend God's perfection; their praise would limit Him to their understanding, so they must first declare Him transcendent of what they delimit. | mentions 42:5, 17:44, 20:110, 16:74
[TABATABAI:1:1-5#3/r3] TABATABAI, d. 1402 · author | holds | God makes the praise and description of His sincerely purified servants His own.
[TABATABAI:1:1-5#4/r1] TABATABAI, d. 1402 · النبي | reports | A report transmitted by both communities from the Prophet says no one can enumerate praise of God as fully as He praises Himself.
[TABATABAI:1:1-5#4/r2] TABATABAI, d. 1402 · author | holds | The opening الحمد لله is taught etiquette: a servant could not rightly utter this praise without God first teaching it and speaking on the servant's behalf.
[TABATABAI:1:1-5#4/r3] TABATABAI, d. 1402 · author | holds | Rabb means an owner who manages what is owned; human ownership is a conventional social relation, unlike real ownership grounded in dependence of existence.
[TABATABAI:1:1-5#4/r4] TABATABAI, d. 1402 · author | holds | God alone has real ownership, which necessarily entails governance because whatever depends on Him for existence also depends on Him in its effects.
[TABATABAI:1:1-5#4/r5] TABATABAI, d. 1402 · author | prefers | Alamin can mean all beings, kinds, or communities; because judgment concerns humans and jinn, the context most suitably means their communities. | mentions 3:42, 25:1, 7:80
[TABATABAI:1:1-5#6/r7] TABATABAI, d. 1402 · الصادق | reports | When al-Sadiq's father recovered a lost mule, he praised God only by saying الحمد لله and explained that every kind of praise is contained in that phrase.
[TABATABAI:1:1-5#6/r8] TABATABAI, d. 1402 · علي | reports | Ali explains that God teaches servants general gratitude because His blessings cannot all be counted or known in detail; the author connects this to praise taught on the servant's behalf.
[TABATABAI:1:5#2/r2] TABATABAI, d. 1402 · author | holds | Hamd praises voluntary excellence, while madh is broader and can praise non-voluntary qualities; the definite article here yields the same result whether generic or comprehensive.
[TABATABAI:1:5#2/r3] TABATABAI, d. 1402 · author | holds | Everything is God's cr
