[TABATABAI:1:5#2/r4] TABATABAI, d. 1402 · author | holds | God creates and acts with knowledge and choice, not under compulsion; therefore every being is His voluntary beautiful act, and all genuine praise belongs to Him. | mentions 39:4, 20:111, 20:8, 7:180
[TABATABAI:1:5#2/r5] TABATABAI, d. 1402 · author | holds | Since God is beautiful in names and acts and all praised beauty comes from Him, every true act of praise is rightfully His. | mentions 20:8, 7:180
[TABATABAI:1:5#2/r6] TABATABAI, d. 1402 · author | holds | The shift to direct address at the worship verse shows that the sura is speech placed on the servant's tongue, teaching how to praise and behave in servitude. | mentions 1:5
[TABATABAI:1:5#3/r1] TABATABAI, d. 1402 · author | holds | Every effect and its perfections depend on their cause; since all causes end in God, all genuine beauty, praise, and thanks ultimately belong to Him.
[TABATABAI:1:6-7#11/r6] TABATABAI, d. 1402 · النبي | reports | The Prophet transmits God's division of al-Fatiha between Himself and the servant: each phrase receives divine acknowledgement and a tailored promise of blessing, mercy, ease of judgment, reward, help, and fulfillment of the servant's requests.
[TABATABAI:2:21-25#11/r2] TABATABAI, d. 1402 · بعض النصارى | reports | He also quotes a Christian's parody of al-Fatiha as another failed counter-imitation.
[ASAD-NOTES:1:2#n2/r1] ASAD-NOTES, d. 1412 · author | holds | “Worlds” covers every category of physical and spiritual existence.
[ASAD-NOTES:1:2#n2/r2] ASAD-NOTES, d. 1412 · author | holds | Rabb combines rightful possession and authority with rearing, sustaining, and fostering something from its beginning to completion.
[ASAD-NOTES:1:2#n2/r3] ASAD-NOTES, d. 1412 · author | holds | With the definite article, rabb is used in the Qur'an exclusively for God, sole sustainer of all creation and ultimate authority.
[ABUDAWUD:821/r2] ABUDAWUD · الله تعالى | reports | In a hadith qudsi transmitted by Abu Hurayra, God divides al-Fatiha between Himself and the servant: praise and glorification receive divine responses, worship is mutual, and the guidance petition belongs to the servant.
[CORPUSCORANICUM:1:2:kommentar/r1] CORPUSCORANICUM · author | holds | The hymn of praise begins the sura’s actual text and gives it the alternative name al-Ḥamd.
[CORPUSCORANICUM:1:2:kommentar/r10] CORPUSCORANICUM · author | holds | To preserve the eschatological dimension, translate rabb al-ʿālamīn as Lord of the worlds, with people implied; translate it simply as people where that reference is explicit.
[CORPUSCORANICUM:1:2:kommentar/r2] CORPUSCORANICUM · author | holds | The doxology was already used in the early Meccan period; in middle Meccan texts it is joined to the epithet rabb al-ʿālamīn, itself attested early. | mentions 52:48, 37:182, 39:75, 83:6, 81:27, 81:29, 69:43, 68:52, 56:80
[CORPUSCORANICUM:1:2:kommentar/r3] CORPUSCORANICUM · Paret | reports | Paret takes ʿālamīn primarily as people, translating the epithet as Lord of people throughout the world or Lord of the world’s inhabitants. | mentions 26:165, 29:6, 2:47, 2:122
[CORPUSCORANICUM:1:2:kommentar/r4] CORPUSCORANICUM · author | holds | Paret’s rendering may be factually right but omits the eschatological force; rabb an-nās would have expressed simply Lord of people. | mentions 114:1
[CORPUSCORANICUM:1:2:kommentar/r5] CORPUSCORANICUM · author | holds | Rabb al-ʿālamīn corresponds to Jewish liturgical ribbon ʿōlām, an eschatological title spanning this world and the next; a Syriac parallel itself lacks that connotation.
[CORPUSCORANICUM:1:2:kommentar/r6] CORPUSCORANICUM · author | holds | Syriac ʿâlam ʿâlmīn could nonetheless evoke the Greek liturgical formula eis tous aiōnas tōn aiōnōn, meaning eternally.
[CORPUSCORANICUM:1:2:kommentar/r7] CORPUSCORANICUM · author | holds | Although ʿālamīn’s sound plural cannot mean worlds morphologically, it can designate a collective of people.
[CORPUSCORANICUM:1:2:kommentar/r8] CORPUSCORANICUM · author | holds | The form may be a cross-language wordplay presenting the emerging community as citizens of both worlds, through a nisba formation from ʿālam and rabbinic Hebrew ʿōlām.
[CORPUSCORANICUM:1:2:kommentar/r9] CORPUSCORANICUM · author | holds | This theological lexicon recasts the negatively charged early Meccan human as homo eschatologicus, belonging to both worlds under God’s rule. | mentions 103:1
[KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:1:2/r1] KURANYOLU-TEFSIR · author | holds | Praise can be given for beauty or good whether voluntary or not, whereas hamd is for good and beauty arising from will and choice.
[KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:1:2/r2] KURANYOLU-TEFSIR · author | holds | Thanks is a verbal or practical response to intentional kindness and a moral duty toward benefactors, human or divine; hamd is spoken praise for all willful goodness, not only gifts.
[KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:1:2/r3] KURANYOLU-TEFSIR · author | holds | Hamd in its complete sense belongs only to God: human good is never fully independent of divine will, while unchosen gifts and qualities are directly the Creator’s work.
[KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:1:2/r4] KURANYOLU-TEFSIR · author | holds | All created things in the material and spiritual, visible and unseen worlds, in this life and the hereafter, are included in the worlds.
[KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:1:2/r5] KURANYOLU-TEFSIR · author | holds | The visible domain is called the realm of dominion and witness, while immaterial existence is the unseen and angelic realm; God alone owns the latter, though worldly ownership can appear to belong to others.
[KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:1:2/r6] KURANYOLU-TEFSIR · author | holds | Revelation compares the visible realm to a drop in the sea and a grain of sand beside the unseen; knowledge of cosmic scale points both to the limits of reason and the immensity of divine creation.
[KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:1:2/r7] KURANYOLU-TEFSIR · author | holds | Contemplating the unseen’s immensity through faith leads from awe at God’s greatness to prostration and then to peace, security, love, nearness, and contentment.
[KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:1:2/r8] KURANYOLU-TEFSIR · author | holds | Used alone, Rabb refers only to God and names His ownership and nurturing; in a construct such as master of a house, it can refer to others.
[SAMARRAI-LAMASAT:p11/r1] SAMARRAI-LAMASAT · author | holds | The author opens the book with al-Fatiha for blessing.
[SAMARRAI-LAMASAT:p11/r2] SAMARRAI-LAMASAT · author | holds | Hamd is praise of beauty, whether a quality or gift, with love and reverence.
[SAMARRAI-LAMASAT:p11/r3] SAMARRAI-LAMASAT · author | holds | Hamd covers praise of intrinsic qualities and beneficence, and is directed only to a living, rational being.
[SAMARRAI-LAMASAT:p11/r4] SAMARRAI-LAMASAT · الرازي | reports | Madḥ is broader than hamd because one may praise beautiful pearls or jewels, but cannot give them hamd.
[SAMARRAI-LAMASAT:p12/r1] SAMARRAI-LAMASAT · بعضهم | reports | One distinction says hamd follows a real benefaction or praiseworthy quality, while madḥ may precede any good deed or be undeserved.
[SAMARRAI-LAMASAT:p12/r2] SAMARRAI-LAMASAT · النبي | reports | The Prophet warns against excessive flatterers, supporting the distinction between deserved hamd and potentially misplaced madḥ.
[SAMARRAI-LAMASAT:p12/r3] SAMARRAI-LAMASAT · النبي | reports | The Prophet says that whoever does not praise people has not praised God, recognizing gratitude for people's real contributions.
